### v0.144 changelog (v0.143 → v0.144)

**`when` is now a keyword for scrutinee-less condition dispatch; `case` always takes a scrutinee (§19, Appendix A).** Through v0.143 a `case` could be written two ways: with a scrutinee (`case x ...`) or without one, in which case each arm was a full boolean condition. The two readings shared the keyword `case`, and the parser told them apart by *source layout* — whether the first arm started on a line after `case`, or whether an `or`/`and`/`=` appeared before the first `=>`. That made a `case`'s meaning depend on where line breaks fell, and it left a genuine ambiguity unresolved: §19.3 has always listed the leading-open range pattern `..<0` as legal, but in `case x ..<0 => …` the scrutinee parser could not tell `x ..<0` (a range scrutinee) from `x` followed by the pattern `..<0`, so the compiler rejected the very pattern the spec admitted. Issue #744.

The fix gives condition dispatch its own keyword. **`when`** (already a reserved word — it introduces a `case`/`catch` arm guard) is now also the scrutinee-less construct: `when Arm ("," Arm)* end`, each arm a boolean condition, first-true wins, valid in both expression and statement position. The construct use and the guard use never collide — the construct `when` heads an expression or statement, the guard `when` follows a pattern inside an arm. With condition dispatch peeled off, **`case` always carries a scrutinee**; a `case` with no scrutinee is now a syntax error. Because the scrutinee is unconditional, the parser parses it above the range precedence level, which makes the leading-open range pattern (`..<0`, `..5`) unambiguous and finally legal.

#### What changed
- §19 retitled "The `case` and `when` Constructs"; §19.1 documents the `case` (scrutinee) form and the `when` (condition-dispatch) form, the latter in both expression and statement position, and states that `case` always requires a scrutinee.
- §19.4 gains a sentence distinguishing the guard `when` from the construct `when` (position disambiguates). §19.6 notes a `when` is never statically exhaustive (no scrutinee to reason about) and needs a `_` arm in expression position. §4.1's `bool`-condition list now names `when`.
- Appendix A: `CaseExpr`'s scrutinee `Expression?` becomes mandatory `Expression`; a new `WhenExpr`/`WhenArm` pair is added and wired into `ConditionalExpr` and `PrimaryAtom` alongside `CaseExpr`. The `RangeExpr` note already documented `..<0` as a pattern; it now actually parses.
- Rationale §11.1 retitled and rewritten around `when`; this changelog.

#### Touched
Spec §4.1 (one clause), §19 (title, §19.1 forms, §19.4 guard note, §19.6 exhaustiveness note, two scrutinee-less `case` examples in §9.6/§10.5 migrated to `when`), Appendix A (CaseExpr mandatory scrutinee + new WhenExpr/WhenArm + two alternative-list wirings), Contents entry. Rationale §11.1 and §11.3 (one clause). No stdlib change. Compiler: the parser drops the layout heuristic (`case` unconditionally scrutinee'd), adds `when` in expression and statement position, raises the `case` scrutinee precedence cap above the range level, and removes the leading-open-range-pattern rejection — landed across #744 stages 1–5.

#### Migration
A scrutinee-less `case` (e.g. `case\n  x >= 90 => …\nend`) no longer parses; replace the keyword with `when`. A `case` with a scrutinee is unaffected. An unparenthesised bitwise (`& ^ |`) or range scrutinee — never shown in any example and not previously idiomatic — must now be parenthesised (`case (flags & MASK) …`). Leading-open range patterns that were previously rejected now compile. The conformance corpus and the project's own test/example sources were migrated with this revision.

**Erratum (same revision) — §19.2 `Classify` example (#748).** The `Classify` helper example used statement-if syntax (`return if score < 0 then "invalid" else "failing";`) in expression position. Bezel's if-*expression* is the postfix form `trueValue if condition else falseValue` (§20); `if … then … end` is the *statement* form (§21). The compiler correctly rejected the example; it now reads `return "invalid" if score < 0 else "failing";`. Documentation-only; isolated (a doc-wide scan found no other expression-position `if … then … else`).

### v0.145 changelog (v0.144 → v0.145)

v0.145 folds three decided amendments: a cast-semantics clarification paired with a new bit-reinterpretation intrinsic, a LINQ standard-library completion, and a grammar-appendix catch-up. All three are additive or clarifying; none changes the meaning of an existing conforming program except where one previously relied on undefined-by-the-spec behaviour.

#### Amendment 1 — same-width signed↔unsigned casts are checked; `BitConverter.Reinterpret<T>` added (spec §5.2, stdlib §2.12; #753)

Spec §5.2's "integer narrowing raises `OverflowException` if the value does not fit" left unresolved whether a *same-width* signed↔unsigned cast (`int(uintValue)`, `ulong(longValue)`) is a checked value conversion or a bit reinterpretation — and an existing codegen test had quietly committed to the latter. The ruling: such a cast is a **checked value conversion** — it raises `OverflowException` when the value is outside the destination type's range (a negative cast to unsigned, or an unsigned value above the destination's signed maximum). This is Reading A; it matches the rationale's standing position that `BitConverter` is the only general bit-reinterpretation surface and that narrowing casts are checked.

To keep a zero-cost bit reinterpretation available — the legitimate "view this `uint` as the `int` with the same bits" need — stdlib §2.12 gains a generic `BitConverter.Reinterpret<TTo>(value): TTo` (target type explicit, source inferred from the argument, same bit width required) that lowers to a register-level reinterpretation. The existing `FloatToInt32Bits`/`Int32BitsToFloat`/`DoubleToInt64Bits`/`Int64BitsToDouble` family are its float/double special cases. The net rule reads cleanly: **a cast converts a value (checked); `BitConverter.Reinterpret` reinterprets bits (always succeeds)** — no new syntax, intent greppable at the call site, consistent with the no-implicit-conversions discipline.

#### Amendment 2 — `Last`/`Single` predicate overloads (stdlib §5; #789)

Through v0.144 the LINQ element-access surface offered a predicate overload only on `First`/`FirstOrNull`; `Last`, `Single`, `LastOrNull`, and `SingleOrNull` had none, so a predicate argument on those was silently accepted and mis-evaluated. The asymmetry was an oversight. v0.145 adds the predicate overload to each — `Last(predicate)`, `Single(predicate)`, `LastOrNull(predicate)`, `SingleOrNull(predicate)` — each defined as the no-argument method applied after `Where(predicate)`, inheriting its missing-element and (for `Single`) more-than-one-match behaviour.

#### Amendment 3 — Appendix A accessor grammar catch-up (spec Appendix A; #691)

The grammar lagged prose the compiler already implements. `AccessorBody` gains the single-statement form `set => _x := value;` (an `AssignmentStmt`, per §13.6) — previously the appendix admitted only `=> Expression` (assignment is a statement, not an expression) or a `do … end` block. `IfaceProperty`/`IfaceIndexer` gain the accessor-block declaration form (`get; set(owned); end;`, per §23.3) alongside the `;`-terminated auto form. No compiler change — the appendix now matches the implemented prose.

#### Touched

Spec §5.2 (one paragraph), Appendix A (`AccessorBody`, `IfaceProperty`, `IfaceIndexer`). Stdlib §2.12 (`Reinterpret` signature + prose; revised the "no unsigned forms" sentence), §5 (four LINQ overloads + one prose paragraph). Rationale: this changelog. Version headers bumped to v0.145 across the language spec, standard library, and design rationale. Compiler (separate lanes, #753/#789): the §5.2 checked-cast guard and the `Reinterpret` intrinsic; the `Last`/`Single` predicate-overload typing and lowering; #691 is doc-only (a conformance test pins the already-accepted forms).

#### Migration

No existing conforming program changes meaning. Amendment 1 is observable only for code that *relied on* a same-width signed↔unsigned cast silently bit-reinterpreting an out-of-range value — that cast now raises `OverflowException`; rewrite it as `BitConverter.Reinterpret<T>(...)` to retain the reinterpreting behaviour. Amendments 2 and 3 are purely additive (new overloads; grammar forms the compiler already accepts).

#### Editorial note

Amendment 1's compiler change overturns one pre-existing codegen test (`long_min_value_literal_exact_bits`) that documented the bit-reinterpret reading; that test is rewritten to observe the literal's bits via `BitConverter.Reinterpret` rather than `ulong(longMin)`, per the CLAUDE.md rule that a test misrepresenting the (now-ruled) spec is fixed.

### v0.146 changelog (v0.145 → v0.146)

v0.146 is an errata revision. It corrects three code-example defects in which an example used syntax the spec itself does not admit; the surrounding prose and every normative rule are unchanged, and the compiler already rejected each of these three examples correctly. No conforming program changes meaning. The defects were surfaced by a triage of the conformance-example corpus and are tracked as #978.

#### Erratum 1 — §17.7 `new()` shorthand example used `:` for a named argument

The §17.7 field-initializer example read `private _config: Config := new(verbose: true);`, using a colon for the named argument. §22.5 defines named-argument syntax as `name := value` (e.g. `Log(level := "ERROR", message := "Failed")`); the colon form does not parse. Corrected to `new(verbose := true)`.

#### Erratum 2 — §27.3 lambda example bound a reserved keyword

The §27.3 expression-body lambda example read `var double := (x: int) => x * 2;`. `double` is in Appendix B's unconditionally-reserved keyword list (the primitive-type alias) and is not a contextual keyword, so it may not be used as a variable name. The variable is renamed to `twice`.

#### Erratum 3 — stdlib §2.14 serialization example used the removed `<owned T>` form

The stdlib serialization example declared `public owned Lines: OwnedArray<owned LineItem>;`. Per §14.4 the `owned` modifier on a generic type argument was removed in v0.97 in favour of the named `Owned…` collection types; the position now rejects the modifier. Corrected to `OwnedArray<LineItem>` — the `OwnedArray` type already carries the owning semantics, so the example's meaning is unchanged.

#### Touched

Spec §17.7 (one example line), §27.3 (one example line). Stdlib §2.14 (one example line). Rationale: this changelog. Version headers bumped to v0.146 across the language spec, standard library, and design rationale. No compiler change — the compiler already rejects all three forms correctly (each erratum is an example that contradicted a rule the compiler already enforces).

#### Migration

None. No normative rule changed; the corrected examples now compile as the surrounding prose always intended.

### v0.147 changelog (v0.146 → v0.147)

v0.147 resolves a standard-library specification ambiguity in stdlib §10.1 (`CString.FromBytes`). It pins a previously-contradictory contract to match both the method's own signature and the compiler's existing behaviour; no language rule changes. Tracked as #982.

#### The defect

Stdlib §10.1 described `CString.FromBytes(bytes: Array<byte>)` as one that "**wraps** an existing byte array; the bytes must already be null-terminated." Two problems: (1) "wraps" implies the result aliases the caller's array, but the parameter `bytes: Array<byte>` carries **no `owned` modifier**, so it is a borrow — and a method may not retain a borrowed value past the call. The signature therefore *requires* a copy, contradicting "wraps." (2) Requiring the caller to pre-null-terminate is gratuitous: `From(string)` appends the terminator itself, and an FFI `char*` cannot carry an interior null anyway.

#### The resolution (copy-in)

`FromBytes` **copies** the source bytes into a fresh, owned buffer and **appends** the null terminator; the source array is unaffected and the buffer is independent. This matches the sibling `RawBytes.From` (§10.3), which already specifies copy-in over the same borrow signature, and it keeps `CString` to a single internal representation (it always owns a freshly-allocated, null-terminated buffer, so its destructor is uniform). The zero-copy alternative was declined: Bezel already serves zero-copy byte access through the span / `OwnedBuffer` family (§4.13–4.16) and `RawBytes.Pointer`, so a "move/adopt" `FromBytes` would be a redundant second way to do it and would force `CString` to carry two internal representations; if such a path is ever wanted it belongs on a separate `owned OwnedBuffer<byte>`-adopting factory, not on `FromBytes`.

#### Touched

Stdlib §10.1 (the `FromBytes` prose paragraph). Rationale: this changelog. Version headers bumped to v0.147 across the language spec, standard library, and design rationale.

#### Migration

None. The compiler implementation already provides exactly the copy-in-and-append-terminator behaviour (the `bz_cstring_from_bytes` runtime helper added with the CString static-call resolution work, #977): it copies the array's bytes and writes a trailing null. The spec prose is corrected to describe what the implementation does; no conforming program changes meaning, and no compiler change is required by this revision.

### v0.148 changelog (v0.147 → v0.148)

v0.148 renames the four `Encoding` singletons from PascalCase (`Utf8`/`Utf16`/`Utf32`/`Ascii`) to all-caps (`UTF8`/`UTF16`/`UTF32`/`ASCII`) to match the spec prose and .NET convention. Tracked as #988.

#### The defect

Stdlib §3.2 defined the four `Encoding` static properties using PascalCase names (`Utf8`, `Utf16`, `Utf32`, `Ascii`). The language-spec prose, however, consistently uses all-caps forms (`Encoding.UTF8`, `Encoding.UTF16`, etc.) — following the established .NET/C# convention where encoding singletons are `Encoding.UTF8` not `Encoding.Utf8`. This mismatch meant every spec example using `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(s)` was syntactically rejected by the compiler with a "has no member" diagnostic (fix #984 made the diagnostic explicit; before that it silently miscompiled). Programmers consulting the spec would write code that the compiler refused.

#### The resolution

The four singleton names are renamed to `UTF8`/`UTF16`/`UTF32`/`ASCII` everywhere: the §3.2 property definitions, the compiler's accepted-name sets in sema (ExprTypecheck_Calls.cpp) and codegen (LlvmBackend_Calls.cpp, LlvmBackend_Exprs.cpp), the diagnostic message, and all tests. The PascalCase forms (`Utf8` etc.) are now unrecognised member names and produce the existing "has no member" diagnostic. The runtime C function names (`bz_encoding_utf8_*`) and the encoding `Name` strings (`"utf-8"`, `"utf-16le"`, `"utf-32le"`, `"us-ascii"`) are unchanged — they are not user-facing Bezel names.

The method/type names that merely contain "Ascii" as a substring — `IsAscii`, `AsAsciiByteSpan`, `TryAsAsciiByteSpan`, `ReadOnlyAsciiByteSpan` — are NOT renamed; they describe ASCII-the-property/type, not the `Encoding.ASCII` singleton, and their PascalCase is correct per Bezel naming conventions.

#### Touched

Stdlib §3.2 (four property declarations and prose). Compiler: sema/ExprTypecheck_Calls.cpp, codegen/LlvmBackend_Calls.cpp, codegen/LlvmBackend_Exprs.cpp. Tests: tests/codegen/encoding_test.cpp (all `Encoding.Utf8/Utf16/Utf32/Ascii` → uppercase; #984 acceptance/rejection tests flipped), tests/codegen/timespan_encoding_525_526_test.cpp. Version headers bumped to v0.148 across the language spec, standard library, and design rationale.

#### Migration

Replace `Encoding.Utf8` with `Encoding.UTF8`, `Encoding.Utf16` with `Encoding.UTF16`, `Encoding.Utf32` with `Encoding.UTF32`, and `Encoding.Ascii` with `Encoding.ASCII` in all Bezel source files. No other changes are needed; method names (`GetBytes`, `GetString`, `Name`) and runtime behavior are unchanged.

### v0.149 changelog (v0.148 → v0.149)

v0.149 is an ownership-soundness pass that closes three holes in the enforcement of the ownership model for method returns and owned temporaries. Two are enforcement of rules the spec already stated; the third adds one normative rule for unbound owned temporaries. Tracked as #1007, #1005, #1006.

#### The defects

Three gaps, all surfaced while clarifying that `OwnedArray<T>` and the other `Owned*` types denote *element* ownership while the `owned` qualifier denotes *container* ownership ([§5.11](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-owning-collections)):

1. **Double-free (#1007).** Returning a *borrowed* owning-collection value — `Identity(a: OwnedArray<T>): OwnedArray<T> => a`, where `a` is a non-`owned` (borrowed) parameter — was tracked at the call site as an *owned* result. The caller then disposed it while the borrow's actual owner also disposed it: a double-free. The cause was an implementation shortcut that classified any owning-type return as owned by its type *name*, conflating the element ownership the name denotes with container ownership.

2. **Owned-field leak (#1005).** §28.6's rule — "an owned field's value may not be returned from a method unless the return type is declared `owned`" — was not enforced. `Take(): T? => move v` (the `move` form) compiled and leaked the moved value.

3. **Unbound-temporary leak (#1006b).** An `owned`-typed value produced as an *unbound temporary* and used only by borrowing operations in a chain — `Folded(src).Sorted()` where `Folded(src): owned Array<T>` — was never disposed, leaking. A named result is disposed via `using var`; an *unnamed* temporary has no name to bind, so nothing disposed it.

#### The resolution

1. **#1007** — a borrow may not be returned through an owning-collection / owning-wrapper return type declared without `owned` ([§28.3](Bezel_Language_Spec.md#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) borrow-lifetime rules); a clean diagnostic replaces the silent double-free. Fresh/owned producers and `owned`-declared returns are unaffected.

2. **#1005** — §28.6's owned-field-return rule is now enforced for the `move`-of-owned-field form. A *bare* owned-field read through a non-`owned` *class* return remains a legal borrow per §28.6's "Methods returning `this`" rule — only the `move` form transfers the value out.

3. **#1006b** — a new rule ([§28.3](Bezel_Language_Spec.md#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries), *Unbound owned temporaries*): an unbound owned temporary used only by borrowing operations is disposed at the end of the full expression, after its uses complete — the unnamed counterpart of the discard contract (§17.13) and the owned-local discharge requirement. Disposed exactly once; the bound / `move`d / transferred cases are excluded.

#### Touched

Language spec: §28.3 (a new borrow-return rule for owning-type returns; a new *Unbound owned temporaries* subsection). Compiler: the ownership pass (src/ownership/Ownership.cpp, Ownership_impl.hpp — the return checks for #1007 and #1005) and codegen (src/codegen/LlvmBackend_Setup.cpp, LlvmBackend_Calls.cpp, LlvmBackend_Exprs.cpp — the unbound-owned-temporary disposal for #1006b, generalizing the v0.148 materializer reclaim along the `owned` axis). Tests: new ownership reject tests (#1007, #1005) and codegen disposal tests (#1006b). Version headers bumped to v0.149 across the language spec, standard library, and design rationale.

#### Migration

A program that relied on any of the three unsound behaviors is rewritten locally: a method that returned a *borrowed* owning-collection value must declare a borrowing (non-owning) return type or return an owned value (#1007); a method that returned a `move`d owned field through a non-`owned` return must declare the return type `owned` (#1005). The unbound-temporary disposal (#1006b) is transparent — affected chains simply stop leaking, with no source change. No change is required of code that already used `owned` returns and `using var` consumers.

#### Deferred

The remaining ergonomic and uniformity questions are tracked separately (#1008): folding the v0.148 materializer carve-out (`ToArray` / `Sorted` / `Reversed`, typed non-`owned` with a compiler-internal reclaim) into the uniform `owned` rule, and the affine-auto-drop-versus-linear decision for a discarded owned value. Returning a *borrowed* owning-collection value (full two-axis container-ownership tracking, as opposed to the #1007 rejection) is likewise deferred. These are expressiveness / ergonomics changes, not soundness; the v0.149 pass leaves the model sound (no leaks, no double-frees) under the existing linear discipline.

---

### v0.150 changelog (v0.149 → v0.150)

v0.150 is the first half of the #1008 ergonomics pass: it makes the ownership discipline **affine** (auto-drop with a must-use warning) and folds the materializer reclaim into one uniform `owned`-driven rule. The borrowed-owning-collection return (Part C of #1008) is soundness-delicate and resolves a separate spec defect, so it lands in its own revision (v0.151).

#### The inconsistency

v0.149 made an *unbound owned temporary* auto-dispose at end of expression ([§28.3](Bezel_Language_Spec.md#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) while a *named* owned local dropped on a normal-exit path remained a hard compile error. Naming a value therefore changed whether the program compiled — `new Foo().Use()` was fine but `var a := new Foo(); a.Use();` was an error — a refactoring hazard, and an asymmetry the language did not actually intend. (The asymmetry already showed through the seams: §17.13's move-only-inline-array discard remedy spoke of `var name := …` "auto-dispose at scope end," while the class case in the same section called the same drop an error.)

#### The resolution — affine auto-drop (Part B / "B4")

The model is now uniformly **affine**, matching Rust/C++ RAII rather than Austral-style strict linearity:

- **Auto-drop** ([§28.3 owned-local discharge](Bezel_Language_Spec.md#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)). An owned local that reaches a normal-exit scope end still-owned (not moved) is disposed implicitly there — the *same* mechanism the exception-path discharge already applied to the unwinding edge, now applied to the normal edge too. The move analysis leaves a transferred value moved-from, so the scope-end disposal skips it; exactly-once on every path is preserved. This *reuses existing machinery*: the implementation is "apply the exception-edge disposal to the fall-through edge," not a new analysis.
- **Must-use warning.** A plain-`var` implicit drop raises a *warning* (not an error), surfacing a possibly-unintended drop; suppressed by `using var` (the explicit scope-bound, non-movable form), explicit `Dispose()`/discard, or move/return. The two keywords keep distinct intent: `using var` = scope-pinned, no warning; plain `var` = movable, warned if implicitly dropped. The warning is a lint over an already-sound program.
- **Discard becomes a disposal form** ([§17.13](Bezel_Language_Spec.md#sec-the-discard-_)). `_ := <owned class / interface / move-only value>` is now legal and disposes at end of statement — the discard *is* an unbound owned temporary. This is the "dispose this owned result now" form (`_ := set.Remove(x);`). It supersedes the prior blanket discard error for non-trivial-dispose classes; the cross-module hazard that forced the *interface* discard error evaporates because the discard disposes the runtime type (correct for any implementation). `Task`/`Task<T>` discard stays an error (disposing a task abandons a running operation — a semantic, not a leak, reason; use `Task.FireAndForget`).

Why affine over strict-linear: v0.149 had already made unnamed temporaries affine; completing the drift is *more* consistent than the split, removes the refactoring hazard, and unifies discard, unnamed temporaries, and named-local drop under one rule ("disposed exactly once — explicitly or at scope end"). The cost — losing the compile-time "you forgot to discharge" error — is recovered as the must-use *warning*, which nudges toward `using var` without rejecting sound code. This is the same trade Rust makes (auto-drop + an unused-`#[must_use]` lint).

#### The resolution — materializer uniformity (Part A)

The standard-library materializers already return `owned` (`ToArray(): owned Array<T>`, `Sorted`, `Reversed`, `ToSet`, `ToDictionary` — owning the *container*, borrowing the elements, [§5.11](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-owning-collections)). v0.150 clarifies ([§28.3 unbound temporaries](Bezel_Language_Spec.md#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)) that an unbound materializer result in a chain (`xs.Where(p).ToArray().Length`) is reclaimed by the *general* end-of-statement rule — the single `owned` return qualifier is the signal, not a special-cased list of method names. (Implementation note: the existing array-materializer reclaim already covers this for `ToArray`/`Sorted`/`Reversed`; collapsing its name-keyed predicate into the `owned`-keyed one is a behavior-preserving cleanup deferred as optional, and extending the end-of-statement reclaim to owned `Set`/`Dictionary` materializer temporaries — an unbound `ToDictionary(...)` result leaks today — is the genuine remaining Part-A2 follow-up, tracked as #1013.)

#### Touched

Language spec: §28.3 (auto-drop + must-use warning rewrite of the owned-local discharge requirement; the unbound-temporary note generalized to all `owned` producers); §17.13 (discard of an owned class / interface / move-only value becomes a legal end-of-statement disposal; only `Task`/`Task<T>` remain restricted); Appendix C.3 (discharge and discard invariants updated); the §28.8 / §28.9 / §28.3-join echoes of the old discharge-error rule. Guide 1 framing updated to "affine." Compiler (Part B, landed): the ownership pass (replace the normal-exit discharge error with scope-end disposal registration + the must-use warning) and codegen (apply the exception-edge disposal to the normal edge). The materializer-reclaim unification (Part A) is deferred as optional cleanup; extending the reclaim to owned `Set`/`Dictionary` temporaries is tracked as #1013. Version headers bumped to v0.150 across the language spec, standard library, and design rationale.

#### Migration

Source-compatible in the safe direction: every program that compiled under v0.149's stricter rule still compiles, and undischarged plain-`var` owned locals that were errors are now warnings (the value auto-drops). A program may *remove* now-unnecessary `using var` / explicit `Dispose()` where scope-end timing is acceptable, or keep them to silence the must-use warning and pin the intent. `_ := ownedExpr;` is newly available as the immediate-disposal form.

#### Deferred (Part C → v0.151)

Returning a *borrowed* owning-collection value remains rejected (#1007). Lifting that requires (1) caller-side reclassification of a non-`owned` owning-collection return with a borrow source as a borrow, (2) relaxing §28.6 so a bare owned-**field** read through a non-`owned` return is a legal receiver-borrow — which also reconciles a §28.6 spec-vs-impl asymmetry (a bare *class*-field read is already a legal borrow in the implementation, while §28.6's text and example call it an error), and (3) a capability restriction forbidding ownership-transferring / disposing operations (`Dispose`/`Drain`/`Pop*`/owning `Add`/indexer-set/`Remove*`/`Clear`) on a borrowed owning container. A mis-step re-introduces the #1007 double-free, so Part C lands as its own revision.

---

### v0.151 changelog (v0.150 → v0.151)

v0.151 is the **specification** for #1008 Part C — returning a *borrowed* owning collection. It reconciles a §28.6 spec-vs-impl asymmetry and defines the borrowed-owning-container capability restriction. The implementation is a separate, double-free-sensitive change (it reworks the caller-side owned-vs-borrow classification) and follows as a tracked PR; until it lands, the compiler keeps the conservative #1007 rejection (spec-ahead-of-implementation, as v0.150 preceded the Part B implementation).

#### The reconciliation

The producers table ([§28.3](Bezel_Language_Spec.md#sec-producers)) has always classified a non-`owned` reference return as a **borrow**. §28.6's prose, however, said flatly that "an owned field's value may not be returned unless the return type is `owned`" and its example called `return _transactions;` an error — even though the Part B / #1005 implementation already treats a bare owned *class*-field read through a non-`owned` return as a legal receiver-borrow (the `GetConn(): Connection => _conn` canary). The owning-collection case was rejected outright by #1007 because the caller's classifier conflates the `Owned*` type *name* with container ownership (a load-bearing name-head heuristic in `producerState`, needed because builtin owned-returning methods like `Shared.Clone` carry no `returnOwned` declaration). v0.151 makes the prose match the model: the bare-field-read borrow is legal and uniform across class and owning-collection fields; only a `move` or a fresh value transfers ownership and requires `owned`.

#### The capability restriction (new normative rule)

A *borrow* of an owning collection may not be **disposed** ([§28.6](Bezel_Language_Spec.md#sec-borrowed-owning-collections)): `Dispose()` on a borrow is rejected, because the actual owner disposes the container — a borrower's `Dispose` would free it a second time. Implementation surfaced a correction to the original design here: the first sketch forbade *all* mutating / transferring operations (a full read-only borrow), but that conflicts with an existing, intended, and memory-safe Bezel idiom — *pass-and-fill*, `method Fill(a: OwnedArray<T>) a.Add(…)`, where `a` is a **borrowed** `OwnedArray<T>` parameter. Bezel's borrowed collections are already mutable. The mutating / transferring operations (`Add`/`Insert`/`Remove*`/`Clear`/`Drain`/`Pop*`/indexer-set) preserve dispose-exactly-once on a borrow — a transferred element is owned by its new holder; the owner then disposes a smaller or empty container — so the *only* operation a borrow-return newly makes unsound is the container `Dispose`. v0.151 therefore restricts exactly that one operation and leaves the rest available. A new reference kind was **not** introduced — "borrowed owning collection" is the ordinary borrow state applied to an owning type, with a single per-method check for `Dispose`.

#### Touched

Language spec: §28.6 (bare owned-field read = borrow; transfer requires `owned`; the new *Borrowed owning collections* capability subsection), §28.3 (the owning-type borrow-return clause generalized to the ordinary borrow-return rules), Appendix C.3 (the two invariants updated). Implementation (tracked follow-up): `producerState` owned-vs-borrow reclassification for non-`owned` owning-collection returns, narrowing the #1007 definition-site rejection to borrowed locals/parameters, caller-side borrow-lifetime tracking of the result, and the borrowed-collection capability check. Version headers bumped to v0.151 across all three documents.

#### Migration

Mostly source-compatible, with one deliberate tightening to flag for review. A method that returns a bare owning-collection field through a non-`owned` return (rejected today by #1007) will compile once Part C lands. A method that *transfers* a field out still requires `owned` (unchanged). Callers of a borrowed owning collection that attempt `Dispose`/`Drain`/mutation get a new, precise compile error rather than a latent double-free.

The tightening: because the caller's classifier cannot see the callee's body, a non-`owned` owning-collection return must mean *one* thing, and v0.151 makes it mean **borrow**. The consequence is that a method returning a *freshly-produced* owning value through a non-`owned` return — `Make(): OwnedArray<T> => new OwnedArray<T>(...)`, which compiles under v0.150 because the caller's name-head heuristic rescues it as owned — must declare `owned OwnedArray<T>` under v0.151. This is a source-breaking change for that pattern (the diagnostic ships with a clear fix-it), and it is the price of distinguishing borrow-returns from owned-returns by signature alone. The alternative — having the caller inspect the callee body / module metadata to decide owned-vs-borrow per call — avoids the tightening at the cost of substantially more machinery; it remains available as a non-breaking future widening should the source-break prove too costly. **v0.151 adopts the tightening.**

---

### v0.152 changelog (v0.151 → v0.152)

v0.152 extends the v0.150 affine auto-drop ([§28.3](Bezel_Language_Spec.md#sec-owned-local-discharge-requirement)) from owned *locals* to `owned` *parameters* on the normal-exit edge — completing the affine model. The third half of the #1008 ergonomics pass's Part B.

#### The gap

v0.150 made an undischarged owned *local* auto-drop at scope end (with a must-use warning) instead of being a hard error. The same edge for an `owned` *parameter* was left as an error: a method that accepted ownership of a parameter and neither moved, returned, disposed, nor reassigned it was rejected. This was an inconsistency — the *exception* edge has always disposed live owned parameters (the §28.3 exception-path discharge names "owned locals and owned parameters"), so only the *normal* edge treated a parameter differently from a local.

#### The resolution

A synchronous, non-iterator, non-destructor method's `owned` parameter that reaches the method's normal exit still owned and is never discharged on any path — and is never reassigned or `out`-overwritten — is disposed implicitly at method end, on both the normal and exception edges, with the must-use warning. The gating is identical to the local case (`everDischarged == 0`, not reassigned, never-moved owner — so the disposal is exactly-once), and reuses the same null-guarded dynamic-dispatch disposal (codegen `dynamicDispose`). Owned parameters of *iterators* are disposed by the state machine (the §29.8 `iteratorAutoDispose` path, unchanged); owned parameters of *async* methods remain a deferred piece.

#### Touched

Language spec: §28.3 (the auto-drop and must-use-warning paragraphs now name `owned` parameters). Compiler: the ownership pass (flag a dropped owned parameter for auto-drop, `ParameterSymbol::autoDropAtScopeEnd`) and codegen (`registerUnwindOwnedParam` registers the flagged parameter for normal+unwind disposal via `dynamicDispose` rather than unwind-only). Version headers bumped to v0.152.

#### Migration

Source-compatible in the safe direction: a method that previously failed to compile because it dropped an `owned` parameter now compiles, the parameter auto-dropping at method end (with the lint). Nothing that compiled under v0.151 stops compiling.

---

### v0.153 changelog (v0.152 → v0.153)

v0.153 closes three ownership-escape gaps surfaced by the implementation sweeps, and corrects one stdlib-doc overstatement. It is a *diagnostic-completeness* revision: it rejects programs that silently leaked or dangled, rather than adding any capability.

#### The gaps

- **Fresh owned value escaping into a non-owning channel (#1020, #926).** §28.6 already made it an error for a freshly-produced owning value to be *returned* through a non-`owned` return type. But the same value stored *into* a non-`owned` (borrow) field, or *returned from a property/indexer getter*, was silently accepted — and leaked, because the destination does not own it and nothing else does. These are the storing-side and getter-side analogues of a rule that already existed for returns.
- **Borrow-bearing record constructed from a temporary (#1066).** §9.7 already stated that a borrow-bearing record value "may not outlive the source of any borrow it contains." A construction argument that is a temporary — a collection/array literal or an unbound fresh call result — has a lifetime that ends at the construction expression, so the record outlives it the instant it is built. This case was accepted and produced a dangling borrow (a crash or a zero-length read).
- **Stdlib overstatement (#1023).** The standard-library text claimed `OwnedArray<int>`/`OwnedArray<MyRecord>` were compile errors. The language spec §14.4 and the implementation (#761) admit value-typed elements (degenerate but harmless — no disposal obligation) and reject only the runtime-managed reference types (`string`, function values). The doc, not the rule, was wrong.

#### The resolution

The §28.6 leak-prevention list gains two enforced bullets: a fresh owned value (a `new`, a call returning `owned T`, a `move`, or an owned operator result) stored into a non-`owned` field is an error directing the author to declare the field `owned`; and a property/indexer getter may not return a fresh owned value, directing the author to a method returning `owned T` (getters cannot carry `owned`, so their result is always a borrow). §9.7 gains an explicit construction-from-temporary bullet specializing the existing borrow-lifetime rule, with the `new Bag([…])` example and the bind-to-a-named-local fix. The standard-library passage is rewritten to match §14.4. No spec capability changes; the accepted set narrows to exclude the three leaking/dangling forms.

#### Touched

Language spec: §28.6 (two leak-prevention bullets + the field-store / getter example); §9.7 (the construction-from-temporary bullet). Standard library: the owning-collection element-constraint paragraph. Compiler (implementation, following this revision): the ownership pass rejects fresh-owned-into-non-`owned`-field (#1020) and fresh-owned-from-a-getter (#926), and rejects constructing a borrow-bearing record from a temporary (#1066). Version headers bumped to v0.153.

#### Migration

Source-breaking only for code that already leaked or dangled. A program that stored a `new`/owned-returning value into a borrow field, returned a fresh owned value from a getter, or constructed a borrow-bearing record from a temporary literal now gets a clear diagnostic with the fix (declare the field `owned`; use a method returning `owned T`; bind the source to a named local). Every such program was already a leak or a dangling borrow at runtime; nothing sound stops compiling.

### v0.154 changelog (v0.153 → v0.154)

v0.154 settles two design questions surfaced by the implementation and clarifies one under-specified rule. Like v0.153 it changes no capability; it states rules the foundations already implied.

#### The questions

- **Null-coalescing ownership (#1029).** §7.7 specified the *value* of `a ?? b` but said nothing about its *ownership* when the operands are owned. `var x := maybeOwned ?? new T()` leaked the right operand when the left was null, because the result was classified as a borrow and never acquired a disposal obligation. The answer was already present elsewhere: `??` is a two-branch expression, structurally identical to an `if`/`else` that assigns `x` on both paths, so it must obey the same ownership-merge (meet) rule the producer table and the two-branch patterns of §28.3 already define. The resolution adds `a ?? b` to the §28.3 producer table — `owned ⊓ owned = owned` (the chosen value is discharged exactly once; the other arm is never produced at runtime, so no leak and no double-free), `borrowed ⊓ borrowed = borrowed`, and an owned arm mixed with a borrowed arm is rejected exactly as the analogous `if`/`else` is — with a cross-reference from §7.7. No new rule: the existing meet rule, applied to an expression form it had not been spelled out for.

- **Reserved primitive-alias type names (#1081).** §3.4 makes each primitive's PascalCase standard-library name (`Int32`, `Single`, …) interchangeable with its lowercase keyword everywhere a type is named. A user type declared with one of those names (`record Single`) therefore *silently shadows the primitive at some use sites and not others*, producing a value the author did not intend rather than an error. The resolution reserves exactly those PascalCase aliases of the primitive value types and `String` as type names: declaring a user type with such a name is a compile error. Only those names are reserved — ordinary library type names (`Array`, `Stream`) remain shadowable under normal name resolution — because only the primitive aliases carry the keyword-interchangeability that makes shadowing ambiguous.

- **Shift operand width (#1094) — clarification.** §6.5 said the shift count is reduced "modulo the operand's bit width" without stating *which* operand or whether a narrow left operand promotes to match a wider count. Bezel's arithmetic is operand-width with checked overflow (§6.1/§6.2 promote only on a width *mismatch*; `byte + byte` stays `byte` and overflows at byte width), so shift must match: the result type is the **left** operand, the right operand is only a count and never promotes the left, and the count is reduced modulo the **left** operand's width. This is a clarification, not a normative change — it tightens "the operand's" to "the left operand's" and states the no-promotion-from-count rule the type system already follows; it makes `<<`/`>>` consistent with the rest of the operator family rather than the lone operator that would promote `byte → int`.

#### Touched

Language spec: §7.7 (the `??`-ownership cross-reference) and §28.3 (the `a ?? b` producer-table row); §3.4 (the reserved-primitive-alias-names paragraph); §6.5 (the left-operand-width shift clarification). No standard-library change. Compiler (implementation, following this revision): the ownership pass classifies `??` by the two-branch meet and discharges the chosen owned value once (#1029); name resolution rejects a user type named after a primitive alias (#1081); codegen masks a shift count by the left operand's width without widening the left operand (#1094). Version headers bumped to v0.154.

#### Migration

Source-breaking only for code that was already wrong. A program that named a user type after a primitive alias was already at risk of silent shadowing and now gets a clear diagnostic (rename the type). A `??` over an owned arm mixed with a borrowed arm now reports the same ownership-merge error an equivalent `if`/`else` already reported. The `??`-ownership and shift fixes otherwise change only previously-leaking or previously-miscomputed programs; nothing sound stops compiling.

### v0.155 changelog (v0.154 → v0.155)

v0.155 settles two standard-library surface questions surfaced by the implementation and corrects one documentation defect. Like the revisions before it, it changes no capability; it pins down values and surfaces the foundations already implied, and removes a sentence that contradicted the rest of the document.

#### The questions

- **Default `DateTime.ToString()` format (#1114).** A `DateTime` inherits `ToString()` from `Object` (language spec §8.1) and additionally declares `ToString(format)`, but the *default* rendering produced by the no-argument form was never stated. The resolution defines it as the round-trippable ISO 8601 form `yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss` — the same value already produced when a `DateTime` is interpolated into a string with no format specifier, so the explicit and implicit no-format paths agree. `ToString(format)` continues to select an explicit format. No new capability: a value the language already rendered one way (interpolation) is now stated for the method form too.

- **Dictionary write surface — there is no `.Set` method (#1112).** The owning- and borrowing-dictionary types expose their write surface as the indexer (`dict[key] := value`, add-or-update) and `Add(key, value)` (insert, raising on a duplicate key); neither §4.8 nor §4.9 ever listed a `Set` method. The resolution states this explicitly and pins the convention for *all* collection types: the write surface is the indexer or the type's own insertion method (`Add` / `Push` / `Enqueue`), and there is no `Set` method on any collection — a `.Set(...)` call is rejected as an unknown member. This follows the established library model (a hash map's update is its indexer, not a named setter) and lets the collection method-surface validation reject `OwnedArray.Set` and its siblings, directing the author to `arr[i] := v`.

#### The defect

- **Owning-collection borrow capabilities listed non-existent materializers (#1109).** §28.6, enumerating the operations available on a *borrow* of an owning collection, listed "the materializers `ToArray` / `Sorted` / `Reversed`." This contradicted stdlib §4.5 — owning collection types deliberately have **no** value-copy materializers at all, because a uniquely-owned element cannot be copied out without double-owning or draining it — and §28.11's element-slot policy, and it was unsound in practice: a borrowing snapshot of an owning collection is an unchecked use-after-free (the snapshot is invalidated by any owning operation, which Bezel does not track). The sentence is corrected to drop the materializers and note that they are simply not part of the owning collection's surface, on a borrow or otherwise. A genuinely sound borrowing-snapshot remains a deferred future feature (it needs the §28.11 borrow-storing-primitive lifetime rules).

#### Touched

Standard library: §2.5 (the `DateTime` no-argument `ToString()` declaration and its ISO 8601 default); §4.8 (the dictionary write-surface paragraph, covering §4.9 by the same convention). Language spec: §28.6 (the owning-collection-borrow read-operation list no longer lists the materializers). No grammar or semantic rule changes. Compiler (implementation, following this revision): the no-argument `DateTime.ToString()` lowers to the runtime default-format formatter (ISO 8601) (#1114); collection method-surface validation rejects a `.Set` call and other non-surface members (#1112 / #920). The §28.6 correction needs no code — the implementation already rejects the materializers on `Owned*` receivers. Version headers bumped to v0.155.

<a id="sec-v0-155-to-v0-156-changelog"></a>
### v0.156 changelog (v0.155 → v0.156)

v0.156 settles four standard-library and language questions surfaced by the implementation and corrects one stale cross-reference. It changes no capability; it pins down behaviours the foundations already implied and makes loud what was silent.

#### The questions

- **Lazy LINQ queries are single-consumption, not re-enumerable (#1226).** §29.11 left repeat enumeration of a lazy iterable "a property of the specific implementation," which the implementation realised as a silent empty second enumeration — a silent wrong result. The resolution states that a lazy query is single-consumption: the first enumeration (a `for` loop or a terminal operator) consumes it as `move` consumes an owned value; a second use is a compile error where statically visible, or `InvalidOperationException` where only dynamically reachable; `ToArray()` materializes an owned, re-enumerable `Array<T>`. This is stricter than C#'s deferred re-execution (which the C# ecosystem itself flags as a likely defect via analyzer CA1851), and it falls out of the existing affine/move machinery — a lazy query is a single-use producer that borrows its source, so re-execution would re-run over a possibly-disposed source. No new mechanism: the query reuses the consume/move analysis, and the dynamic guard reuses the §29.12 mutation-during-iteration failure mode.

- **A span boxes into `IReadOnlySpan<T>` for a call-bounded use (#970).** Stdlib §4.14's iteration paragraph read as a categorical ban on boxing a span into an interface, contradicting language spec §8.6 (which permits a short-lived box of a borrow-bearing record) and the stdlib's own §4.16 `IReadOnlySpan<TElement>` parameter surface. There is no design conflict — §8.6's rule already sanctions the call-bounded box and rejects escape, and the `IReadOnlySpan` interface is escape-free by construction (no `GetEnumerator`, `Slice`, or borrow-retaining handle). §4.14's parenthetical is reworded to name the *escaping* enumerator as the forbidden case (which is why spans do not implement `IEnumerable`) and defer to §8.6 for the call-bounded box, and §8.6 gains the `IReadOnlySpan` example. No semantic change.

- **`string.LastIndexOf(value: string)` (#1249-B).** §9.6 declared only the `char` overload, but the natural counterpart to the existing `IndexOf(value: string)` was implemented and useful; the `string` overload is now documented.

- **Equality/formatting overrides disqualify auto-equality (#1249-A).** §9.2's "not auto-equality-bearing" list named explicit fields, side-effecting computed properties, and non-trivial constructor bodies, but not the case of a record that declares its own `override Equals`, `GetHashCode`, or `ToString` (without the `operator =`/`<>` overloads) — under which the synthesized structural `=` would silently ignore the author's override. The disqualifier is added to the list; `=`/`<>` and the direct `.Equals`/`.GetHashCode` calls are a compile error on such a record unless the operators are also declared.

#### The clarification

- **A `for` loop variable is freshly bound — body assignment never changes the iteration count (#1243).** §21.4 already specified fresh per-iteration binding; a clause is added making explicit that assigning to the loop variable inside the body affects only that iteration, even when the source is a `Range<T>` the compiler optimizes into a counted loop. No rule change; the counted-loop optimization must preserve the fresh-binding observable.

#### Touched

Language spec: §29.11 (single-consumption lazy queries); §8.6 (the `IReadOnlySpan` boxing example + escaping-vs-call-bounded distinction); §9.2 (the equality/formatting-override disqualifier); §21.4 (the fresh-binding/body-assignment clause); §29.2 (the stale `§9.7.1`→`§8.6` boxing cross-reference). Standard library: §4.14 (the iteration parenthetical reworded), §4.16 (the stale `§9.7.1`→`§8.6` reference), §9.6 (`LastIndexOf(string)`), §5 (the single-consumption LINQ note). Design rationale: §5.15 (the stale `§9.7.1`→`§8.6` reference). Compiler (implementation, following this revision): a lazy-query second enumeration becomes a compile error / `InvalidOperationException` (#1226); the span→`IReadOnlySpan` non-escaping box is permitted (#970); `LastIndexOf(string)` accepted (#1249-B); a body record with an equality/formatting override rejects `=` (#1249-A); the counted-loop codegen preserves fresh-binding under body assignment (#1243). (`AppendFormat`'s composite-format grammar, #1179, is deferred to a following revision.) Version headers bumped to v0.156.

#### Migration

Source-breaking only for code that was already wrong or relied on an unspecified value. A `.Set(...)` call on a collection now reports an unknown-member error (use the indexer `coll[k] := v` or the type's insertion method). A no-argument `DateTime.ToString()` that previously produced an empty/garbage string (and crashed when its result was used) now returns the ISO 8601 rendering. Nothing sound stops compiling.

---

<a id="sec-v0-157-to-v0-158-changelog"></a>
### v0.158 changelog (v0.157 → v0.158)

v0.158 is the **grammar-normativity and equality revision**: parse rules that lived in grammar comments become normative text, Appendix A becomes able to derive the language the prose describes, record equality is consolidated into one recursive rule, and two equality-consistency rules become compiler-enforced. One conversion ruling (bool↔integer asymmetry) settles a fork exposed by implementation. (Issues: #1320, #1321, #1322-ruling, #1325, #1326, #1338, #1341, #1368; #1381 filed as the split-out enum-operators fork.)

#### Normative promotions (were grammar comments; now rules)

- **Case scrutinee level** (#1320): §19.1 states the rule — the scrutinee parses at the *multiplicative* level; additive/shift/bitwise/range/relational scrutinees must be parenthesized, which is what lets a first pattern begin with `-10..-6`. The A.7 comment (previously *mis-stating* the level as "above range") corrected to match the implemented and now-normative rule.
- **Generics-vs-less-than** (#1368): the balanced-`<…>`-plus-follow-token rule is now normative prose in §22.12 (purely syntactic, no name-resolution feedback; `f(a<b, c>(d))` is a generic call; parenthesize for the relational reading).

#### Grammar repairs (Appendix A derives the prose language)

- **Pattern alternatives factored to the arm level** (#1321): new `ArmPattern ::= Pattern ("," Pattern)*`; `Pattern`'s constant-alternatives production reduced to a single `Constant`. Inside a positional destructure list the comma is now unambiguously the slot separator (the #1300 ambiguity closed at the grammar level); §19.3 states the per-slot rule and the guard workaround.
- **Range patterns** (#1341): dedicated `RangePattern`/`PatternBound` productions (no bare-expression leg, no `step`, `-`-prefixed bounds); `Constant` admits `-`-prefixed numeric literals; §19.3: alternative-list members must resolve to constants (a type is an error; grouped type tests = separate arms).
- **Derivability** (#1325): `PrimitiveType` production added to `TypeNoNullable` and `PrimaryAtom` (with the `T?(x)` type-reading-wins note); `UnaryExpr` made right-recursive (`not not x`, `- -x`); `NullCoalesce` admits `?? throw …`; the retired pre-v0.97 `where T is owned` constraint form and `ModifierConstraint` deleted, the orphaned accessor `GenericConstraints?` removed, the SetterParamSpec comment recited to §22.3/§23.3. The enum-operator fork is **not** bundled: filed as #1381.

#### Record equality, consolidated (#1326)

§9.2 restated as **one recursive rule over storage components**; admissible component types now include `T?` (null-safe `=` per §8.4/§7.11) and non-owning inline arrays (element-wise per §8.3); the undefined "sealed reference type with content equality" clause **deleted**. §8.3's stale "Body-only record | compile error" row corrected. §9.3 gains the combined-form eligibility rule (positional fields count as storage components; disqualifiers suppress with the use-site error) and extends the use-site-error discipline to purely-positional records with non-admissible fields (closing a reference-equality footgun). §9.8 delegates to §9.2 instead of paraphrasing. **#1249-A narrowed:** an `override ToString` now suppresses only auto-`ToString`; equality survives (through v0.157 it revoked the whole package — the v0.156 reasoning never argued formatting should kill equality). §8.5 aligned.

#### Equality consistency, enforced (#1338)

- **Co-declaration rule** (§25.2): a record/enum overloading homogeneous `=`/`<>` must also declare `Equals(T)` and `override GetHashCode` — compiler-enforced, mirroring §8.3's Equals→GetHashCode rule. (IntPtr/UIntPtr intrinsics exempt.)
- **Equality-bearing** joins the §3.6 derived-property table; `Dictionary`/`OwnedDictionary` keys and `Set`/`OwnedSet` elements require it **at the instantiation site** (stdlib §4.8/§4.10), replacing the unenforceable "must provide consistent Equals and GetHashCode" prose.

#### Conversion ruling (§5.2, from #1322's merge adjudication)

Explicit `bool`→integer is **admitted** (total: `false`→`0`, `true`→`1`; the `int(r = null)` exit-code and branchless-counting idioms). `bool(n)` remains an error in both forms — partial and truthiness-shaped — as does `bool`→`float`/`double`/`decimal`/`char`. The asymmetry is deliberate and recorded in §5.2.

#### Migration

Mostly source-compatible. Tightenings: the §25.2 co-declaration rule (a record overloading `=` without `Equals`/`GetHashCode` now errors — the fix is stating them); hash-container instantiation over non-equality-bearing record keys/elements now errors at the instantiation. Loosenings: `int(b)` compiles; records with `override ToString` regain auto-equality; negative constant patterns and `T?`/inline-array record components become expressible/eligible. Compiler alignment for the new checks and eligibility extensions follows in-run; the parser already implements the #1320/#1321 rules.

<a id="sec-v0-158-to-v0-159-changelog"></a>
### v0.159 changelog (v0.158 → v0.159)

v0.159 is the **conversions-and-typing revision**: four families of rules the compiler already implemented but the spec never stated are now normative. Nearly docs-only (probe-level verification in-run). (Issues: #1323, #1324, #1337, #1340; also settles #184's documented-vs-rejected fork.)

- **Constant narrowing** (§5.1, #1323): a compile-time integer constant implicitly converts to any integer type containing its value; out-of-range constants error (never truncate). Cross-referenced from §15.4/§10.2/§18.1.
- **MinValue literals** (§4.2): the 2³¹/2⁶³ magnitudes admitted solely as immediate operands of unary `-` — `int.MinValue`/`long.MinValue` become writable.
- **Typed-context widening** (§4.2/§18.1, the #184 fork settled): an oversized unsuffixed decimal literal is admitted at an explicitly-declared integer target it fits; untyped contexts still error toward a suffix. Rationale: the width is taken only from a written target and range-checked — the suffix discipline's purpose survives; rejecting would break the corpus for no safety gain.
- **Common-type (join) rule** (§20/§19.1/§21.9, #1324): A-into-B-or-B-into-A only (widening, T→T?, subtype→base); no sibling LUB (deliberately unlike §31.2.1 catch bindings); throw arms bottom-typed; condition-first evaluation and selected-arm-only evaluation stated; case/when expression type = left-fold of arm types; §21.9's discard rules applied per arm in statement position (resolving its tension with §19.1).
- **`?` idempotent under substitution** (§7.10 + C.4 + stdlib §5 note, #1337): `T?` at T=`U?` is `U?`; no two-level optional; the `*OrNull`-at-nullable-T ambiguity documented with the recommended shapes; bare-T storage follows §7.9.
- **Range `Contains` vs direction** (§16.3/§16.4/§16.6, #1340): normative extent formula (min/max endpoints, exclusivity, null-open sides, Step-independent) — `50 in 100..0` is true; `IsEmpty` reworded to iteration; **range patterns read bounds directionally as written** (reversed patterns match nothing) with the deliberate pattern-vs-Contains asymmetry recorded; the circular §17.5 reference in the surrogate paragraph fixed.

#### Migration
None expected: every rule codifies implemented behavior. (In-run probes verify: reversed-range pattern non-match, MinValue literal forms, `T?`-idempotence corners; divergences found become implementation fixes, not spec changes.)

<a id="sec-v0-159-to-v0-160-changelog"></a>
### v0.160 changelog (v0.159 → v0.160)

v0.160 is the **members revision**: the call/parameter-modifier composition matrix gets defined, extensions and operators get their resolution cores, the arrow-body family gets its one missing form, and two small syntax seams close. (Issues: #1335, #1343-remainder, #1344, #1345, #1346, #1347.)

- **out-var annotations** (#1335): §22.6's stray annotated forms struck — the inline `out var x` never takes a type annotation (§22.4 was always explicit); typed disambiguation = pre-declared local.
- **Modifier composition** (#1344): A.4 Argument gains `out owned var` (the thrice-stated prose form is now derivable) and restricts named arguments to plain values (`M(out var x := n)` has no reading); `out _` defined against both out kinds (owned discard = unbound owned temporary, end-of-statement disposal; both-overloads-present ⇒ ambiguity error); defaults permitted only on unmodified/`owned` parameters, with the trailing-defaults rule stated; primary constructors take plain/`owned` parameters only.
- **Arrow bodies** (#1345): a unit-returning method takes the assignment arrow the accessors always had (`method SetX(v: int) => _x := v;`); the remaining per-context divergences recorded with reasons in rationale §3.5 (lambda `;`-collision, operators value-only, methods already have the bare block).
- **Extensions** (#1346): the implicit type-parameter binding rule stated (bare single-segment identifier in argument position of the extended type binds fresh, always, with a shadowing warning — the only implicit type-parameter binding in the language; "resolution-wins" declined as action-at-a-distance); extension members are `public`/`internal` only; extension properties expression-bodied only.
- **Operators** (#1347): declaring-type-operand requirement; the two-operand-types union resolution rule with no auto-commutation and the both-types ambiguity error; `public` made normative (A.4 narrowed); C.10 bullets added.
- **Syntax seams closed** (#1343 remainder): type aliases bind with `:=` (was `=`, the sole exception — "all bindings introduce with `:=`" is now exceptionless; 9 examples migrated); `destructor` parens-less form recorded as intentional (rationale §3.6).

#### Migration
Tightenings: named ref/out/owned arguments (were undefined-but-parseable) now rejected; non-public operators rejected; protected/private extension members rejected; block-bodied extension properties rejected; defaults on ref/out rejected. Type alias `=` → `:=` is source-breaking but trivially mechanical. Compiler alignment for all of v0.160 rides the wave-3 lanes (the `out owned var` parse is #1305's fix; the owned-`out _` disposal semantics subsumes the #1315 scratch-slot family for owned outs).

<a id="sec-v0-160-to-v0-161-changelog"></a>
### v0.161 changelog (v0.160 → v0.161)

v0.161 is the **ownership-honesty revision**: the one remaining zero-disposal path closes, the soundness claims are rescoped to exactly what is checked, and the owning-enumeration protocol loses its anomalous destructive getter. (Issues: #1328, #1331, #1349, #1360.)

- **Drop-on-overwrite** (§28.7 rewritten, #1328): assignment to an owned field or plain-`var` owned local now disposes the displaced live value (RHS-first; null/moved-from displaced values dispose nothing; explicit prior `Dispose()` stays legal via idempotence, so all correct v0.160 code is behavior-preserved). The "compiler warning on undisposed overwrite" subsection is deleted; the disposers-don't-throw discussion is rewritten for the new ordering (the manual pattern's exception-unsafe window no longer exists on the implicit path). New Appendix C.3 invariant. §28.8's commentary updated. The §28.3 exactly-once claim becomes true without carve-outs. Move-only inline-array whole-value reassignment retains §15.3's manual discipline (deferred with its own issue — #747 interaction). *Compiler: locals half already shipped (#913/#1054); the fields half is a wave-4 ownership lane; spec-ahead-of-implementation until it lands.*
- **Borrow honesty** (§28.3, #1331): the producers-table borrow row and the factory-methods text are restated structurally (instance ⇒ receiver-sourced borrow; static ⇒ owned-with-warning; documentation phrases carry no classification weight — `owned` is the only transfer signal); the borrow-into-field bullet separates the decidable assignment-site check from the trusted caller-side lifetime obligation, naming the checked-mode `DisposedAccessException` backstop and the unchecked-mode UB honestly; the closing soundness sentence is rescoped to what is actually guaranteed.
- **`TakeCurrent()`** (§29.1/§29.2/§30.7 + stdlib §4.13, #1349): the owning enumerators' destructive `Current: owned T` property is replaced by an ordinary owned-returning method — the language's only destructive property getter is removed (it violated §28.6 as written; §23 itself prescribes a method for transfer-out). Protocol misuse (read/take before first advance, after exhaustion, double-take) is a **defined `InvalidOperationException`** (was undefined behavior), normative for stdlib/compiler-generated enumerators, contractual for user ones. *Compiler: builtin-member rename + desugaring + IOE guards ride wave-4.*
- **`using var` as readonly-local** (rationale §17.8, #1360): the no-op-disposal admission documented honestly (tolerated for uniformity, not the endorsed idiom; runtime-`const` stays on the deferred list). No diagnostic added — §28.10 sanctions scope-pinning.

#### Migration
Drop-on-overwrite is behavior-preserving for all correct code and un-leaks previously-leaking code. `TakeCurrent()` is a mechanical rename for owning-enumerator users (the for-desugarings are compiler-internal). No other changes.

<a id="sec-v0-161-to-v0-162-changelog"></a>
### v0.162 changelog (v0.161 → v0.162)

v0.162 is the **async-and-exceptions revision**, executing the #1362 deadlock proposal and closing the async/exception findings of the 2026-07 review; it also carries the owner-prompted range-membership correction. (Issues: #1362, #1332, #1333, #1340-revision, #1350, #1352, #1379; RFC #811 resolved by ruling.)

- **Blocking waits are contextual** (§30.3/§22.13, #1362): `Wait()`/`Result` on an incomplete task are legal only outside domains (startup code on the main thread — the same mechanism that drives async `Main`); inside a domain continuation they are a deterministic deadlock and become a compile error in `async` bodies plus a runtime `InvalidOperationException` elsewhere. §22.13's previously-prescribed (and deadlocking) `Wait()` static-init pattern is replaced by eager-init-in-async-`Main` and the lazy-task-accessor patterns. New C.6 posture throughout.
- **Pattern A slots are owned or chained** (§30.5, #1332): a `return await <source>` transfers the *source task* into the outer task (destructor disposes the chain link, never the borrowed result) — "disposing the task disposes the result" holds transitively. **`Task.WhenAny` returns `Task<int>`** (the winner's index): the former `Task<Task>` was unconstructible under this section's own rules. Rationale §12.2 Step 4 rewritten (the "task borrows from the repository" story was unimplementable).
- **OwnedTask spends on all edges** (§30.4/§30.5/C.6, #1352): the first await consumes the operand regardless of outcome (fault/cancel included; retry = bind a fresh task); C.6 now distinguishes owned operands (second await = compile-time moved-from read) from borrowed ones (runtime IOE).
- **`OwnedTask<T>.Result` blessed** (§30.3, #1379): a completed-task read in an owned-consuming position transfers ownership exactly like `await` (the implementation's #1250 semantics, now normative); subject to the same blocking-context rules.
- **TCS closure-capture exception defined** (§30.11, #1333): four compiler-checkable conditions replace "recognized by shape"; the registration callback must be one-shot; repeating registrations are outside the exception (the old keyboard-event example — itself a use-after-dispose under the structural proof — replaced by a one-shot block-device read).
- **Exception model completed** (§31/§22.7/stdlib, #1350 + RFC #811): the base `Exception` surface is declared for the first time (ctors, `Message`, `StackTrace: string`, `CauseChain`); **cause chaining is by snapshot** — the `(message, cause)` constructor borrows the cause and copies `ExceptionInfo` records (type/message/stack) into the new exception's flattened `CauseChain`, never retaining the instance — resolving #811 inside the caught-exception-is-a-borrow model with zero new ownership rules (a live `InnerException` on user exceptions is deliberately declined; `TypeInitializationException`'s stays the one runtime-owned live reference, now stated to be process-lifetime-owned and exempt from dispose-after-arm). The throw-in-finally supersede rule is stated in §31.2 itself (superseded exception disposed exactly once — same for guard supersede); wrapping constructors take the caught exception as a borrow and snapshot it; `ArgumentException`'s surface declared; `StackTrace` is a `string` (guides fixed).
- **Range membership corrected** (§16.3/§16.6 + stdlib §9.8, revising v0.159 after owner review of #1340): `Contains(v)` = *nonempty under iteration* ∧ within-extent — an empty range contains nothing (`50 in 100..0` is now `false`, matching Rust/Python); `IsEmpty` and `Contains` agree; range patterns and `in` agree exactly on stepless forms (the v0.159 asymmetry is deleted); constant reversed range patterns get a mandatory never-matches warning; stepped descending ranges keep their members.

#### Migration
Tightenings: in-domain `Wait()`/`Result` (was a deadlock at runtime — now diagnosed); `50 in 100..0`-style extent membership over iteration-empty ranges (write `Math.Min/Max` comparisons for unordered intervals). `WhenAny` consumers switch from the (unconstructible) winner task to its index. Everything else is definition of previously-undefined or unstated behavior. Compiler alignment rides wave-4: the Wait/Result sema-reject + runtime guard (unblocked by #1377's RaiseAsync re-lower), WhenAny index, spend-on-fault, Contains flip + warning, Exception surface/CauseChain, TakeCurrent (v0.161), fields drop-on-overwrite (v0.161).

<a id="sec-v0-162-to-v0-163-changelog"></a>
### v0.163 changelog (v0.162 → v0.163)

v0.163 is the **domains-and-system revision**: the statics side door closes, termination gets defined, FFI callbacks are inverted to the forms that actually lower, the sendability coordination text is reconciled, and event-raise reentrancy is pinned. (Issues: #1363, #1364, #1366, #1367, #1369. The module-system chapter, #1365, is deliberately its own following revision.)

- **Statics and domains** (§22.12 + §30.14, #1363): statics are process-global; lazy initialization is runtime-synchronized once-semantics; a *mutable* static of non-synchronized type is a compile error; readonly immutable content is unrestricted; class-typed readonly singletons carry a declaration warning naming the cross-domain obligation; static events' subscriber lists are runtime-synchronized. §30.14's headline invariant now cites the statics rules instead of silently excluding them.
- **Sendability list reconciled** (§30.14, #1364): `Shared<T>`'s v0.140 conditional rule replaces the stale blanket exclusion; `Mutex`/`Semaphore`/atomics stated sendable (their purpose), `Lock` guards domain-bound.
- **Termination defined** (§33.3, #1366): uncaught exception ⇒ exit 70 + typed/chained report to stderr, shutdown sequence still runs; live spawned domains at `Main`'s completion are **abandoned** (join explicitly if their work matters); `Environment.Exit` initiates the same shutdown from any domain and never returns.
- **FFI callbacks inverted** (§32.8/§32.10, #1367): static methods and *non-capturing lambdas* are admitted (both are bare fn pointers); bound instance references and capturing lambdas are rejected (they need an environment the FFI does not define) — the previous rule admitted exactly the wrong set. Environmentless callbacks may be retained by native code past the call (process-lifetime code addresses; foreign-thread discipline per §30.12/§30.14 governs what they may touch). The `errno()` example corrected.
- **Event raise takes a snapshot** (§24.5, #1369): in-flight raises are unaffected by subscribes/unsubscribes from handlers; self-unsubscribing one-shot listeners are thereby well-defined.
- **Diagnostic identity is implementation-defined** (Appendix D, #1369): conformance classifies accept/warn/reject; no error-code registry until multiple implementations exist.

#### Migration
Tightenings: mutable non-synchronized statics become errors (the sanctioned shapes: synchronized types, readonly immutables, or domain-confined design); capturing/bound FFI callbacks become errors (pass state through the C user-data pointer). `WhenAny`-era note: none. Compiler alignment rides waves 4–5 (statics checks, static-event sync, snapshot raise, FFI admission flip, exit-code path).

<a id="sec-v0-163-to-v0-164-changelog"></a>
### v0.164 changelog (v0.163 → v0.164)

v0.164 is the **module-system revision** — §2 grows from ~70 lines to a real chapter, closing the review's one chapter-sized hole (#1365).

- **Circular imports compile as one unit** (§2.5): import cycles form strongly-connected components; an SCC is the compilation unit (sources compiled together, one artifact per member still emitted; partial-SCC builds are errors naming the missing members); between SCCs resolution stays artifact-based in condensed topological order. This replaces the jointly-impossible pair "resolution reads compiled artifacts" + "circular type-level imports are permitted".
- **Import aliases** (§2.2 + A.1): `import M.N as X;` — a file-scoped qualifier; bare names and the full module name stay usable.
- **Collision rule** (§2.2): same public name from two imports ⇒ the bare name is ambiguous (error citing both; qualify or alias); imports never shadow one another; current-module declarations shadow imports for bare-name purposes.
- **Dotted-name resolution** (new §2.7): leftmost-first, type-wins, no backtracking; longest-module-prefix fallback; shadowing warning when a type and module prefix compete; adding an import can un-error a chain but never silently re-mean one.

#### Migration
Additive except the collision rule, which turns silent first-import-wins behavior (where an implementation had any) into an explicit ambiguity error. Compiler alignment (alias parse, ambiguity diagnostic, §2.7 order, SCC build mode) is a wave-5 lane with probe-first discipline — the implementation's current behavior for each corner is measured before changing it.

<a id="sec-v0-164-to-v0-165-changelog"></a>
### v0.165 changelog (v0.164 → v0.165)

v0.165 is the **standard-library rules revision** — the review's stdlib findings land as one batch. (Issues: #1327, #1342, #1353, #1354, #1355, #1356, #1357, #1358, #1359, #1375.)

- **Owning-collection elements are class/interface only** (#1327): the three-way contradiction resolved in the v0.102-recorded direction; stdlib §4.2 rewritten, spec §14.4's "proper class types" phrase corrected; value-typed elements rejected at instantiation.
- **Stream read contract** (#1375): `Array<T>` gains the sized constructor `(size, fill)`; the windowed Read/Write forms range over `Count` (never grow); span-taking Read/Write/Async overloads added (#1355) as the preferred forms — the canonical read loop is finally writable.
- **Byte-worlds bridges** (#1358): deserializers accept `ReadOnlyArraySpan<byte>`; the endianness accessors are mirrored onto the Array-span family; `File.WriteAllBytes` takes `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` — file→parse and serialize→file are zero-copy.
- **Inline arrays join the ecosystem** (#1342): intrinsic `ToArray(): owned Array<T>` and `Contains` (making `x in arr` work through §17.5) — §15.1.2/§17.5 rewritten.
- **Lazy-query consumption points** (#1353): the normative three-point list (enumerate/terminal, compose, pass-as-IEnumerable) with the untracked-callee honesty note; no Query<T> head type (declined — it would break the §5 surface and re-erase at the upcast).
- **Collection-family consistency** (#1354): SortedDictionary/SortedSet gain their IReadOnlyCollection conformance (making documented iteration legal); SortedDictionary.TryGetValue takes `out V`; SortedSet gets Add/TryAdd per the §4.10 convention; Dictionary Keys/Values become read-only views; borrowing Stack/Queue retype to IReadOnlyCollection with explicit Contains. The hash-vs-sorted comparer split and the literal duplicate policies are kept and recorded (rationale).
- **Directory/Path/Convert normativity** (#1356): full surfaces enumerated; the Convert elisions expanded; Convert ruled a kept familiarity alias (rationale §15.x) with no cross-primitive role.
- **Temporal ordering and construction** (#1357): DateTime/TimeSpan/DateOnly/TimeOnly/Guid gain IComparable/IEquatable with stated CompareTo semantics (ticks; Guid = canonical-byte lexicographic — the .NET trap called out), component constructors, Ticks/FromTicks, Unix conversions, Guid.FromByteArray, and full DateOnly/TimeOnly declarations.
- **Naming conventions recorded** (#1359): acronym/width rules stated (IEEERemainder and IeeeEquals both correct under one rule); Random.NextLong → **NextInt64**; the enumeration-interface I-prefix resolves in #1372's rename train.

#### Migration
Tightenings: value-element owning collections (`OwnedArray<int>`) become instantiation errors — use `Array<T>`/`OwnedBuffer<T>`; SortedSet.Add's bool form becomes TryAdd. Everything else is additive or a documented alias. Compiler alignment is the wave-5 stdlib lane (instantiation check + ~8 test migrations, intrinsics, retypes, new members).

<a id="sec-v0-156-to-v0-157-changelog"></a>
### v0.157 changelog (v0.156 → v0.157)

v0.157 is the **documentation-currency revision**: it brings every body section of the five documents up to date with decisions already landed (chiefly the v0.97 `Owned*` naming and the v0.150–v0.152 affine model), corrects the mechanical defects catalogued by the 2026-07 documentation review, and records previously-unrecorded syntax decisions. It changes no language capability. (Issues: #1317, #1318, #1319, #1329, #1330, #1361, #1373, plus the recording halves of #1343.)

#### Currency sweep (stale-premise text updated in place)

- **Rationale §12.1–§12.2** respelled from the retired `Task<owned T>` to `OwnedTask<T>` with a spelling note; §12.2 retitled (#1317). Historical/changelog mentions untouched.
- **Affine-model echoes swept** (#1329): spec §29.2 (iteration-variable discharge — twice), §30.1, §30.5, Appendix C.3, and stdlib §4.5/§4.13 no longer state the pre-v0.150 "compile error" rule; all now delegate to §28.3's auto-drop-with-must-use-warning. *Compiler note:* the implementation still hard-errors on an undischarged owned **iteration variable** (the §28.3 auto-drop machinery requires a plain local); this revision is spec-ahead-of-implementation on that path, as v0.151 was for Part C — the compiler follow-up is tracked in #1329.
- **Guide 1** (#1330): §5's factory guidance rewritten — the old text taught `using var fresh; … return fresh;`, which the spec rejects ("cannot move out of `using var`"), and pre-affine leak-error framing; it now teaches plain-`var` factories (exception-safe via the §28.3 exception-path discharge) and `using var` as scope-pinned. §7's closing rewritten for auto-drop. §6's dangling "Guide 4" reference now cites spec §28.8.1/§28.11 (#1319).
- **Field-narrowing justification re-led** (rationale §6.1, spec §7, Guide 2 §1): the "another thread" rationale is incoherent under the serial-domain model (v0.131); the operative reasons are unseen writers — method calls, aliases, closures, re-entrancy, and continuation interleaving at `await` — with FFI threads as the residual concurrent case.
- **Rationale §5.1** gains a supersession note (data races closed by the domain model §12.5/§12.6; the discharge error superseded by the affine model).
- **Both guides re-pinned** to the current revision (#1318), with the standing rule below.

#### New rationale body sections

- **§3.3 The value-position conditional is value-first** — records the owner ruling on #1373: the Python-style `a if c else b` is kept deliberately; the prefix `if c then a else b end` expression form and C's `?:` are recorded as considered-and-declined; the statement/expression word-order asymmetry is the accepted cost.
- **§3.4 Compound assignment is spelled `+=`, not `+:=`** — records the deliberate C-family seam in the Pascal-family operator set (#1343 recording half), with `+:=` and no-compound-assignment as considered-and-declined.
- **§5.23 The affine model** — hoists the v0.150–v0.152 why-affine reasoning from this changelog (which is "not part of the language definition") into the rationale body (#1330).

#### Mechanical defect sweep (#1361)
