### v0.267 changelog (v0.266 → v0.267)

**One graduation: proposal [0114](proposals/0114-lifted-operators-rejected.md), accepted by the owner on 2026-08-20 — arithmetic, bitwise, shift and relational operators no longer lift over nullable value types.** This is the **first retirement of a shipped operator behaviour** in the register's history, and it is the one change in this batch that removes rather than adds. The evidence is recorded separately and in full at [`docs/research/2026-08-20-null-lifting-investigation.md`](research/2026-08-20-null-lifting-investigation.md); this entry records the decision, the declined alternatives, and what moves.

- **The rule (§7.11).** `a + b`, `a & b`, `a << b`, `a < b` and their unary, compound-assignment (§6.6) and `++`/`--` (§17.6) forms are **compile errors** when an operand's static type is a nullable value type. The diagnostic names the remedies the language already has: unwrap with `!` or `??`, or narrow under §7.4. **§8.4's null-safe equality is retained**, and so are the marked propagating forms — `??`, `?.`, `?(args)`, `??=`. §7.11's existing rejection of `and`/`or`/`not` over `bool?` stops being an unexplained exception and becomes the section's general rule, stated once.
- **Why, in one line each.** The defence everyone gave for propagation — that §7.4 quarantines the null — **is false**: it holds for every numeric exit, but the null escapes into `bool` through two total exits needing no narrowing, because **relational lifting yields `bool`, not `bool?`**, and §8.4 equality is total. Composed, `if (flags & ADMIN) <> 0` is **true** when `flags: uint?` is null — a fail-open authorization test. The spec also contradicted itself twice: §7.11's *Safety* paragraph claimed *"Lifting never silently produces a non-nullable value from nullable operands"*, refuted by its own *Relational* paragraph twenty lines above; and §18.5 held that a null participant in ordering *"has no defensible result"* — which is why §4.6 makes `string? < string?` an error — while §7.11 said the defensible result is `false`. **Both sentences are now true.**
- **What the cross-language evidence actually established.** Eight of eight languages that enforce nullability by **flow analysis** reject lifted arithmetic and lifted ordering; the only lifters are SQL, C#, VB.NET, and F#'s LINQ corner. The predictor is **not** designed-in versus retrofitted — TypeScript retrofitted and still rejects — it is **mechanism**: flow analysis rejects, a runtime value wrapper lifts. Bezel has C#'s representation but not C#'s excuse. Three findings carried the decision: **C#'s own designers declined to repeat it** for C# 8's nullable reference types (*"just propagates nulls"*, and it would *"flag the problem 'at the end' rather than on the first undesired null"* — the sticky accumulator, named by them as a reason not to lift); **Swift shipped lifted ordering and removed it in a breaking release** (SE-0121), with semantics strictly better than Bezel's, so the evidence applies a fortiori; and **Bezel's `<` was worse than SQL's**, because SQL's three-valued logic keeps `NOT (x < 5)` unknown while Bezel's two-valued collapse made `not (x < y)` definitely **true**.
- **The principle the ruling actually enforces**, which is narrower than "propagation is wrong" and is the reason the marked forms survive: **every propagating construct in Bezel already carries `?` in its spelling** — `?.`, `?(`, `??`, `??=`. Lifted `+` and lifted `<` were the **sole unmarked exceptions**. Rejecting them makes the language's own convention exceptionless.
- **The pattern-position companion (§19.3, §16.6), and it is a gain rather than a cost.** Relational and range patterns over a nullable scrutinee rode §7.11's lifting, so they are ruled here too: they **reject**, rather than silently never matching. The decisive argument is internal — §16.6 already claims range patterns *"agree exactly with `in`"*, which was **false at v0.266**, since `n in 1..5` over an `int?` is a compile error (§17.5, stdlib §9.8's non-nullable `T`) while `case n of 1..5` silently never matched. The claim is now true. This costs **no implementation change**: nullable relational and range patterns lower on a path separate from the operator's lift, and the rule they implement was stated in **no normative document** — so the revision writes down a rule the compiler already enforced silently.
- **Three alternatives declined with reasons, all recorded in `DECLINED.md`.** *(a) A runtime fault* — the owner's own first alternative — is **incoherent**, and not for cost: it needs no new exception type. A faulting lifted operation can never *yield* null, so its result type is `T`, which makes it this ruling with the diagnosis moved from compile time to production; it also contradicts Appendix C.1, §7.8's explicit-postfix-`!` design (it is an unspelled `a! + b!`), and the posture §5.4 and §6.5 both take of using static rejection wherever available. *(b) Rejecting only compound assignment* contradicts a recorded decision — rationale §11.6 (v0.254): *"Rejecting sugar whose normative expansion is legal would carve §6.6's equivalence for no semantic gain"* — and its premise fails anyway, since `total := total + p;` reproduces the trap it was meant to close. *(c) F#-style marked lifting operators* (`?+?`, `?<?`) fit Bezel's own `?`-marking convention and are declined on surface cost, with a stated reopening bar rather than dismissal. Two further rows record *retaining relational lifting alone* — the position one investigation lane argued and lost — and the **closure of §7.11's user-defined-operator deferral as a decline**, deferral being incoherent once nothing lifts.
- **The rationale is written, which was half the defect.** `Bezel_Design_Rationale.md` had **zero** coverage of this area — §7.11 stated the rule and nothing recorded why. New **rationale §6.4** carries the decision, the alternatives, and the unmarked-propagation principle.
- **§6.6's reconciliation is visible, not silent.** v0.265 ruled #2158 by typing nullable compound assignment on the underlying types, which made `byte? += 1` well-typed; this revision rejects it. The §6.6 text says so and cites both revisions, so a reader who finds the v0.265 entry does not conclude the documents changed their mind without saying so. That ruling is not withdrawn — it remains correct about *typing*, and the incoherence it fixed (`int? += 1` accepted, `byte? += 1` rejected, for a reason unrelated to nullability) is exactly the symptom that led here.

**Kernel classification (the v0.198 obligation): no contact.** No rule of §28 or §30.5 is touched. §28.8.1's throwability set **cannot grow by deleting forms**, and the spec now states that rather than leaving it to be re-derived. The register stands at eleven axioms and four tombstones, as at v0.266.

**Body-locality classification (0105 §1): local.** The rejection is decided from the operands' own static types at the operator. The generic carve-out is **empty**: §25.2 resolves `a + b` on a type parameter only through static-interface constraints, §7.10 gives nullable value types no type-bound constraint, and §7.11's keying is pre-substitution — so lifted arithmetic in a generic body was **already** a compile error at declaration, and no per-instantiation clause is added.

**Migration.**

- **Newly rejected.** Every lifted arithmetic, bitwise, shift and relational operation over a nullable value type, in every spelling — binary, unary, compound-assignment, `++`/`--` — plus relational and range **patterns** over a nullable scrutinee. The remedies are the existing ones (`!`, `??`, §7.4 narrowing) and the diagnostic names them.
- **Newly accepted: nothing.** This revision only removes.
- **Migration cost, counted rather than estimated: zero across every artifact that is not the compiler's own test suite.** Zero sites in the spec's examples (§7.11 carries no code block; §6.6's has no nullable targets), zero in the stdlib, zero in all six guides, and zero in all 571 conformance cases. Twelve corpus files declare a nullable value type; none performs a lifted operation on one. **This is the last revision at which the change is free** — Bezel has no external users, and the only migration is to the project's own artifacts.
- **One idiom is genuinely worse, and is named rather than buried:** an `invariant` over a **mutable** nullable field, where §7.4's narrowing (locals and `readonly` fields only) is unavailable. Two remedies are verified and behaviour-preserving: the short-circuit form `invariant(_port <> null and _port! >= 0 and _port! <= 65535)`, total because §17.2 makes `and` short-circuit — the shape §22.16's own `requires(x <> null and x.Count > 0)` example already uses — or declaring the field `readonly`. Zero instances exist in the documents or the corpus. Deliberately-propagating accumulation also goes from one line to four; that is by design in every language surveyed.
- **Unchanged:** §8.4's equality, `??`, `?.`, `?(args)`, `??=`, every ownership rule, every kernel rule, and every stdlib signature — this revision adds no member, removes none, and changes none.
- **Guides:** untouched, all six keeping their pins (01 v0.259, 02 v0.259, 03 v0.250, 04 v0.261, 05 v0.265, 06 v0.260). **Verified rather than assumed:** the only nullable-value binding across all six is Guide 02's `?.` (never an operand), and Guide 05 already teaches `best = null or s.Score > best!.Score` — the post-ruling idiom.
- **Doc-only:** `DECLINED.md`'s six new rows and recomputed size line (**187 → 193**: 89 `rejected` · 56 `deferred` · 30 `declined-at-proposal` · 6 `non-goal` · **12** `retired` · 0). The `retired` count moves for the first time since the register was published.
- **Conformance corpus:** no case is added, edited, or invalidated.
- **Spec-ahead-of-impl:** one delta, tracked as [#3298](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3298) — the rejection itself. The compiler lifts today; the fix **widens a gate that already exists**, since `ExprTypecheck_Exprs.cpp:4443–4482` already rejects lifting for **user-defined** operators with the diagnostic *"unwrap the operand(s) with `!` or `??`"*, and the sema site already computes whether every nullable operand is proved present. Codegen is a net deletion. Roughly 18 lit acceptance files and a bounded set of gtest blocks move.
- **Bookkeeping:** proposal 0114 carries `graduated-v0.267` in its Status row; its README cell moves to **Graduated**.

### v0.268 changelog (v0.267 → v0.268)

**Three graduations, accepted by the owner on 2026-08-20 and landed as one slate:** proposal [0107](proposals/0107-record-invariants.md) (constructor-only records), proposal [0112](proposals/0112-terminal-accessor-warning-widening.md) (the terminal-accessor warning predicate, widened), and proposal [0113](proposals/0113-exception-tostring.md) (`Exception.ToString()`). They are independent designs sharing a revision, so each is recorded on its own terms below and the composition gate ran over the union.

- **0107 — constructor-only records (§9.9, new).** One §3.6 derived type property is minted: a record is **constructor-only** when it declares a constructor carrying a `requires` **or `ensures`** clause. Two consequences — the record is **not defaultable**, and **`with` is rejected** on it — plus a §9.3 declaration rule making positional fields beside a clause-bearing constructor a compile error, on the verified symmetry that a class primary constructor admits no clause either. §3.6's table stands at **twelve** rows.
- **Why this design and not the instrumented invariant, which is what 0107 was.** The original design failed **three independent adversarial rounds**, each finding a new admitted forge or reopening a closed one, and was withdrawn from v0.264 rather than landed on an argument that had not held. The redesign closes the same fabrication hole by quantifying over **producers** — a set §9.8 enumerates itself — rather than over stores, so all five recorded forges plus a sixth found during the redesign (**F4**: a `static readonly` class-typed singleton with a settable auto-property falsifies a record invariant with *no mutable static anywhere*) fail to land **structurally**: there is no runtime predicate for a forge to falsify. A **ninth** fabrication route, §22.5's default-value form, was found in the process and closed free. F4's corollary is recorded rather than buried: **the class-invariant rule has the same frame defect today**, surviving only because re-entry checking converts a missed violation into a spurious `ContractViolationException`.
- **Two things 0107's own text did not have, found while authoring the edits.** The proposal claimed the change was **spec-only**; it is not. stdlib §4.14 does not key on §17.11 — it *paraphrases* defaultability field-by-field (*"records with default-able fields do"*), and a constructor-only record has default-able fields and no default, so that sentence went **false** at the landing. It now cites §17.11 and names the exclusion. And §9.4's receiver-store diagnostic directs the author to *"return the updated value, built with `with` (§9.5)"* — a remedy this ruling **rejects for exactly the records that hit that rule**. Both are repaired here; neither was named in the proposal.
- **The predicate is spelled byte-identically in exactly six places**, every other consumer keying on the property name alone, with a sweep for near-miss variants returning zero. That discipline is not decoration: a predicate restated in slightly different words across sections is precisely how the first 0107 died, and this design states it more times than that one did.
- **0112 — the terminal-accessor warning, widened (§29.11, §29.2, stdlib §5).** v0.243's provenance warning covered only *minting* iterators; it now covers **adopt-then-yield** — an iterator that adopts a value and yields it, whose elements die on advance identically under §29.2's dispose-on-advance rule. v0.266 landed the **term** half of this as a clarification; the predicate widening needed a proposal and is what lands here.
- **The widened predicate is not zero-false-positive, and the proposal said it was.** *Adopt, yield, then transfer out* — `yield return d; sink.Add(move d);` — leaves an element that is **dead** at an abandoning accessor (`First`, `FirstOrNull`, `ElementAt`) and **live** at an exhausting one (`Last`, `Single`, `Min()`, `Max()`). No refinement fixes it: excluding transferred-out bindings would silence the `First` case, where the fault is **certain**. So §29.11 now carries an explicit **over-approximation** clause beside its under-approximation list — **the first time that section admits an over-warn**. Suppressing it would have made §29.11 assert something false, which is the worse trade.
- **Two narrowings the authoring pass forced on 0112's design.** D1's *"quote §29.4's list verbatim"* imports a false positive: §28.10 admits a `using var` initialized from a **borrow**, which owns nothing, so `using var d := docs[i]; yield return d;` is sound and would have been warned — every edit now carries the ownership qualifier and an explicit exclusion. And D3(b)'s **type-keyed** propagation over-warns, conflating a *grouping* with an *element of a sequence-of-sequences* at `IEnumerable<T>`; propagation is keyed on the **`GroupBy` operator** instead, which is what D3's own body-locality claim says it reads. Also corrected: 0112 §1's motivating contrast does not hold against v0.267 text — both spellings are adopting and both are silent today — so the *newly warned* line names the plain-owned-local spelling explicitly.
- **0113 — `Exception.ToString()` (§31.4, §32.8, §33.3).** §31.4 promised a rendering that **no declared member delivered**; v0.266 recorded the gap honestly, and this revision closes it. `Exception` gains a declared `override method ToString(): string`, the two promise sentences stop making independent *content* claims, and §32.8/§33.3 each gain one clause stating that report content is the enumerated list rather than a call to `ToString()`. §22.13 is deliberately untouched, defining itself as *"the same content §33.3 prints"*.
- **One site was mis-briefed and the lane declined it with reasons, correctly.** `Exception` is **not declared in the stdlib at all** — stdlib §2.17 states that the hierarchy *"is normative in the language spec … this document does not repeat it"* — so a mirroring line there would have stated the rendering promise **twice in two documents**, which is the defect this train closes. No stdlib edit.
- **The member is unmarked, and the proposal's reason for that was wrong.** Its allocation argument fails (§22.15 admits string composition) and its calls-to-pure-members argument is weakened by §22.15's own *Intrinsic purity* paragraph. The decisive reason is **dispatch**: §22.15 rules 1+3 propagate a `pure` override down the chain, so marking it would newly **reject** every derived exception type's existing override, including shipped corpus code. Same verdict, sound reason — an absent contract is recoverable, a false one is not. Two further corrections: the §2.8.6 delta is **widening**, not `identical` (§2.8.6's own member-added row), and *"the full diagnostic chain survives into `ToString()`"* would have over-promised entry stack traces.

**Kernel classification (the v0.198 obligation): no contact, all three trains.** No rule of §28 or §30.5 is touched. The register stands at **eleven axioms and four tombstones**, as at v0.267.

**Body-locality classification (0105 §1).** 0107: **local** — the trigger is read from the record's own declaration. 0113: **local**. 0112: **fact-discharged**, naming a tri-valued yield-ownership valuation; the category is unchanged from v0.243, which predated 0105's checklist line and never stated one, and lifting the cross-module bound would require that value **carried** as a §2.8.2 fact.

**Migration.**

- **Newly rejected (0107).** `default(T)` and `with` on a constructor-only record; positional fields beside a clause-bearing constructor; and — closing the tenth fabrication route, found while authoring — a `serialized optional` component (or choice payload field) whose type is **not defaultable** (§9.8, Appendix C.8), which reaches **every** non-defaultable component type, not only constructor-only records.
- **Newly defined (0107).** §9.8's deserialization construction step: a selected constructor's `requires` or `ensures` evaluating `false` raises `SerializationException`, the `ContractViolationException` carried in its `CauseChain` — the input is data, not a caller's broken promise. **Reclassification is zero**, re-verified four independent ways: the stdlib declares no contract clauses at all, the spec's only sites are §22.16's `Account` **class**, Guide 6's clause is on a free method, and all corpus files carrying clauses were read individually.
- **Newly warned (0112).** Adopt-then-yield iterators at a class-element terminal accessor, including the plain-owned-local spelling. One shape is **over-warned** and the text says so.
- **Newly defined (0113).** `Exception.ToString()`, and what a conforming implementation must emit.
- **Guides: both re-traced pins were earned, not asserted.** **Guide 05 v0.265 → v0.268** and **Guide 02 v0.259 → v0.268** — nine revisions in the latter case. Both authoring lanes had moved their pins while stating the re-trace was **not** performed; both were reverted and the work done. The other four keep their pins (01 v0.259, 03 v0.250, 04 v0.261, 06 v0.260).
- **A v0.266 miss, recorded rather than silently repaired.** That entry states *"nothing in this revision touches what [Guide 5] teaches"* while landing #3286, which rewrites exactly its line 64 — the guide taught that `OwningArray<T>` has no copy-forms, so a reader was told `pool.ToArray()` does not exist. It does, on every owning collection, it is sound as a borrowing snapshot, and **its lifetime hazard was unnamed anywhere in the guide**. The changelog is pinned history and is not edited retroactively; the correction is recorded here, at the revision that made it. This is the **third** instance of one class — a changelog asserting something about text nobody re-checked — after the two the v0.266 and v0.267 composition gates caught.
- **Guide 02 carried a second staleness the pin move surfaced:** §3 taught the `Result` combinators without v0.265's eager-fallback ruling, while §1 primes the reader to expect the opposite. `.UnwrapOr($"bad port: {raw}")` builds that string on the `Ok` path too, and the guide now says so.
- **Doc-only:** `DECLINED.md` **193 → 207** rows (89 `rejected` · 58 `deferred` · **42** `declined-at-proposal` · 6 `non-goal` · 12 `retired` · 0). The `declined-at-proposal` count moves most, because a graduation records what its proposal declined and not only what it landed.
- **Spec-ahead-of-impl:** two trackers, covering all three trains. **[#3301](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3301)** — 0107's whole surface: the §3.6 property and its §2.8.2 carriage, the four compile-time rejections (`default(T)`, `with`, positional-fields-beside-a-clause, and §9.8's non-defaultable `serialized optional`), and §9.8's new `SerializationException`-with-`CauseChain` fault route. **[#3302](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3302)** — 0112's widened predicate (with the three-valued diagnostic, the borrow-initialized `using var` that must stay **silent**, the `GroupBy` operator keying, and the over-approximated transfer-out shape that must warn) and 0113's declared member (unmarked, not `pure`; §32.8/§33.3 reporting **not** routed through it; sequenced behind `SupersededChain`, unimplemented at HEAD).
- **Guide 01 takes a corrective edit and keeps its pin at v0.259, deliberately.** Its line 374 carried `// warning-free` as a bare code comment on the exact adopt-then-yield spelling for which §29.2 (twice), stdlib §5 and Guide 05 were all amended this revision to add *at the producer* — the only unqualified instance left in the corpus. The annotation is qualified and the consumer-side consequence named. A targeted correction is **not** a re-trace, so the pin does not move: moving it would assert work nobody did, which is the failure this entry calls out two paragraphs above.
- **Conformance corpus:** no case is added, edited, or invalidated.
- **Bookkeeping:** all three proposals carry `graduated-v0.268` and move to the README's Graduated ledger; the index stands at 114 files / 114 rows, live 47 / graduated 67.

**Composition gate: PASS-WITH-FIXES — no design defect, and that distinction is the result.** All three trains survived attack, every cross-train seam constructed either composed cleanly or was silent by a rule the text already stated, and a twenty-route forge hunt against 0107's provenance closure found nothing open. **All four blocking findings were failures in the *record*, not in the rules** — which is the class this project's mechanical gates cannot see, and the third consecutive revision where that is where the gate earned its keep.

*(1)* The revision **filed no spec-ahead-of-impl trackers at all**, while landing four new compile-time rejections, a widened must-warn predicate, a new declared member and a new runtime fault route — an omission of process §5 item 3, now closed by [#3301](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3301) and [#3302](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3302). *(2)* §29.11's new *"exhaustive list of what stays silent"* was **false**: it omitted the largest silent class, a same-unit iterator none of whose yields is enumerator-owned — the plain filter-and-project shape — which is in none of its seven items, and which §29.2's own new three-valued summary gives a value with no home in §29.11. The predicate was correct; the exhaustiveness assertion was not, and the assertion was new at v0.268. *(3)* Guide 01's bare `// warning-free`, addressed above. *(4)* **Two §9.8 rules landed entirely unrecorded**, one of them a newly-rejected program shape whose reach is **wider than 0107's population** — a `serialized optional` component of any non-defaultable type, constructor-only record or not — plus a new `SerializationException` route that §22.16 would otherwise have answered differently.

**Verified clean, and worth recording as evidence rather than assumed:** the 0107 predicate is byte-identical in **exactly six** sites with a near-miss sweep returning zero; `DECLINED.md`'s 207 rows re-derive as 89·58·42·6·12·0 under an escaped-pipe-safe parser; §3.6 carries twelve rows; the axiom register is untouched at eleven and four; the four headers agree at v0.268; and the v0.267 **TABLE** check was proven to bite this revision's *new* `DECLINED.md` rows by fault injection rather than by passing quietly. **Attacks that found nothing** are recorded too: the 0107 × 0112 seam (a record element type is a hard stop in both sections), the Appendix C collision (four different bullets in four different subsections), the §31.2 supersession seam on 0113's new `CauseChain` route (an ordinary catch is not supersession), and 0113's conformance re-derivation (`Object.ToString` is virtual-not-pure; trivial-dispose keys on destructors and `owned` fields, never member count; no stdlib exception type declares `ToString`).

### v0.269 changelog (v0.268 → v0.269)

**An owner-directed audit revision. No rule changes; two sweeps of the *record*.** The spec's every code example was audited for correctness-in-context, and the decline index was completed. Both were prompted by a single defect — §30.1's async example calling `HttpClient`, a type the standard library does not declare (#3306) — and the owner's judgement that it was unlikely to be alone. It was not.

- **The example sweep: eleven lanes, all 330 Bezel code blocks in the specification.** Roughly 68 findings, 10 severe. **57 example corrections land here; 6 findings are routed to issues** because closing them would state a rule the spec does not state, which CLAUDE.md rule 1 forbids doing silently. 20 are recorded as considered-and-dropped rather than silently discarded.
- **The check that found them is not "does it parse".** §30.1's example is syntactically perfect; its defect is that it names an API that does not exist. Each lane asked four questions of every block: does every named type and member exist (rule 2, verified against the standard library); is it well-formed at v0.268; does it obey the ownership rules it is *not* about; and — the one that found the most — **does it support the claim the surrounding prose makes about it**.
- **The dominant defect class is a name that does not exist.** `new Stream()` at **11 sites** (`Stream` is `public abstract class Stream`, stdlib §7.1 — none of them can build); `HttpClient` at 2; `Stream.Clone()`; `EventHandler`; `IComparer<in T>`, a contravariant interface the library deliberately does not provide; `FrozenArray<Priority>` named without the import that resolves it. All are corrected.
- **The `Stream` fix is a rewrite, not a disclaimer, and the distinction is the reasoning.** A disclaimer is sanctioned for a name the library *lacks* — §28.12 and §30.7 each carry one for the deferred `System.Net` module. `Stream` is a name the library **owns** and the same sections use correctly as a *type*. So declared types stay `Stream` and only **constructions** become `new FileStream(...)`; `new` stays `new`, because §28.8.1's non-throwable-`new` paragraph reasons about that construction.
- **`HttpClient` took three edits, not two.** Both sites are the same body, copied — §30.1 and §30.6 — so a fix covering one would have left the defect standing at the other. And §30.1's *prose* names `DownloadAsync` and `client.GetAsync(url)`, so fixing the fences alone would have left the surrounding text citing a call that no longer exists.
- **The second class: constructs a past revision retired, surviving in examples.** `readonly` on an expression-bodied property — a **compile error** since **v0.214**, whose changelog records stripping "the stdlib's thirteen decorative uses" — survived 54 revisions in the wrapper-class pattern §32.10 and §32.13 both point readers at. §27.1's `EventHandler` is a survivor of the v0.85 rewrite that retired the identical shape; `grep` finds it exactly twice in the corpus, here and in the changelog entry that retired it. Pre-v0.246 marker spellings survived where the marker was *dropped* rather than respelled — including `return new Wrapper(s)` on an `owned` parameter, which teaches the silent consume K3.13 forbids.
- **The third class was not on the sweep's list, and two lanes found it independently: a valid example the prose over-claims about.** §17.13's ceremony-exemption bullet says an undiscarded trivial-dispose result warns "neither way" — but §21.9 warns on any expression statement with a non-`()` result, and the fence's own `items.ToArray();` line is one, making the discard non-cosmetic. §28.6's comment forbids "dispose **or drain**" on a borrowed owning collection while §28.6's own subsection fifty lines below says `Drain` is memory-safe and *"Only `Dispose` is restricted"*. §30.7 asserts an example is well-formed on a fact the reader cannot see. This is the class §30.1 belongs to, one level up — and the class no parse-level check can reach.
- **Coverage took two corrections to become real.** The partition enumerated ```` ```bezel ```` fences at column zero and so assigned **8 indented** blocks to no lane; a keyword filter, keyed on tags, then missed untagged ones entirely. Two added lanes swept the **18** blocks known at that point — the 8 indented plus the **10** untagged the first pass surfaced — and the FENCE census written afterwards found **4 more**, for **14 untagged fences** in the corpus. (The 18 is a lane count and the 14 a census count; they are different sets, not a discrepancy.) All 14 proved to be EBNF or schematics — correctly untagged, and now tagged `ebnf` (8) and `text` (6) — but that was luck, not a guarantee, so **every opening fence now carries a tag and `check_docs.sh` gains a FENCE census** that fails on a bare one. The changelog is exempt, being pinned history whose fences are historical quotations.

**The decline index is now a complete register: 207 → 410 rows.** Six lanes swept every home the file names.

- **203 of the 410 rows record decisions taken and written down long ago that the index did not list.** Its opening sentence — the single ground-truth for *where* every recorded decline lives — was not true until this revision.
- **The gap was structural.** The rationale's two **registers** (§17, §18) were swept clean when the index was built. **Everything else never was**: topical rationale sections, spec per-section decision records, the **stdlib** (a home the opening paragraph did not even enumerate, although rows already cited it), and above all the **graduated proposals**, whose decline registers had ~20 of 69 headings cited. Proposal 0042's purity declines were absent despite rationale §9.7 recording four of them.
- **The highest-value single row: axiom A7** — a **live** axiom recording a decline (no `move` in `??`-operand or operator-operand position), gated on one named ruling, indexed nowhere.
- **Two scope rules are recorded in the file so they are not re-argued each sweep.** *Status gates the record*: a decline is indexed when recorded in a graduated proposal, an accepted one, or as a delegated ruling under the owner's standing delegation — the pre-existing *Typed modular arithmetic* row already cited an `accepted` proposal, so this is precedent rather than invention. *A recommendation is not a verdict*: under-review drafts are excluded and the `recommended — awaiting owner ruling` class stays empty, because populating it would add rows that all change on acceptance — churn, not ground truth.
- **Six citation defects in pre-existing rows repaired**, found by the inverse half of the audit: all four axiom tombstones omitted the changelog revision the spec tombstone names as the decision record's home; the serialization-back-edge row cited rationale §5.19 where both its quoted phrases are in §5.22; D-0001's register body cited `proposal 0003 §3.3`, which does not exist (the reasoning is §3 item 3); the move-only-value-types row named only the buffer/span trio where the §28.11 deferral covers both collection families; the generic-leaves row recorded no reopening bar where §19.6 states one; and `README.md` still described the file as holding only its own D-numbers and gap review.

**Kernel classification (the v0.198 obligation): no contact.** No rule of §28 or §30.5 is touched — every §28 edit corrects an example or a comment, never a rule. The register stands at eleven axioms and four tombstones.

**Body-locality classification (0105 §1): vacuous.** The revision adds no compile-time rule.

**Migration.**

- **Newly rejected: nothing. Newly accepted: nothing. Newly defined: nothing.** Every program that compiles at v0.268 compiles at v0.269 with identical meaning. This revision changes what the documents *say about themselves*, not what the language admits.
- **Six findings are routed, not fixed**, and each is a decision rather than a correction: §28.3's uninitialized-`var` adoption, stated only by two worked examples ([#3309](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3309)); §15.4.1's `RingBuffer<T>` protocol, well-formed only at value-typed `T`, where three symptoms point at `ReadOnlySpan<T>`'s class-`T` case being an unclosed seam ([#3310](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3310)); Appendix A.7's `MoveExpr` taxonomy, which read literally rejects `return move _f;` — the one spelling §28.8 calls mandatory ([#3311](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3311)); and three smaller ambiguities in §22.8, §17.5 and §32 ([#3312](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3312)).
- **Two normative texts were repaired, and are itemized here because "no rule changes" must mean it.** Appendix A.3's `PolyCase ::= StringLiteral ":" TypeName` cited a nonterminal that appears nowhere in Appendix A; it now reads `QualifiedName`, and the adjacent comment, which still said *"each TypeName must name a type…"*, was brought with it. One consequence is worth stating rather than leaving to be discovered: `QualifiedName ::= Identifier ("." Identifier)*` admits no `GenericArgs`, so a polymorphic registry cannot name a generic instantiation. §9.8 states no rule either way; this is the grammar's answer, not a new restriction. And §9.2's admission list for a body record's members read *"methods, expression-bodied properties, additional constructors, and operator overloads"* while its own example declares two auto-properties, and *"additional"* is meaningless where there is no primary constructor; it now reads *"auto-properties, methods, expression-bodied properties, constructors, and operator overloads"*. Neither repair changes what any program means.
- **The standard the sweep applied to example fragments, stated once.** A fenced block is a *fragment* unless it is a whole compilation unit: it need not declare the names it uses, and the sweep did not add declarations for them. What it did add — and what a fragment does owe the reader — is an `import` comment wherever a name resolves only through one, since that is the difference between a name that exists and a name that does not (§26.1's `ToArray` gained `import System.Collections.Linq;`, §10.4's `FrozenArray` likewise). Undeclared `items` in §17.13 and `path` in §28.3 are therefore correct as they stand, not oversights.
- **Guides:** untouched. **Guide 02 and Guide 05 keep the v0.268 pins they earned**; 01, 03, 04 and 06 keep theirs (v0.259, v0.250, v0.261, v0.260). The new PIN check now prints their staleness on every run — Guide 03 is **19 revisions** behind — which is a finding this revision surfaces rather than fixes.
- **Tooling:** `check_docs.sh` gains **PIN** (derived-document staleness, failing past three revisions for the code-generation reference and reporting for the guides) and **FENCE** (every opening code fence carries a language tag). `check_proposals.sh` gained **TABLE** at v0.267. The code-generation reference is re-pinned to v0.269 and had three defects of its own corrected — two of them inherited verbatim from the spec examples this sweep was auditing, which is the derived-document drift risk arriving within a day of the document being written.
- **Doc-only:** `DECLINED.md` **207 → 410** rows (the 235 and 208 figures quoted during this work were unlanded mid-branch states of this same sweep) (170 `rejected` · 104 `deferred` · 109 `declined-at-proposal` · 7 `non-goal` · 20 `retired` · 0). The v0.268 entry's figure of 207 is correct as of that landing; these rows postdate it.
- **Conformance corpus: 44 cases invalidated — the one figure in this entry that a later measurement contradicted.** This line originally read *"no case is added, edited, or invalidated"*, carried over from the five preceding entries, and it is wrong: a revision that edits 57 fenced examples necessarily invalidates the cases extracted from them. Measured content-addressed (case ids are positional and a regeneration renumbers, so comparing by id compares different blocks): of the 571 committed case bodies, **34** had already vanished from the docs at v0.268 and **78** have at v0.269 — this revision accounts for the 44-case difference. A further 174 extracted bodies have no case at all, 82 of them from the code-generation reference, which the corpus does not cover (it is derived, not normative) though `extract_doc_examples.py` now reads it. **No regeneration is attempted here**: the corpus was last regenerated at v0.247 and its catch-up is already tracked ([#3262](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3262), [#3297](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3297)); regenerating needs a `bezelc` to classify against, which the docs lane does not build. Recorded here so the debt is stated rather than implied by a boilerplate line that says the opposite.

### v0.270 changelog (v0.269 → v0.270)

**The ruling revision — six of the v0.269 sweep's seven routed findings are decided, and four of them were not the question that was filed.** Each was researched by an independent lane against the spec, the stdlib, the rationale's records, the changelog's history, and the compiler's source; each ruling below states the alternatives and why the losing one lost. **Four of the seven issues turned out to rest on a false premise** — which is the argument for gating a ruling behind evidence rather than closing it on the framing it arrived in.

**§22.8/§23.1's `readonly` assignable context is per-instance, not per-type (#3299 — a soundness fix).** #3299 asked whether the positional wording (*"in a field initializer or in a constructor body"*) was deliberate. It was not a silence: **§9.9, landed at v0.268, states the per-type reading as fact** in a parenthetical inside a *record* section that no reader of §22.8 will find — *"§22.8's and §23.1's `readonly` assignable context is a constructor body, **not an instance**"*. So the question was not what to fill in but whether to overturn.

- **Per-type is unsound against §7.4.** §7.4 licenses narrowing on a `readonly` field by asserting that outside its construction window the field has *"no writer on any path, **through any alias**, so **no call** … can invalidate a fact"*. Under per-type a call **can** reach a writer: a constructor of `C` writing a *different* `C`'s field. §7.4's invalidation list is explicitly closed (*"beyond the forms above, nothing invalidates a local's narrowing"*) and a plain borrow argument is not on it, so `if c._f <> null then … new C(c) … c._f.Length` reads null under a non-null narrowing. The same shape works from a `this`-rooted fact, which §7.4 names first.
- **Two neighbours already assume per-instance.** §22.15's pure-constructor birth-store rule is stated `this`-rooted, justified by *"unreachable from any other holder"* — false cross-instance; and §9.4 justifies the constructor carve-out by *"the value under construction"*.
- **Blast radius: zero.** Three independent sweeps of `docs/`, `tests/`, fenced blocks and test string literals found **no** shape the restriction rejects. The only occurrence in the tree is the attack itself, in proposal 0107's Revision record, annotated as a forge.
- **Alternative declined:** keep per-type and make it explicit. It costs a §7.4 soundness hole to buy a capability nothing uses. **Recorded caveat:** per-type was never *decided* — 0107 §13.3 identified it as **forge B**, an attack that helped kill that proposal's first design. §9.9's parenthetical described the then-current reading in a disclaimer; it is repaired, not reversed.

**An uninitialized local adopts the ownership state of its first assignment (#3309).** §28.3 stated adoption for exactly one case — the polymorphic null state — while its two normative worked Patterns depended on the general rule, which no clause stated.

- **The two Patterns are jointly decisive, not merely suggestive.** Both declare `var x: Stream;` — *the same form and the same type* — and end in **opposite** states: Pattern 1 borrowed, Pattern 2 owned. No property of the declaration can fix the state; only the assignment can. Any non-adoption rule makes one of the two normative examples wrong.
- **The gap had a structural cause, and stating it is the fix.** §28.3's state-match rule derives from **K1.7 + K3.11** — one-holder and drop-on-overwrite — both about a *displaced* value. An uninitialized LHS displaces nothing, so the paragraph's own derivation is contentless there. Adoption is now stated once over the two **valueless** LHS states, as a two-member enumeration whose shared predicate is only what both members share, with the *"first non-null"* qualifier attached to the polymorphic-null member alone.
- **The issue's third question rested on a misreading, corrected here.** *"The patterns imply equalize-to-borrowed"* is wrong: Pattern 1 equalizes to borrowed, Pattern 2 to **owned**, and **the program** equalizes — K7.3 rejects a mismatched join and never equalizes. The genuinely unruled join is **uninitialized ⊓ classified**, whose answer follows from §7.9 (unreadable after the join) plus K3.14 (per-path disposal), the machinery K7.4 already names.
- **Kernel classification: derivation** (K1.7 + K3.11 for the adoption clause; K3.14 + K7.4 for the join). **The axiom register is untouched at eleven axioms and four tombstones.**

**Appendix A.7's `MoveExpr` taxonomy is restated by what the operand denotes (#3311) — and the issue's sharp end was wrong.** #3311 argued that read literally the grammar rejects `return move _f;`, *"the one spelling §28.8 calls mandatory"*. It is not mandatory: **a terminal move is rejected at every return type, `owned` included** — §28.8.1 admits *"no terminal-move dispensation"*, the return edge being itself an unrestored exit, and v0.223 (#1814) declined sanctioning it as unsound (double-free). Grammar and rule agree; there was no contradiction there.

- **The spelling actually broken is `var old := move _resource;`** — the RHS-root bare-field take the spec prints a dozen times and a test pins as a clean compile. It matches no written form and fails form (c)'s naming condition. The taxonomy now classifies operands by what they **denote** (owned field / owning slot / named binding) with the shapes as illustrations, which closes the `!` gap and the bare-field gap together.
- **A regression, not a decision:** the taxonomy was sound before v0.246, whose transfer-marker unification added form (c) plus *"Any other operand is a compile error"*, giving bare identifiers a second and narrower home. Proposal 0090 recorded (a)/(b) as *"unchanged"*.
- **A live user-facing defect rides along.** §28.6 bullet 2 still carried pre-#1814 wording — ownership reaches the caller *"only as `return move _f;` through an `owned` return type"* — and `src/ownership/Ownership.cpp:8494` **quotes it in a diagnostic**, instructing users to write the spelling the compiler rejects two checks later. #1814 fixed §28.6's example and not its bullet. The bullet is corrected; the diagnostic is filed as a compiler-lane issue.

**Field initializers may read statics of any type, not only of any class (#3312.1).** §22.8 said *"static members of any **class**"* while its own neighbouring example reads `DateTime.Now`, and `DateTime` is a **record**. The escape hatch is closed: the stdlib states `Now` is *"computed at each access"* and not a constant, so the example reaches the rule through exactly the item that excludes it.

- **Original drafting, never a ruling** — the sentence and the example are both unchanged since the earliest revision in git history, where `DateTime` was already a record. One occurrence in the entire document set; no changelog entry; fifteen revisions unremarked.
- **No soundness argument exists for the narrow reading.** §22.13's initialization order is stated over *"distinct types"*, enum statics are specified to follow *"the same rules as class static fields"*, and §22.12 keys on a static's declared type, never its declaring kind. The prohibition §22.8 actually enforces is *"must not observe `this`"*, which no static of any kind can.
- **A survey of 3,152 field and auto-property initializers across `docs/`, `tests/` and `src/`** found fourteen reading class statics and **eight reading statics of non-class kinds** — one record, six enum, one choice — not one of them pinned as a §22.8 rejection. The compiler enforces only the negative list; no positive-list check exists anywhere.
- **Alternative declined:** keep *"class"* and fix the example. It would make the spec contradict **itself** — §22.5 blesses `DateTime.Now` **by name** as a default parameter value, so the same expression would be legal in one initializer position and illegal in another with no principle separating them.

**`in` states no nullability rule of its own (#3312.2) — neither of the filed alternatives was right.** §16.6 cited §17.5 for a hard rejection §17.5 never stated. The answer is neither "make it an error" nor "soften the citation": **`x in c` *is* the call `c.Contains(x)`, so the left operand is admitted exactly when it is admissible as that call's argument.**

- **Over a range that rejects unconditionally**, and for §7.11's own reason: `Range<T>.Contains` takes a non-nullable `T`, `T?` does not implicitly convert, and range membership is an **ordering** test, which admits no absent participant. §16.6's parity claim is now true, scoped to ranges, and cites the authority that actually carries it.
- **A blanket rule would have been false and would have contradicted v0.267's own D2.** `Array<int?>.Contains(item: int?)` and the span forms accept nullable arguments deliberately, with a guard test whose comment says it *"guards against a false-reject"*. Under a blanket rule `arr.Contains(n)` would compile and `n in arr` would not, for the same question — a fresh instance of the *"same shape, opposite answers, decided by spelling"* defect proposal 0114 cited as its own motivation. That membership test is §8.4 equality, which v0.267 explicitly **retained**.
- **v0.267's authorities already used the derived rule**, not a blanket one: both the changelog and proposal 0114 justify the rejection as *"§17.5, stdlib §9.8's non-nullable `T`"* — never §17.5 alone. Membership by equality answers a question that has an answer; membership by ordering does not.

**§32's two near-identical names are disambiguated by renaming the one that stated a falsehood (#3312.3), and a live defect is fixed.** The issue reported two sets differing *"exactly by `Ptr`"*. **They are incomparable:** *FFI-pointee scalar* held `Ptr<T>` and no records; the *FFI-pointee set* holds C-compatible records and no `Ptr`. Neither contains the other, so any rename framed as "X minus `Ptr`" would have been wrong.

- **"FFI-pointee scalar" → "FFI-compatible scalar"** (five spec sites, one rationale site). The old name asserted that `Ptr<T>` **is** an FFI pointee — the exact proposition §32.12 denies in order to reject `Ptr<Ptr<U>>`. The replacement is not a coinage but the corpus's existing composition (*"FFI-compatible types"*, *"FFI-compatible function types"*), and it converts a false implied containment into a true one. The gate keeps its name: it is the term the rename protects.
- **The trap had already sprung.** stdlib §4.14's `DangerousPointer` prose used the name *"FFI-pointee scalar"* while enumerating the **other** set's membership, rescued only by re-rejecting `Ptr<U>` three clauses later; and its code-block comment carried the phrase with **no** rescue, which read against the definition admitted `OwningBuffer<Ptr<U>>.DangerousPointer()` — reconstructing the declined `Ptr<Ptr<U>>`. Both now cite §32.12's set directly instead of re-deriving it.
- **Two contrast sentences added** (§32.12 and stdlib §10.5) stating that neither set contains the other, so the `Ptr<Ptr<U>>` rejection is derivable from the names rather than from a restatement. Appendix C.9's inline restatement **stays**: Appendix C's genre is one actionable check per bullet, and it already restates other derivable facts in the same section.

**#3310 is not closed — it is routed to a proposal, which is the honest verdict.** §15.4.1's collection-literal protocol is ill-formed at class-typed `T`, but neither candidate the issue offered was right. The defect is that the borrowing form **names the wrong span family**: `ReadOnlySpan<T>` is the *owning*-family view backed by `OwningBuffer<T>`, which **owns** its class-`T` slots, while `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>` is the borrowing-family view backed by `Array<T>`, which borrows them — stdlib §4.15 states they *"are not interchangeable … because the underlying storage models differ"*. A protocol whose elements are defined as borrows is declared to receive the owning view: not a nullability mismatch but an ownership incoherence. **The compiler already disagrees with the spec** — codegen lowers the borrowing form onto Array-family storage with no element disposer, via the same helper `Array<T>.AsReadOnlySpan()` uses. Restricting the protocol at class `T` is self-defeating, since §28.11 places borrow slots *only* in the class/interface row. Closing it is a source-breaking signature change to a protocol already scheduled for interface promotion (#3247), so it takes §6's proposal path, not a ruling.

**Kernel classification (the v0.198 obligation): derivation only.** #3309's adoption clause derives from K1.7 + K3.11 and its join answer from K3.14 + K7.4; #3311 restates an operand class without changing what the kernel admits; #3299 constrains a store the kernel never licensed. **No axiom is extended and none is added — the register stands at eleven axioms and four tombstones.**

**Body-locality classification (0105 §1): local.** Every rule here is decided from information already in the body being checked — #3299's per-instance context is an lvalue-root test, #3309's adoption reads the assignment in front of it, #3312.2's admission is the ordinary argument check. No new cross-body fact is minted.

**Gate round (adversarial composition gate, same revision).** One pass; verdict **BLOCK** — six blocking findings, all applied before landing, none declined. Two were edits this entry did not describe, which is how they escaped review in the first place; both are now described here.

- **A false rule had been written into the normative grammar.** Appendix A.7's `NewExpr` comment was edited to say the `with` suffix is *"legal when the constructed type is a **defaultable** record"*. §9.5 requires only that the source be **record-typed**, and the `PrimarySuffix` comment a hundred lines above said so correctly. As written the grammar outlawed `new Person("a", 1) with(Age := 2)` — the shape §9.5 blesses by name. Corrected to *record-typed*. This is the sharpest kind of defect this gate exists to catch: a ruling revision inventing a restriction nobody ruled.
- **A placeholder shipped.** A new Appendix C bullet cited *"[§22.x *Object initializer blocks*]"*. `check_docs.sh` passed it because the **anchor** resolves; nothing checks a citation's display text. Now §22.11.
- **#3311 was half-done.** The new A.7 comment cites §28.8.1 as its authority, but §28.8.1's identifier-operand form still read *"`x` a named local binding or `owned` parameter"* — so `move _resource`, the very spelling the ruling exists to legalize and which the spec prints thirteen times, still matched nothing in the prose the grammar points at. §28.8.1 now admits the bare in-scope field spelling, and says which forms carry the restoration obligation.
- **#3299 contradicted itself on statics**, and the contradiction was the one the ruling was about: the clause permits writing a `static readonly` field from a constructor body, then claimed §7.4's no-writer assumption was thereby satisfied — but §7.4 narrows `TypeName._s` too, so a plain `new C()` reaches a writer of a static by exactly the route the ruling rejected for instance fields. The §7.4 claim is now scoped to instance fields and the static case is recorded as **not decided here**.
- **Two figures were wrong.** *"nine reading statics of non-class kinds — one record, six enum, one choice"* sums to eight. And the Migration note claimed *"Newly accepted: nothing"* in a revision that **deletes** §17.5's *"If the left operand is nullable, it must be checked before use"* — see the corrected note below.

**What the gate attacked and could not break**, recorded so the next reader knows what was actually checked: `DECLINED.md`'s 413 rows re-counted by parsing all six tables (the breakdown sums exactly); the axiom register verified as eleven live plus four tombstones; the four version headers confirmed in lockstep; the guides confirmed untouched with pins intact; the conformance corpus confirmed untouched; the #3312.3 rename confirmed complete (zero *"FFI-pointee scalar"* left in spec or rationale, pinned history intact, every *"FFI-pointee set"* site correct); the code-generation reference's terminal-move correction confirmed **true** against §28.8.1; every new §-citation opened and confirmed to say what the citing text claims; and an independent sweep of `tests/` for cross-instance `readonly` writes returned fourteen candidates, all in ordinary methods — confirming #3299's zero blast radius. The gate could not build or run anything, so every claim here about compiler behaviour rests on reading `src/`, not on observing it.

**Migration.**

- **Newly rejected: one shape, which nothing in the corpus writes.** #3299 rejects a write to another instance's `readonly` storage from inside a constructor of the declaring type, and the `ref`/`out` binding that is the same store by other syntax. Three sweeps found zero occurrences outside a withdrawn proposal's attack record.
- **Newly accepted: one shape at the spec level.** §17.5 previously carried *"If the left operand is nullable, it must be checked before use"*; #3312.2 removes it, so `n in arr` over an `Array<int?>` — where the selected `Contains` parameter is itself nullable — is admitted by the text for the first time. This *aligns* the spec with what the stdlib declares and what the call spelling `arr.Contains(n)` already accepted; it is nonetheless an admission the previous text refused, and is recorded as one rather than as a clarification. #3312.1 by contrast widens a *stated* admission set to what the compiler already enforced and the corpus already relied on; no program that failed now compiles on its account.
- **Newly defined:** #3309's adoption rule and its uninitialized-⊓-classified join answer, both of which state obligations already in force rather than adding any.
- **Unchanged in meaning:** #3311 (a taxonomy restatement — the parser enforces no closed operand set and no test pins the shapes), #3312.3 (a rename plus two defect fixes in prose that named one set and enumerated another).
- **Spec-ahead-of-impl:** #3299's four compiler sites are filed as a tracking issue — `ExprTypecheck.cpp`'s `readonly` gate is a bare `if (inConstructor_) return;`, unqualified by declaring type, so today *any* constructor may write *any* `readonly` field of *any* type; the diagnostic it prints is already narrower than the code, and the definite-assignment tracker keys on field name with no receiver test.
- **Guides:** untouched; all six keep their pins. No idiom in any guide changes.
- **Code-generation reference:** re-pinned to v0.270, and **one v0.269 error of mine is corrected**. v0.269 rewrote its terminal-move paragraph to record the question as *"open"* and cite #3311. That was wrong — §28.8.1 had ruled it, and v0.223 had declined the permissive reading. The correct statement was replaced with a hedge on the strength of the issue's framing without checking §28.8.1; it now states the rule and names the revision that made it.
- **Conformance corpus:** no case is added or removed. The corpus remains at its v0.247 regeneration with the drift v0.269 measured (78 stale bodies, 174 uncovered), tracked by #3262 and #3297; this revision's edits are prose and grammar-comment text, and the one stdlib code-block comment it changes is comment-only and cannot flip a classification.

### v0.271 changelog (v0.270 → v0.271)

**The follow-through revision — five findings routed by v0.270 are decided, two of them refuted, and one graduated proposal's stale draft is annotated.** Every finding was researched by an independent lane before any edit was written; two came back saying the reported defect was not real, which is recorded below rather than quietly dropped.

**§22.8 now states the single-assignment rule that three other sections cite (#3315 item 1 — a ruling).** §22.8 stated only *where* a `readonly` field may be assigned, never that it may be assigned at most once. **Three** places cited the missing rule, not the two the issue reported: §7.4 twice (*"§22.8's single-assignment rule"* and *"the field's single assigned value, final by §22.8"*), §21.1, and rationale §6.1. `src/sema/DefiniteAssignment.cpp` says the gap out loud — it derives the rule *from the citations* because the cited section lacks it, which is the inversion this sweep exists to find.

- **The unit is one instance construction, not one constructor** — initializer and every constructor body in the `this(...)` chain counted together — and the bound is **at most** once, not exactly once: §7.9, not §22.8, is what demands that an assignment happen at all. The corpus already answered both parameters, and the ruling adopts what it answered: assignment is tracked **per path**, and an initializer plus a constructor-body store counts as **two**.
- **It is scoped to `readonly` fields, and deliberately does *not* travel to auto-properties.** The first draft of this ruling said it did. The composition gate found why that was wrong: `tests/module/xmod_record_body_ctor_field_store_3207_test.cpp` pins the opposite twice — `readonly property X: int := 100;` followed by `this.X := x;`, asserted to compile **and** to yield the body's value — in blocks named `t3_imported_init_then_ctor_store_overrides_initializer` and `t3b_same_module_…`. That is not incidental to those tests; it is their stated point, established by #3207's fix. So the language today rejects initializer-plus-body for `readonly` **fields** (pinned by `…2187__initializer_then_body_rejected.bzl`) and admits it for `readonly` **auto-properties**, both deliberately. Unifying them is a ruling with its own blast radius, not a consequence of this one, and §22.8 now says so in as many words.
- Appendix C gains the checkable form; the loop over-approximation the compiler already applies is promoted to normative.
- **Blast radius, corrected: nothing newly rejected.** The first draft claimed *"exactly one file"*, counting a lit test whose `:= 5` is incidental. The gate found two further sites in `tests/module/xmod_record_body_ctor_field_store_3207_test.cpp` where the shape is **not** incidental but asserted. Narrowing the rule to fields (above) resolves all three: every one of them declares a `readonly` **auto-property**, which this rule does not reach. The `this(...)`-chain double write has **zero** occurrences anywhere in the tree.

**§22.8's admission list admits choice case construction (#3315 item 2 — a clarification), and v0.270's widening did *not* absorb it.** The lane was asked to confirm or refute that guess and **refuted** it: v0.270 widened the *declaring kind* of a static (class → any type), not the *entity kind*, and a choice case is not a static member — §35.2 enumerates a choice's members after the case list, §35.1 says a choice has no constructors, and §2.4 lists *"enum constant, static member"* as different segment kinds. Enum constants escape through the list's **constants** item because §17.14 admits them; §17.14 admits no choice case in either form. And §35.3 *routes programmers into the gap*: the bare-case reading explicitly does not extend to field initializers, so the qualified form is the only spelling available — and it matched no item in the list.

Three tests pin the under-included shape as **accepted and executing**, one asserting an exit code; the single rejection in the corpus cites §9.7 only, never §22.8. The edit adds case construction **and** one sentence stating that the list enumerates *names, not expression forms* — the same under-inclusion left `B._b + 1` unadmitted, a shape pinned nine times in one test file. **Nothing is newly rejected.**

**Appendix C.1's "relational" is disambiguated (#3315 item 4 — editorial).** Read against §17.1's precedence table, which names level 10 **Relational** and puts `in`, `is`, `is not` and `as` in it, C.1's blanket rejection of a nullable operand at a *"relational"* operator contradicted three passages — §12.7 (which licenses `is not null` as *the* narrowing form), §7.11's own closing paragraph, and §17.5 as v0.270 ruled it. The decisive tell is internal: C.1's qualifier reads *"built-in or user-declared"*, and §25.1 makes `is`/`is not`/`as`/`in` **not** user-declarable — so the qualifier is only coherent under the ordering reading. Nothing was ever mis-ruled, only mis-worded. **The band is deliberately not renamed:** that would touch thirteen sites including three grammar productions and would not even eliminate the two-sense usage, since §17.2 keeps it. §17.2's own spelling — *relational (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`)* — is the house precedent the parenthetical follows.

**§15.4's fresh-producer list gains one parenthetical, and the reported defect was not real (#3315 item 5).** The claimed ownership ambiguity does not exist: the rule is stated **positively** (*"each element expression … must be a borrow"*), which rejects a nested literal whatever the gloss enumerates; §15.4 already calls FCL targets *"User-defined collection types"*; §15.4.1 says the literal's ownership treatment is *"identical to"* a built-in literal's; and §28.3's producers table classifies it Owned. What *is* real is a **reading hazard**, and it has been taken in writing — a compiler comment declines that arm for a difficulty that does not arise for a user target. The parenthetical names the §15.4.1 target inside the arm, changing nothing about what compiles and narrowing #3307's residual.

**Proposal 0114's D5 is annotated as the declined alternative, and a false cost claim is corrected (#3315 item 3).** The issue reported that D5 *"landed inverted"*. It did — but **deliberately**, and the determination matters more than the fact:

- **This was an override, not a mis-transcription.** The graduating commit **itself** added a `DECLINED.md` row declining D5's position by name — *"Relational and range patterns over a nullable scrutinee (retaining the never-matches reading)"*, class `rejected`, reopening bar *"—(none stated)"*. A transcription failure does not author a decline record naming the thing it failed to transcribe. The v0.267 entry states the verdict in a dedicated bullet, rationale §6.4 carries the decline with reasons, and four spec sites plus the code-generation reference agree. **The only missing artifact is the annotation on the draft**: the graduating commit changed the proposal file by exactly one line, its `Status` row.
- **So the light-gate correction runs the other way.** Editing §19.3 back to D5 would contradict two recorded decisions — rationale §6.4 and the `DECLINED.md` row — which spec-change-process §2 makes a **design change** requiring a fresh proposal, not a correction. What is editorial is annotating the stale draft, and that is what lands here. 0114's D5 section now carries a landing note marking it the declined alternative, with both grounds that decided it.
- **The cost claim is false and inherited, in three artifacts.** v0.267 says the pattern companion *"costs no implementation change"*; the commit message and #3298 repeat it. That sentence is **D5 reason 4**, which justified the *opposite* verdict. Verified from source: no `RelOpPattern`/`RangePattern` site in `src/sema/` gates on nullability, and codegen still implements D5's `hasValue AND cmp`. The landed rule needs a new sema rejection, the **deletion** of that lowering, and the conversion of **8** test blocks across **2** files — the second file being one the issue did not know about. #3298 refutes itself: it waives the code change its own acceptance criterion requires.
- **The standing lesson, recorded because it generalizes:** a graduation that inverts a proposal's decision must **re-derive that decision's cost paragraph, not transcribe it**. The verdict was re-argued and the price was carried over unchanged. This is the fourth instance of the class the v0.268 entry named, and the first where the unchecked text describes the *compiler* rather than a document.

**Kernel classification (the v0.198 obligation): no contact.** No rule of §28 or §30.5 is touched. The axiom register stands unchanged at eleven axioms and four tombstones.

**Body-locality classification (0105 §1): local.** §22.8's single-assignment rule is decided from the constructor chain of the type being checked; it mints no cross-body fact.

**Migration.**

- **Newly rejected: one shape, pinned by one test.** A `readonly` auto-property written both by its initializer and by a constructor body. The test that pins it as a clean compile is named in the spec-ahead-of-impl issue rather than edited here — the compiler does not yet enforce onceness for auto-properties (`PropertySymbol` is not a `FieldSymbol`, so the shape never reaches the check), so flipping a test expectation to match a rule nothing enforces would leave a false failure for whoever builds next.
- **Newly accepted: nothing.** #3315 item 2 admits a shape three tests already pin as accepted and executing; it corrects the *text*, not the compiler.
- **Unchanged in meaning:** items 4 and 5 (both editorial), and item 3's proposal annotations, which touch no normative rule.
- **Spec-ahead-of-impl: two deltas, both re-counted after the gate.** (i) §22.8's **cross-constructor** once-ness across a `this(...)` chain: `src/sema/DefiniteAssignment.cpp` states in writing that it does not enforce this (*"the #2206 route B residual, out of scope here"*), so the chain clause is ahead of the implementation even though the single-constructor case is not. The auto-property delta the first draft listed here does not exist, the rule having been narrowed to fields. (ii) v0.267's pattern rule, whose real cost v0.267 did not state.
- **Code-generation reference:** updated and re-pinned to v0.271. It stated neither v0.270's per-instance `readonly` context nor this revision's at-most-once rule, and both are rules a generator can violate. The gate caught the first version of that edit dropping the *instance* qualifier, which made the sentence false for `static readonly` — a different context (bare name or `TypeName.F`) and a different unit (one type initialization). Both are now stated separately.
- **Guides:** re-validated in a separate guide-only pass, which spec-change-process §5 item 5 treats as not-a-revision.
- **Doc-only:** `DECLINED.md` **413 → 415** rows — the two declines this revision records, which §9's checklist binds and the first draft omitted: the §17.1 precedence-band rename (item 4 took the parenthetical instead) and the extension of §22.8's single-assignment rule to `readonly` auto-properties (narrowed out after the gate).
- **Conformance corpus:** no case added or removed; the corpus remains at its v0.247 regeneration with the drift v0.269 measured, tracked by #3262 and #3297.

### v0.272 changelog (v0.271 → v0.272)

**Proposal 0115 graduates: §15.4.1's borrowing form named the *owning* span family, and now names the borrowing one.** Ruled under the owner's 2026-08-21 delegation. Class: **design change → ruling-class landing** (spec-change-process §2, §6).

**The defect.** §15.4.1's collection-literal protocol has two forms. The borrowing form — the one whose elements §15.4.1 itself defines as **borrows** — declared its carrier as `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, which is the **owning** family's view, backed by `OwningBuffer<T>`, which *owns* its class-`T` slots. The borrowing family's view is `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>`, backed by `Array<T>`, which borrows them. The standard library states the two "are not interchangeable … because the underlying storage models differ." So a protocol defined over borrows was declared to receive the owning view: **an ownership incoherence, not a nullability mismatch.** The visible symptom reported at #3310 — a `T?` indexer at class-typed `T`, so `rb.Push(elements[i])` fails to type-check — is one of three the mis-named carrier caused; the others are that `string` elements were unreachable (the owning buffer rejects them) and that the element borrow's source was the dying temporary rather than the original owner.

**D1 — the carrier becomes `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>`.** The one serious objection is that it views a *resizable* collection while a literal has fixed extent. It does not survive the spec's own §15.5 table, which lists `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>` in the **fixed-extent** buffer/span family by name: what is resizable is the `Array<T>` *source*, while the span's `(Start, Length)` are fixed at construction, and at a literal site the backing array is compiler-materialized and named by no binding. Four further properties decided it: a **category-uniform** indexer (`[i: int]: T` for every `T`, which is what dissolves the reported symptom), **zero** new stdlib surface, agreement with the **shipped lowering** — codegen already emits Array-family storage with no element disposer, via the same helper `Array<T>.AsReadOnlySpan()` uses — and admission of every element category the borrowing family admits.

**The provenance, recorded because it explains rather than excuses.** `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>` landed at **v0.107**, four revisions *before* v0.111 chose the owning view by analogy to C#'s `Create<T>(ReadOnlySpan<T>)`. The right carrier existed and was not chosen; the analogy simply does not carry, because C#'s `ReadOnlySpan<T>` does not own its elements and Bezel's does. The rationale now says so at the point where the choice is described, so the next reader meets the correction rather than the analogy.

**D4 — a borrowing-form target is a borrowing-family target for §15.4's fresh-producer rejection, and this is mandatory rather than opportunistic.** §15.4's borrowing-family rule opens with a **closed list of built-ins**; a user type declaring the borrowing form is not on it, and §15.4.1 states no element-ownership rule of its own. Today that hole is unreachable *only because the class-`T` borrowing form does not type-check*. **D1 makes it reachable.** Landing D1 alone would convert an ill-typed program into a **well-typed leak** — strictly worse than the defect being fixed — so D1 does not land without D4. Kernel classification: **derivation** (K1's per-slot classification plus K2.3/K4.3's stored-borrow treatment, through §28.11's existing borrow column); no axiom is added or extended, and the register stands at eleven axioms and four tombstones. Body-locality: **local** — the existing §15.4 predicate applied to one more target class, not a parallel rule.

**D3 — the stack-allocation permission retires.** *"The storage for the span may be stack-allocated"* is a permission no conforming implementation can exercise once the span's source is an `Array<U>`, and the shipped compiler already declines it in as many words in its own comment. Retiring a permission nobody can take is a subtraction, not a restriction, and no program's acceptance changes. The clause's load-bearing half — the factory must not retain the span, §28.6 — is retained verbatim, and applies unchanged because `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>` is a borrow-bearing record exactly as `ReadOnlySpan<T>` is.

**R3 — declined: no `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>.ToArray()` rides this fix.** The asymmetry is real and is the migration's one genuine loss: `ReadOnlySpan<T>` declares `ToArray(): owned Array<T>` at value `T`, this type does not, and a factory body spelled `elements.ToArray()` stops compiling. In-tree uses are **zero** and there are no external users. It is declined anyway, because a stdlib addition riding a signature fix is the *"while we're at it"* expansion the project's operating rules forbid, and surface is debt. It has a row in `DECLINED.md` with its reopening bar rather than a quiet inclusion. Options B, C and D stay declined with their bars — B on the argument #3310 never considered, that a fixed-extent *borrowing* view needs fixed-extent *borrowing storage*, which §28.11 explicitly defers.

**Composition check, performed rather than assumed.** D4 and v0.271's §15.4 edit amend the **same sentence** from opposite directions. The composed sentence was read whole before landing: D4's clause qualifies a **target** (*"declares the borrowing form"*), v0.271's qualifies a **producer** (*"whose `FromCollectionLiteral` result is `owned`"*). Both cite §15.4.1, with visibly different predicates and no contradiction.

**Migration.**

- **Source-affecting, with no affected sources.** A borrowing-form declaration's parameter type name changes. External users: none exist. In-tree: ten declaration sites, all at value element types, all declaration **text** — no test's semantics change. Three conformance rows are affected and all three were already skipped; none is reclassified.
- **Newly rejected: one shape that could not previously be written.** Under D4, a fresh producer of non-trivial-dispose class type in a user borrowing-form literal is rejected at the literal site. Before D1 that literal did not type-check at all, so nothing that compiled stops compiling.
- **Newly accepted:** the borrowing form at class-typed, runtime-managed and interface element types — which is the point of the change. §15.4.1's `RingBuffer<T>` example body is **unchanged** and now type-checks at class-typed `T` as well as value-typed `T`.
- **Unchanged:** the owning form and its `where T: class`; the *"exactly one of the two forms"* rule; every §28 ownership rule.
- **Sequencing:** this lands **before** [#3247](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3247)'s first promotion, which was recorded on that issue at v0.271 — it had said *"any order among the three."* §11.8's zero-source-change promise is a property of the current signature; promoting first would freeze the wrong carrier into `ICollectionLiteralTarget` and turn a signature correction into an interface-breaking change. Promotions 2 and 3 are unaffected.
- **Spec-ahead-of-impl:** the compiler's discrimination is by head name at two sites; it already emits Array-family storage, so D1 is a rename there rather than a behaviour change. D4's rejection is new sema work.
- **Doc-only:** `DECLINED.md` **415 → 416** rows (R3). Proposal 0115 flips to `graduated-v0.272` and its README row moves to Graduated.
- **Guides:** untouched; none names either span family in a collection-literal context.
- **Conformance corpus:** no case added or removed; the corpus remains at its v0.247 regeneration with the drift v0.269 measured, tracked by #3262 and #3297.
