### v0.273 changelog (v0.272 → v0.273)

**Two contradictions closed, and both issues' framings were wrong in the same way: each named the right defect at the wrong address.** Class: **ruling** for the freeze scope, **clarification** for the range-pattern reason.

**§28.14's admission freeze on captured sources lifts at the bounding local's scope exit; v1 bound 2(a) is the defect ([#3318](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3318)).**

The issue reported this as a dispute about **§28.3's consume-site freeze**. It is not. §28.3's freeze is **live-range-scoped** — *"A borrow is live at a consume site when some path from the site reaches a later use of it"*, a backward dataflow question — so it is neither method- nor block-scoped and needs no edit under any reading. The dispute is entirely about §28.14's **admission freeze** (K5.7), a separate rule with a separate compiler mechanism. Correcting the address is what made the answer visible.

- **The split is three to one, and the outlier says so about itself.** Three normative sites state that the freeze ends at the bounding local's scope exit — §28.14's own admission text (*"Until `L`'s scope exits, the captured local sources are **frozen**"*), the `scoped`-argument rule, and §22.3's parameter-modifier entry. Against them stands only v1 bound 2(a), which says the freeze *"persists to the end of the enclosing method body, not merely to the bound's scope exit"* and concedes in the same breath that it is *"conservative — may over-reject mutation after an inner block closes."*
- **Bound 2(a) is mis-filed.** The v1 bounds are licensed as covering *"corners the original text left silent."* This corner was never silent: the admission text states the rule. 2(a) is an implementation shortfall recorded as though it were a design bound — no rationale entry defends it, and `DECLINED.md`'s §28.14 row scopes itself to bounds 3, 5 and 6.
- **Nothing is protected by the excess.** Quiescence plus `using var` scope-end disposal means no captured source can be observed after the bounding block closes, so a freeze extending past that point guards nothing. Narrowing costs one stored `SourceLocation` — spans are already stamped on every statement — not "more analysis."
- **Blast radius: zero.** The `do … end` lift idiom appears in **no** test and **no** conformance case; all six existing §28.14 freeze tests are flat bodies where the two readings coincide.
- **Proposal 0099 repeated this rule; it did not decide it.** It quotes the admission text, derives the `do … end` remedy, mandates it into Guide 01 and into its own acceptance tests — and never quotes, cites, or reasons about the v1 admission bounds; its one mention of a "bound" is about `scoped` on a constructor parameter. Under the precedent v0.271 set, that makes this ruling a **confirmation** of 0099 rather than an override, so it takes no `DECLINED.md` row and 0099 gains a confirming landing note rather than a correction.
- **Consequence for the teaching documents: they were right.** Guide 01 §10 and stdlib §2.21 both taught the `do … end` lift, and both followed the three-site majority. Neither is rewritten. **Guide 01's pin moves to v0.273** — it was held at v0.259 through the v0.271 guide pass precisely because its §10 taught a shape bound 2(a) rejected, and that blocker is now removed by ruling the spec wrong rather than the guide.
- **Kernel classification: derivation.** K5.7 is unchanged; what changes is the interval over which it is applied. The axiom register stands at eleven axioms and four tombstones. **Body-locality: local** — the interval is the bounding local's own scope.
- **One residual, shipped with an explicit clause rather than left implicit.** Bound 2(b) claims back-edge moves are caught by the general moved-from rules, but a test in the tree calls capturing a moved-from local *"a pre-existing general capture gap"* and asserts no error. The narrowed rule therefore states the loop case explicitly, and the capture gap is filed separately.

**§19.3's nullable-scrutinee rejection keeps its verdict, gains an honest reason, and the bare `..` pattern's meaning is stated for the first time (the [#3315](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3315) item-3 residual).**

The residual reported that §19.3 over-reaches: a **bare** `..` performs no ordering test, yet §19.3 rejects it citing *"ordering admits no absent participant."* The premise is correct, and correct **normatively** rather than by appeal to the compiler — §16.3's own `Contains` formula says a `null` endpoint *"imposes no bound on its side and never makes the range empty"*, so with both bounds absent the ordering test is vacuous.

- **Narrowing the rejection was nonetheless declined, because it would re-open rather than correct.** v0.267 deliberately overrode proposal 0114's D5, and the graduating commit recorded that with a `DECLINED.md` row naming D5's position and carrying no reopening bar. That row says *"range patterns"*, unqualified. And **v0.271's own accounting already counted the two bare-`..` test blocks** among the eight the landed rule newly rejects. So the unbounded form is inside the decline as landed; narrowing it is a design change requiring a proposal, not a clarification.
- **The alternative's cost decided it.** Narrowing would make the verdict depend on **how many bounds are written**: `case n of ..` would compile over an `int?` while `case n of int.MinValue..int.MaxValue` would not, at identical extent. That is a fresh instance of the *"same shape, opposite answers, decided by spelling"* defect proposal 0114 gives as its own motivation — the very defect the rule exists to remove.
- **The real defect underneath was silence.** The spec never stated what a bare `..` *means*. §19.3 illustrates only `..<0` and `31..`; §16.6 gives the match rule only for bounded forms; the code-generation reference omits it; the guides never mention range patterns. The bare leg existed only in the Appendix A grammar. That is why the rule's reason and its verdict drifted apart, and it is now written down.
- **The honest cost, stated rather than hidden:** the rejection of the unbounded form is now defended by uniformity rather than by the ordering argument, and the text says so instead of implying a reason that does not reach it. Appendix C.1 and §7.11 need no edit — both are already form-independent — and the grammar is untouched, so the conformance corpus is untouched.

**Migration.**

- **Newly accepted: one shape.** Mutation of a captured source after the bounding local's scope exits, where an enclosing method body continues. Nothing in the corpus writes it, so no test changes; the *reference implementation* rejects it today and is now behind the spec.
- **Newly rejected: nothing.**
- **Unchanged in meaning:** §19.3's verdict, in every form; §28.3's consume-site freeze, which this revision does not touch and which the issue mistakenly named.
- **Spec-ahead-of-impl: one delta.** `scopedFrozen_` is a per-method map with no scope hook — three references in the whole tree, no clear, no erase — and `checkScopedFreeze` is a one-sided offset test whose own diagnostic string already claims the block-scoped rule it does not implement. Filed.
- **Guides:** Guide 01 re-pinned to **v0.273** and otherwise untouched by this revision; the other five keep their pins.
- **Conformance corpus:** no case added, edited, or invalidated. The grammar is unchanged and no fenced example moves.

### v0.274 changelog (v0.273 → v0.274)

**The standard-library and rationale audit — the sweep the v0.269 revision did not do.** v0.269 read all of the specification's Bezel code blocks and found ~68 defects, ten severe. It read **neither** the standard library nor the rationale. This revision closes that: **seven lanes over 176 blocks** — the stdlib's 157 and the rationale's 19 — asking the same four questions, of which the fourth (*does the surrounding prose over-claim what the block shows?*) was the one v0.269 discovered by accident and which found the most again here. **~51 findings, roughly fifteen severe.** Class: **ruling** for the six decisions below, **clarification/editorial** for the rest.

**The partition was made provable before the sweep ran.** v0.269's `^```bezel` recipe silently dropped eight indented fences. This one enumerated with an open/close-tracking scan, and the stdlib turned out to contain exactly one indented fence — which the old recipe would have missed again, and which lane S5 independently confirmed by finding 26 where its range holds 27. Every lane reported its own count back as a check, and all seven matched.

**Three defect classes are new to this project.**

- **Unreachable by construction.** `Array<T>`'s and `OwningArray<T>`'s default-comparer `Sort`/`Sorted` were declared as `extension` members — but §26.5 rule 1 commits instance resolution by **name**, *"of any arity"*, and both types already declare those names, so *"extension blocks are **never consulted**"*. `myArray.Sorted()` is a compile error. Not a missing name: a name that exists and can never be reached. The prose compounded it (*"`Sorted` comes in two forms"*) while stating the governing rule **correctly** two sentences later about `OwningArray<T>.ToArray()`.
- **Ungrammatical syntax, thirteen times.** §6.8 `Domain` and §6.12 `Parallel` constrain two type parameters in one clause — `where A: sendable, class, R: sendable, class`. Appendix A.4 admits **one** identifier per clause with `GenericConstraints*` repetition, so `R` parses as a *type bound on `A`* and the following `:` fails. The specification uses this form **zero** times and puts the same constraints in comments instead; the asymmetry is the tell.
- **Self-contradiction.** §4.5's reference implementation drops the `pure` its own surface declares — a compile error under §22.15 dispatch rule 1 — while *restating* it would also be rejected, because the body calls the non-pure `OwningBuffer<T>.Length`. The surface and the implementation of one type cannot both be right.

**Six rulings, each recording what it declined.**

1. **The four temporal/`Guid` types are not orderable, and the claim goes rather than the operators arriving.** `DateTime`, `TimeSpan`, `DateOnly` and `Guid` each carried a comment asserting that *"the `<,>,<=,>=` operator group agrees with `CompareTo`"*. **None of the four operators is declared anywhere in the document** — the only `operator <` declarations in the standard library are `INumber<T>`/`ISteppable<T>`'s constraint members — and records auto-generate `=`, `<>`, `GetHashCode` and `ToString` only, never ordering. So `if deadline < DateTime.UtcNow then` did not compile. **Declined: declaring the operators.** That is a stdlib surface addition carrying §25.2's whole-group and co-declaration obligations; `CompareTo` already serves ordering. Deleting a false claim is a correction, adding four operator groups is feature work.
2. **The unreachable extensions are deleted, not renamed.** The lane proposed `SortNatural`/`SortedNatural`. **Declined:** inventing two public names is a design decision riding a correction sweep — the *while-we're-at-it* expansion the operating rules forbid, and the same ground on which v0.272 declined `ReadOnlyArraySpan<T>.ToArray()`. The extension is not reachable, therefore is not API today, therefore deleting it loses no capability. A comment records **why** it cannot exist, so the next editor does not re-add it. Whether the language should offer default-comparer sorting at all is a design question, filed.
3. **`RaiseAsync` loses its `async` marker.** §6.5's only worked async-handler example takes a **borrow-bearing** payload record, which §30.1 bars outright as an async-lambda parameter — and this is structural, not an example bug: `AsyncEventSource<T>` declared `public async method RaiseAsync`, and §30.1 re-applies the check after substitution, so *every* payload following §6.5's own recommended convention was rejected at the instantiation site. §28.12 makes `async` implementation-side and invisible in signatures, and §30.1 exempts non-`async` `Task`-returning methods, so deleting the marker fixes the declaration without touching the rule. **Not decided here:** whether async events may carry borrow-bearing payloads at all. Filed.
4. **`Ptr<T>` gains `Equals`/`GetHashCode`.** It overloads homogeneous `=`/`<>` and declared neither, which §25.2's co-declaration rule makes a compile error. Its exemption names `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` **only**, on the stated ground that they *predate* the rule — and the changelog refutes the transfer: the rule landed at **v0.158**, `Ptr<T>` at **v0.186**, twenty-eight revisions later. The block's own comment invoking *"the §10.0 `IntPtr` precedent"* is the over-claim that hid it: the **reason** transfers, the **exemption** is dated and does not. §25.2's now-false justification is filed separately.
5. **`DateTime.Date` and `TimeOfDay` are declared, because the prose already declares them** — §9's prose gives both with exact signatures, so the omission was in the block, and writing them down records existing documented API rather than adding surface.
6. **`pure` is added to `Count` alone, not to `Capacity`.** The proposed edit marked the `Capacity` half *"requires E6"* — an edit deliberately routed out of this revision. Applying both would have declared `pure` on a body calling a non-pure member: a **fresh** contradiction introduced while fixing one. Filed with its two candidate remedies.

**Taxonomy drift, a hundred revisions of it.** §4.14's value-type categories were pinned at **v0.102** and never re-read against §35. Choices became move-only at **v0.200**: the stdlib said move-only value types are *"currently only the owning inline arrays"* while §15.3 says the kinds *"are **two**"*, the second being the owning-classified choice — over-permissive, so a reader concluded `OwningBuffer<SomeOwningChoice>` was admitted. Corrected. The related gap — that the value-typed category lists omit choices entirely, so a *value-like* choice falls through the class bullet, the value bullet **and** the exclusion list — is a ruling and is **filed, not fixed**; the lane recorded a recommendation and correctly wrote no edit.

**Two findings land on this project's own work, and both are recorded rather than quietly repaired.**

- **v0.272 shipped with proposal 0115's Edit 8 missing.** The rationale named the withdrawn `ReadOnlySpan<T>` carrier as current in **two** places, one of them a paragraph directly above the sentence repudiating it, and §18's deferred-list summary in the present tense. Root cause: the edits were extracted as e7 and e9 — **the identifiers themselves recorded the gap** — and **no composition gate was run on v0.272**, the only revision this month without one. The missing-edit audit is precisely that gate's highest-value attack. Both sites are corrected here.
- **`check_docs.sh`'s FACTS check is structurally blind to the stdlib's copy of the synchronized set.** §2.16 lists seven members where §28.13 lists eight, `CancellationTokenSource` having been granted at v0.263 — whose entry enumerates the five sentences it amended and missed this one. The check keys on the *specification's* phrasing, so a divergent duplicate elsewhere is unpoliced **by construction**. Corrected here; the checker gap is filed.

**The three designated high-risk areas came back clean, and that is a result.** Spans are family-correct at every site, stated in full at three independent places; all nine FFI touches name the set they enumerate, with one sentence getting the incomparability explicitly right; and `new Stream()` — v0.269's most-repeated defect, eleven occurrences — has **zero** hits in the standard library. (The entry first claimed *corpus-wide*; the composition gate found one survivor in the **rationale** at §11.4, a stale quotation of a spec passage v0.269 had already corrected to `new FileStream(_path, FileMode.Open)`. The verification had been run against the stdlib alone and generalised. Corrected here.) The v0.270 and v0.272 rulings held.

**Gate round (adversarial composition gate, same revision).** One pass; verdict **BLOCK** — eight blocking findings, all applied before landing, none declined. Three were of the class the gate exists for: *did the fix break what it touched?*

- **The prose applied a rename this entry's own ruling 2 declines.** The code blocks correctly deleted the unreachable extensions, but §4.4's covering paragraph was rewritten to tell readers that `Array<T>` has *"the parameterless `SortedNatural()`"* and that *"the extension members take **distinct names** deliberately"*. `SortedNatural` existed nowhere in the corpus except that sentence and the line declining it — **an invented stdlib API, shipped by the revision whose subject is invented APIs.** The ruling was reviewed and the *declarations* were patched to match it; the *prose* edit encoding the same decision was not.
- **The code-generation reference was re-pinned to v0.274 while still declaring what v0.274 deleted.** The pin bump was the file's only change, and its §4.4 block still carried the `Array<T>` extension this revision calls a compile error. `check_docs.sh`'s PIN check compares revision **numbers**, not content, so it passed a document asserting validation it had not received. That is the same shape as the FACTS blind spot recorded above: a check aimed at the wrong half of its own claim.
- **The `Parallel` `where` fix reached five overloads and not three**, and the covering sentence was rewritten from *"sendability is the stronger compiler-checked requirement"* to *"the `where` clauses state the full requirement"* — so the edit both left three clauses incomplete **and** deleted the sentence that had made their incompleteness harmless. The three `ForEach` clauses now spell `sendable`.

Also applied: a duplicated `);` that made the `JsonOptions` fence a syntax error — in a revision whose headline class is *ungrammatical syntax*; the §6.5 payload restrictions withdrawn (above); the five `DECLINED.md` rows §9's checklist binds, whose omission was the same one v0.271 was caught on; and the register's size line, which **v0.272 never updated** after adding a row — a third consequence of that revision running no gate.

**Migration.**

- **Newly rejected: nothing** — and this survived a challenge. The first draft of §6.5 added two payload restrictions (no borrow-bearing record for the async pair, no move-only value type for either), which would have made the claim false. The gate refuted both derivations: §30.1 binds `async` **lambdas**, so a plain lambda or method reference returning a completed task is unaffected — an absolute rule had been drawn from a conditional; and §15.3 **defines** move-only parameter passing as by-value-move rather than rejecting it, so it was cited for the opposite of what it says. Both clauses are withdrawn and the interactions are stated as interactions; the questions are filed. Every deletion in this revision removes a claim or a declaration that could not be used: the operator claims described operators that do not exist; the extensions could never be consulted; the `where` clauses did not parse.
- **Newly accepted: two shapes at the document level** — `DateTime.Date` and `TimeOfDay`, which the prose already promised, and `Ptr<T>.Equals`/`GetHashCode`, without which `Ptr<T>`'s own declaration was a compile error. Neither is a new capability; both make a declaration match what the document already asserted.
- **Unchanged:** every ownership rule, every kernel rule, the axiom register at eleven and four tombstones. **Kernel classification: no contact** — no §28 or §30.5 rule is touched. **Body-locality: vacuous** — this revision adds no compile-time rule.
- **Guides:** untouched; all six keep their pins.
- **Conformance corpus:** the stdlib's fenced blocks are extracted, so the corrected blocks change; the corpus remains at its v0.247 regeneration with the drift v0.269 measured, tracked by #3262 and #3297.

### v0.275 changelog (v0.274 → v0.275)

**The rulings v0.274 routed — and the correction of a v0.274 ruling that was wrong.** Seven questions were routed out of the standard-library audit rather than answered inside it. Three ruling lanes took them, and **five of the seven premises turned out to be wrong** — including one of this project's own. Class: **ruling** throughout, with one **reversal**.

**⚠ v0.274's ruling 2 was wrong, and this revision reverses its substance.** That ruling deleted `Array<T>`'s and `OwningArray<T>`'s parameterless `Sort`/`Sorted` on the reasoning that §26.5 rule 1 makes an extension of an already-declared name unreachable, therefore the declarations were not API, therefore *"deleting lost no capability because there was none."* **The last step does not follow, and it is false.** The capability **ships on `Array<T>`**: a sema admissibility gate keyed on `T: IComparable<T>`, lowering, interface-element dispatch and cross-module paths, **twelve test files** across four areas, and **five** hardening issues — one of them a *measured* silent-wrong-answer bug. The compiler never implemented it through the extension. So §26.5's argument was sound about the **extension** and unsound about the **capability**, and for one revision the documents asserted a compile error for a call that compiles, runs and sorts.

- **The restoration uses the mechanism the compiler actually has**, not the one v0.274 deleted: arity-0 overloads on `Array<T>` itself ([§22.6](Bezel_Language_Spec.md#sec-overloading)), admitted only where `T: IComparable<T>`, with the condition checked and reported **at the call's instantiation**. That is not a new device — `OwningBuffer<T>.DangerousPointer()` has had exactly this shape since v0.186: a member of a generic class whose admissibility is conditioned on the enclosing parameter, stated in prose, with no `where` clause.
- **`OwningArray<T>` stays absent**, and that is a scope correction this revision would have missed: the sema gate reads *"Only on `Array<T>` (not `OwningArray<T>`)"*, so that half was never implemented. It is genuinely new work and is filed, not restored.
- **What remains declined is only the extension spelling.** Renaming to `SortNatural`/`SortedNatural` stays declined as inventing vocabulary inside a correction sweep. The register row is corrected rather than deleted, so the reversal is legible.
- **A per-member `where` on an unconstrained generic class is *not* the mechanism**, and the check mattered: it is grammatical (A.4's `MethodDecl` carries `GenericConstraints*`) but semantically undefined — §14.2 defines `where` as filtering substitutions at instantiation, and a conditional-member reading exists nowhere. The changelog said so **218 revisions ago**, which is *why* the extension was written in the first place.

**The root cause behind two of the seven, named for the first time.** **v0.200 added a tenth kind to §3.1 and no revision re-read the taxonomies derived from it.** Its migration note reads *"no existing type's classification, layout, or rules change"* — true of every **type**, and false of every closed **enumeration over types**. §3.1 was updated; stdlib §2.13 (pinned v0.113) and §4.14 (pinned v0.102) were not, and both still enumerated a nine-kind world seventy-five revisions later.

- **`Type` gains `IsChoice`.** Choice was the **only** §3.1 kind with no predicate — the mapping is otherwise total, both flattenings and the one exception stated. The paragraph carried **three** falsehoods for a choice, not one: the exactly-one claim, the `IsValueType` disjunction (which contradicts §3.2's *"choices … are value types"*), and the exception list. The addition costs provably nothing: `typeof`/`GetType` are unconditional compile errors in both sema and codegen, and `IsValueType` appears nowhere in the compiler.
- **§4.14 admits value-like and borrow-bearing choices; owning choices stay excluded.** The value-typed set turned out to be §15.3's copyable set with one member silently dropped. Appendix D.3 independently forces the exclusion — it asserts that *Buffers and spans* does not depend on *Move-only value types*, so admitting owning choices would falsify a normative claim.
- **v0.274 fixed one of *five* copies of the move-only undercount** (the first draft of this entry said three — the gate found two more, in the rationale's §5.15 design home and a further spec site, and the pattern this paragraph names caught the paragraph itself). The **normative specification** (§14.4) and the rationale (§18) both still named the move-only kinds as the owning inline arrays alone, against §15.3's *"are two"*. Both are corrected here. The pattern is worth naming: v0.274 fixed the instance it was shown and did not ask where else the claim was stated.

**§25.2's exemption is retired rather than re-grounded, because the proposed new ground is false.** v0.274 recorded that the exemption's stated reason — that `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` *predate* the co-declaration rule — cannot cover `Ptr<T>` (rule at v0.158, `Ptr<T>` at v0.186). The obvious repair was to re-ground it on the *reason* rather than the date: zero auto-properties, so no synthesis to defer to. **That reason is refuted by §9.2** — such a record **is** auto-hashable and receives an every-pair-equal `=` — and by stdlib §10.0's own words, that this synthesis *"is **wrong** for pointer comparison."* It is a reason to **declare**, not to be exempt. And the census settles it: the only homogeneous `=`/`<>` overloads in the normative documents are `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr` and `Ptr<T>` — so the exempted set was never "the ones that came first", it was **the complete set of types that fail the rule**. Under one reading of §9.2, `Dictionary<IntPtr, V>` silently aliases every handle. **The fix is nonetheless withheld, and this is the gate's doing.** Adding `override GetHashCode` to `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` strips them of **auto-hashable** (§9.2's disqualifier list), which by §9.2's recursive component rule strips it from **every user record with an `IntPtr` field** — their `=`/`<>` and hash-container use become compile errors. Whether that happens at all depends on whether an equality-*operator* overload already disqualifies, and **§9.2's eligibility and disqualifier lists contradict each other on exactly that**. The blast radius is therefore unknowable until that contradiction is ruled, so the ruling is recorded and the edit is routed: `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` keep the exemption, with a comment saying why, and §9.2's self-contradiction is filed as the blocker.

**`const Zero` becomes `static readonly property`.** The three sites violate §22.12's restriction of `const` to a primitive value type or `string`, **and** fall outside §17.14's scoping of compiler-provided constants to primitive *wrapper* types — so their `const`-ness was already inert: nothing could use them in a constant position and nothing tried. The tree already carries the convention (`Guid.Empty`, `DateTime.MinValue`, `TimeSpan.Zero`, `CancellationToken.None`), and `CancellationToken.None` proves the property spelling reaches even default-argument position. Compiler impact: zero — `IntPtr.Zero` is not modelled as a `const` at all.

**Async events keep their payload type unrestricted, and the real obligation is written down instead.** The routed framing was half the story. The handler-side point is correct but minor — a `(T) -> Task` slot need not be an `async` lambda, so §30.1 need never fire. **The load-bearing fact is raiser-side and was nowhere stated:** `RaiseAsync` *retains the payload until the returned task settles*. The runtime proves it — it heap-copies the payload so later chain steps can read it after the originating continuation returns, and holds it to settlement. That is exactly the frame §30.1's parameter rule polices, so v0.274's fix moved the declaration out of the rule's **syntactic** scope while leaving it inside its **semantic** one. No restriction is invented; the retention and the raiser's held-until-settlement obligation are now normative.

**§4.5's purity contradiction was smaller than filed, and its premise was refuted.** **No interface pure-declares `Capacity`** — not `IReadOnlyCollection`/`IReadOnlyList`, not `IOwningCollection`/`IOwningList` — so §22.15 dispatch rule 1 never fires, and both v0.274's entry and its register row mis-cited it. The contradiction is internal to §4.5: a `pure`-declared surface against its own unmarked reference implementation. `OwningBuffer<T>.Length` is made **pure**, its non-purity having been established as *incidental* — outside the #2089 purity pass, merely observed by a later gate, and outside the deferral that names only the four span types. Blast radius: one spec site, three stdlib, zero tests, zero programs newly rejected.

**Tooling: `check_docs.sh` gains SETS**, closing the blind spot v0.274 recorded ([#3323](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3323)). FACTS cross-checks every *formula* carrier against the spec's phrasing and is therefore blind, by construction, to a passage restating a normative set's **membership** in its own words. SETS keys on members: it finds every passage naming the set and enumerating it, and fails when a restatement diverges. Fault-injected against the real defect — dropping `CancellationTokenSource` from the stdlib restatement alone yields a violation and exit 1. Its reach is narrower than the first draft of this entry claimed. It does **not** find *every* passage naming and enumerating the set: the gate demonstrated that rewording `currently` to `at present` passes clean, that a restatement shrunk to two members passes clean, and that an editorial parenthetical mid-list produces a spurious failure. What it reliably catches is the shape the historical defect took. It is parameterized by one set marker, and discovering restatements generically remains the harder half of #3323.

**Gate round (adversarial composition gate, same revision).** One pass; verdict **BLOCK** — six blocking findings, all applied. Neither project checker sees any of them.

- **The reversal was itself incomplete.** §4.4 restored the declarations and, twenty lines later, still carried *"There is **no** parameterless natural-order form … the call would be a compile error rather than a fallback"* — a sentence this revision exists to retract, traced by `git log -S` to v0.274's own gate-fix commit. The revision named the pattern (*"fixed the instance it was shown and did not ask where else the claim was stated"*) and then committed it against its own headline change.
- **"One of three copies" was wrong: there are five.** The rationale's §5.15 — the *design home* of the buffer and span family — still undercounted, and carried the value-typed-set defect beside it. Two spec sites more. Corrected; a third suspected site was checked and is **not** an undercount, so it was left alone.
- **The `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` co-declaration would have been a breaking change announced as none** — see above. Withheld.
- **The SETS claim overstated the check.** The gate fault-injected past it three ways.
- **`DECLINED.md`'s reclassed row kept its old *group*.** The Class cell said `deferred` while the row sat under `### rejected`, against the file's own *"rows are grouped by verdict class"*. Section counts said 181/104; the size line said 180/105. Moved; both now agree.
- **An absence was asserted that cannot be verified here.** The entry stated `OwningArray<T>` "has no such form". Sema's admissibility arm is `Array`-only, but **codegen's `Sort()` arm carries no receiver guard** and a regression test comments that *"OwningArray<T> in-place Reverse()/Sort() work"*. Settling it needs a build this lane does not have — and writing an absence into this document for a call that works is precisely v0.274's error. The claim is withdrawn and the question filed rather than answered.

Also applied from the non-blocking set: the code-generation reference never received the two restored members, leaving §9's obligation undischarged for the revision's headline change — in the one document written to be copied from.

**Migration.**

- **Newly accepted: `Array<T>.Sort()`/`Sorted()` at the document level** — restoring what v0.274 wrongly removed. Nothing changes in the compiler; the documents catch up to it.
- **Newly rejected: nothing.** `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` gaining `Equals`/`GetHashCode` makes their declarations legal where they were not; §2.8.6 classifies an added-purity, off-slot member as preserving.
- **Newly defined:** `Type.IsChoice`; §4.14's admission of value-like and borrow-bearing choices; the `RaiseAsync` retention obligation.
- **Unchanged:** every ownership rule and every kernel rule. **Kernel classification: no contact.** **Body-locality: vacuous.**
- **A spec-ahead-of-implementation inversion, recorded because the process has no slot for it.** `spec-change-process.md` §5 item 3 covers *spec ahead of implementation*. This revision's central finding is the mirror: the **implementation was ahead of the documents**, and the documents asserted its behaviour impossible. Nothing in the checklist would have caught that, and the gap is filed.
- **Guides:** untouched; all six keep their pins. **Conformance corpus:** three `skip` rows are touched by the `IsChoice` addition; the corpus remains at its v0.247 regeneration.

### v0.276 changelog (v0.275 → v0.276)

**One ruling, and the four things it turned out to touch.** §9.2's two membership lists have under-determined the same input since v0.158: the eligibility list admits *"an overload of a **non-equality** operator"*, and the disqualifier list names only an `override` of `Equals`/`GetHashCode`. An author who overloads `=` itself falls between them. Read one way, the record keeps **auto-hashable** and receives a synthesized `Equals`/`GetHashCode` computed by a rule its own `=` has just replaced; read the other, the overload disqualifies it and §25.2's co-declaration rule supplies the pair. This revision rules the second — **a homogeneous `=`/`<>` overload strips auto-hashable; a heterogeneous one (`T = U`) does not** — and writes it into **both** lists, so neither can be read alone and be wrong. §35.7's choice restatement moves with it, Appendix C gains the invariant, and rationale [§7.6](Bezel_Design_Rationale.md#sec-equality-operator-strips-auto-hashable) is the new decision record.

The decisive argument is structural rather than textual. §25.2 states the hazard it exists to prevent: *"`a = b` true while a `Set<T>` treats them as distinct."* Under the rejected reading, §25.2's co-declaration rule is the **only** guard against it, so **any exemption from §25.2 becomes a soundness hole** — which is observably how the `IntPtr` bug arose and what v0.275 found. Under the ruling the overload strips auto-hashable by itself, §9.2's use-site error blocks equality until the author supplies it, and an exemption is harmless. Three supports, in descending force: §3.6 defines the property as one a type has *"for which `=`, `GetHashCode`, and `ToString` are **synthesized**"*, which an overloading record is not; the word *non-equality* appears in two sections and is drafting noise under any other reading, which §9.2's own `equality skip` discipline names as a defect class; and `src/sema/SymbolCollection.cpp:1373-1377` (the token test at `:1374`) has enforced it since v0.158 with no recorded objection.

**Why not the broad reading the compiler implements.** `src/` rejects **any** `=`/`<>` overload token, operand types unexamined. Aligning §9.2's trigger with §25.2's instead — which frees heterogeneous overloads explicitly — is what makes §25.2's *"the **auto-generated or user-supplied** `Equals(Object?)` and `Equals(T)` methods continue to exist"* a live two-case split rather than a sentence with a dead arm. The counter-argument was stated at full strength and loses on cost, not on plausibility: operator overloads are `public static`, and §9.2's gate reads *"every **instance** member"*, so on the letter the gate never examines them. That reading is genuinely available. It makes a normative bullet inert in two sections and contradicts §3.6's definition of the property, and §35.7 enumerates *"statics, **and** non-equality operators"* as two items — the drafters do not fold operators into the static exemption.

**The stated cost, not minimised.** §9.2's recursive component rule admits *another record that is itself **auto-hashable***, so a record with an `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr`, or `Ptr<T>` component is not auto-hashable: the spec's own `record Sqlite3Db(Raw: IntPtr)` shape cannot use `=` or key a hash container. The wart is not created by this ruling — it is created by the component rule saying *auto-hashable* where it arguably means *hashable*, which is what the compiler's own comment at `src/sema/SymbolCollection.cpp:1268-1269` says while the code calls the auto-hashable predicate. **Widening it is declined here and routed** (`DECLINED.md`, `deferred`): *hashable* would admit a user-equality record carrying a **class**-typed field as a component, smuggling reference equality inside a value record's `=` — §35.7's *"virtually never the intended semantics"*. That is a design change owing its own proposal, not a rider on the ruling that exposed it.

**Four consequences the ruling forced, none of them in the routed question.**

- **§9.8 needed a carve-out, or serialization would have broken silently.** Its body-record bullet reads eligibility *"under exactly the auto-equality membership conditions of §9.2 … applied here **unchanged**"*. Applied unchanged, the new disqualifier would make every record that overloads `=` **not serialization-eligible** — `IntPtr` and `UIntPtr` first. An overloaded `=` states how two values compare and says nothing about which components serialize. §9.8 now reads the disqualifier **out**, on the one-directional-gate discipline §9.2 already carries for `equality skip`, and says the same of the `override Equals`/`GetHashCode` disqualifier, which was always read out for the same reason without saying so. Choice serialization is untouched: its gate is *value-like* (§35.4), not auto-hashable.
- **§25.2's retirement parenthetical became false one revision after it was written.** v0.275 retired the `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` exemption on the ground that *"§9.2 generates the zero-property every-pair-equal `=` … for exactly such a record"* — which is true only under the reading this revision **rejects**. The verdict survives; the ground is restated: the overload strips auto-hashable by itself, so the exemption deferred to no synthesis at all — it left two types whose purpose is comparison by address carrying an overloaded `=` with no `Equals`/`GetHashCode` beside it, hence outside **hashable** (§3.6) and unusable as a `Dictionary`/`Set` key. That is the same divergence reached from the other side. The retirement was independently carried throughout by stdlib §10.5's `Ptr<T>`, which has always declared all four members.
- **§25's opening list omitted choices** — *"Records, enums, and classes may overload operators"* — while §35.2 admits of a choice body *"exactly what an enum body may … and operator overloads"*, and §35.7 has restated §9.2's operator clause for choices all along. The list is corrected, and §25.2's co-declaration rule and Appendix C's invariant row now name the choice spelling (the enum's, since §35.2 carries §10.5's plain-member replacement rule over).
- **The code-generation reference had no line on any of it.** It is written to be copied from by a model that will not read the spec, and it did not say that overloading `=` obliges `Equals(T)` and `override GetHashCode` beside it — a generator following it would emit a record that does not compile. §22's member-forms table gains an *Equality operator* row: **write all four or none**.

**§25.2's `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` retirement is now complete, and the fear that blocked it does not materialise.** v0.275 landed the spec and code-generation-reference halves and withheld the stdlib half at its gate, on the recorded worry that co-declaring would strip auto-hashable *"from every user record with an `IntPtr` field"* — leaving the spec asserting *"There is no exemption"* while the stdlib still claimed one. Under this ruling **co-declaring is a no-op**: the two operators had already stripped the property, so adding `Equals(T)` and `override GetHashCode` triggers a disqualifier that has already fired and reclassifies nothing. (The *ruling* does reclassify such records — that is the stated cost above — but the *retirement* does not, and those are the two things the v0.275 gate note ran together.) v0.275's own Migration bullet announced this as landed; it was written before the gate withheld it. It lands here. Empirically the affected population is three FFI examples (`Sqlite3Db`, `Sqlite3Stmt`, `SigAction`), none compared or hashed anywhere in `docs/` or `tests/`, with **zero** `Dictionary`/`Set` keyed on any pointer type in the tree.

**`OwningArray<T>.Sort()` is restored — the half of v0.274's deletion that v0.275 undid only half of.** v0.274 deleted the parameterless natural-order sort from **two** types; v0.275 reversed the ruling and restored one, recording `OwningArray<T>` as *"NOT DOCUMENTED HERE, AND DELIBERATELY NOT DENIED"* because its own gate had just caught it asserting an unverifiable absence. Reading settles it in the admitting direction: three sema sites admit it positively — §22.5's owning-container allow-list names `Sort`, the result-typing arm names `OwningArray` explicitly, and the sole rejection arm covers `Reversed`/`Sorted` and omits `Sort` — codegen reaches it because `OwningArray` is array-backed, the form was declared from v0.242 to v0.273, and the code-generation reference has told writers to *"reorder in place with `Reverse()`/`Sort()`"* on an owning array since `2a65e27a` (2026-08-20) — which is to say it contradicted v0.274's deletion from the day after that line was written, not since the member was first documented at v0.242. **The declaration carries its own defect note:** the `T: IComparable<T>` gate is `Array`-only in the compiler, so an owning array of a class without `CompareTo` is admitted where it should be rejected — [#3325](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3325), the owning-side twin of #2790. Per the obligation this revision's process amendment adds, the reading is stated as a reading and the settling probe is named; it is not asserted as a measurement.

**Two claims v0.275 made are false, and are corrected here rather than in its own entry** (this file is pinned history — an entry is written at its revision and never retroactively edited).

- *"A conditional-member reading exists **nowhere**."* §35.2's *"Compiler-provided per-instantiation members (v0.233)"* paragraph is one, and it is complete: admissibility rule, rejection site, diagnostic contract, and the compiler-known-standard-library reservation. Read as a claim about a **`where`-clause** reading the sentence is exactly right; read as the claim it makes, it is false — and the false reading is what left the restored `Array<T>.Sort()` with prose and no anchor.
- *"Twelve test files across four areas."* `grep -rln '\.Sort()\|\.Sorted()' tests/` returns **ten**, across **three** (`codegen`, `module`, `ownership`). The claim was made in the entry that reversed a ruling for overstating what did not ship, which is the reason it is corrected in full rather than quietly.

**The recurring failure this revision was built to not repeat.** v0.275 named it — *fixed the instance it was shown and did not ask where else the claim was stated*. Every one of the four consequences above was found by asking that question of a ruling whose routed brief was two sentences long: §9.8 because §9.2's membership rule is **reused**; §25.2 because the ruling's own text sat in the paragraph the previous revision had just rewritten; §25 and Appendix C because §35.7 restates §9.2 for a kind §25 does not list; the code-generation reference because the process's own checklist asks what a writer must now do differently. None is visible to either mechanical checker.

**Proposal [0116](proposals/0116-conditional-members.md) lands at `draft`.** Members whose *admissibility* depends on the enclosing type argument: the stdlib ships **five**, the language defines **one** of them — completely, in the *Choices* chapter — and nothing points the other four at it. It recommends lifting §35.2's rule into a new §14.2 subsection carrying a closed **register**. Its normative text and its four decline rows land **at graduation, not now**: `DECLINED.md`'s ruled scope rule 2 forbids indexing an under-review draft's recommendations, and the proposal's own coordinator section asks for them anyway — a discrepancy recorded in both files rather than resolved by following the looser instruction. Two of the proposal's findings refuted premises the routed question stated, including the *"nowhere"* claim corrected above.

**Process: the impl-ahead-of-spec obligation** (`spec-change-process.md` §5 item 3b, and a matching §9 checklist line). v0.275's central finding was the mirror of the case the process had a slot for: the **implementation** carried a capability the spec was about to deny. Before a revision states that something does not exist, is not admitted, or is a compile error, it must check `src/` and `tests/`; where the check cannot settle it, the revision records what is known and names the probe rather than asserting the absence. *An unverified absence is worse than a silence, because a reader trusts it.* Both new absence-adjacent statements in this revision are written to that rule.

**Gate round (adversarial composition gate, same revision).** One pass; verdict **BLOCK** — nine blocking findings and twelve non-blocking, all applied. `check_docs.sh` saw none of them. The pattern is worth stating because it is the same one this entry claims above to have been built to avoid: the revision asked *where else is this stated* of the four sites it thought of, and the gate found **seven more** by asking it exhaustively.

- **A value-like choice that overloads `=` was left non-hashable and unrescuable.** §3.6's *hashable* row has a *"nor declares user equality"* arm for **records only**; its choice clause rejects anything not value-like auto-hashable, full stop. So the choice half of this ruling obliged an author to declare an equality surface under §25.2 and then refused to let the language use it — the exact opposite of what the same revision argues two documents away about `IntPtr`. §3.6 and §35.7 both gain the arm. The compiler sides with the un-amended §3.6: `recordHasUserDeclaredEquality` exists (`src/sema/SymbolCollection.cpp:1489-1497`) and has no choice twin.
- **The §9.8 carve-out read out one of the two statements the revision had just made.** This entry's own claim is that the rule is written into **both** §9.2 lists *"so neither can be read alone and be wrong"*. §9.8 applies the §9.2 **member list** *"unchanged"* and the carve-out excused only the *disqualifier* — leaving the membership-list exclusion in force, so a record overloading `=` was still serialization-ineligible, reached through the other half of the same amendment. The carve-out failed at precisely its stated purpose.
- ***"Records and enums may overload `=` and `<>`"* survived in two more places** — §8.4, the section a reader consults about `=`, and §25.2's own restriction bullet **seven lines above** the co-declaration rule this revision rewrote. §25.2 said in one bullet that only records and enums may overload `=`, and in the next paragraph that a choice doing so incurs the obligation.
- **§8.5 restates §9.2's conditions and was skipped**, and with it the auto-`ToString` consequence — see the Migration note, which now carries it and the finding that the compiler was never doing otherwise.
- **§35.7's enumeration of the ways a choice fails the property**, one paragraph below the sentence this revision amended, still read as exhaustive and was not.
- **The stdlib and the code-generation reference both still said *"Callers pass a comparer"*** three lines under the `OwningArray<T>.Sort()` this revision restored — and the code-generation reference had been **re-pinned to v0.276 without gaining the member at all**, which is v0.274's gate-B3 failure repeating exactly: the PIN check compares numbers, not content.
- ***"The set of newly non-compiling conforming programs is empty"* was false**, and the delta it hid was unfiled — see the Migration note. Two further unfiled deltas came with it: §35.7's choice disqualifier, and the retired `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr` exemption still hard-coded in sema.

Non-blocking, all applied: §9.2's `equality skip` consequence list and §9.3's exemplar both enumerated two disqualifiers; §19's named-pattern gloss used *"non-auto-hashable record"* as a synonym for *"does not bear `=`"*, which this ruling pulls apart; three stdlib sites still argued from the ground this revision declared unsound; two compiler citations in this entry were off by a line or two and are corrected above; the delta list named two of **three** identical operator arms; the new `DECLINED.md` row broke that file's alphabetical-within-group rule; proposal 0116's status notes describe as uncommitted what this commit lands. One item was **recorded rather than decided** ([#3335](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3335)): §25.2's obligation now names choices, while §35.2 carries §10.5's member-replacement rule over only *"for the boxable classifications"* — so whether an owning choice can discharge the obligation at all is unsettled, with an affected population of zero.

**Migration.**

- **Newly rejected: two shapes, and the set of newly non-compiling conforming programs is *not* empty.** The first draft of this bullet said it was; the composition gate falsified it.
  - **(i) A choice** that overloads homogeneous `=`/`<>` without `Equals(T)` and `GetHashCode`. §25.2's co-declaration rule reached *"a record or enum"* at v0.275 and reaches choices from here, so this shape was conforming and is not. It is **not** rejected by the compiler: `src/sema/TypeResolution_Checks.cpp:2260-2262` skips every `t->kind` that is not `Record` or `Enum`. Nor is §35.7's choice disqualifier implemented — `isAutoEqualityBearingChoice` (`src/sema/SymbolCollection.cpp:1533-1589`) never inspects body members, and **its own comment at `:1526-1531` predicted this revision**: *"a `=`/`<>` overload … **would** [disqualify]; but the choice surface is so constrained that this is a non-issue in practice — flagged in case a future admission widens it."* The flag was picked up by the gate, not by the ruling. Filed as [#3333](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3333). The affected population is zero: no choice in any document or in the corpus declares an equality operator.
  - **(ii) A body record** carrying a homogeneous overload, which loses auto-hashable — **and this one the compiler has rejected since v0.158**, so the set of newly non-compiling *record* programs is genuinely empty: §25.2's co-declaration rule already compelled the members. Downstream, a record with an `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr`/`Ptr<T>` component loses `=` and hash-key use; that corpus population is zero (§2.8.6: breaking, and stated as such).
- **A rendering consequence, stated because no normative text carried it.** Auto-hashable gates auto-`ToString` (§3.6, §8.5), so a **body** record that overloads homogeneous `=` — `IntPtr`, `UIntPtr`, `Ptr<T>`, and any user record on the §25.2 route — renders by §8.5's qualified-name default rather than `"TypeName(Prop: value)"`, and §25.2's co-declaration rule obliges nothing that restores it. **This is not a behavior change**: `recordIsAutoBearing` and `spec85NameOnlyDefaultIsQualified` (`src/codegen/LlvmBackend_impl.hpp:5584-5613`) both gate on the same `isAutoEqualityBearingBodyRecord` predicate, so the compiler has rendered these records by the qualified name all along — the documents were promising a field listing the implementation never produced. That is a third independent confirmation that the implementation carries this ruling. A **positional** record is unaffected: §8.5's split is by declaration form, and `recordIsPositional` is tested first. A body record that wants the property-listing form declares its own `ToString`.
- **Newly accepted: `OwningArray<T>.Sort()` at the document level**, and a **heterogeneous** `=`/`<>` overload no longer disqualifying — the second is a **widening the compiler has not caught up to**.
- **Newly defined:** §9.2's third disqualifier and its eligibility counterpart; §9.8's read-out of the equality-package disqualifiers; the choice spelling of §25.2's co-declaration rule.
- **Unchanged:** every ownership rule and every kernel rule; the axiom register stands at eleven axioms and four tombstones. **Kernel classification: no contact** — no §28 or §30.5 rule is touched. **Body-locality classification: local** — auto-hashable membership is computed from declarations and their component types' declarations, and consumes no information from any body.
- **Deltas filed, not asserted.** (1) **Spec ahead of implementation:** `src/sema/SymbolCollection.cpp:1375-1377` rejects any `=`/`<>` overload token regardless of operand types, so the compiler over-rejects the heterogeneous case this ruling frees; the same arm appears at `:1453-1457` (`isPositionalRecordEqualityBearing`) and a **third** time at `:1489-1497` (`recordHasUserDeclaredEquality`, which implements §3.6's *declares user equality* rescue rather than a disqualifier, and must agree with the other two about what *homogeneous* means or a heterogeneous-only record comes out both auto-hashable and user-equality-declaring). The homogeneity test to reuse already exists at `src/sema/TypeResolution_Checks.cpp:2274-2285`; three hand-rolled copies of *homogeneous* is how the two-list divergence this revision rules on arose in the first place. (2) **Implementation ahead of spec:** `IntPtr` resolves to a Named `TypeRef` with a **null** declaration (`src/sema/TypeResolution_Names.cpp:344-352`) and `isAdmissibleComponentType` returns the conservative `true` for a null declaration (`src/sema/SymbolCollection.cpp:1265`), so the compiler **today accepts** `record Sqlite3Db(Raw: IntPtr)` as auto-hashable by a fallthrough the operator rule never reaches. This revision therefore states the rule and does **not** write that such a record is rejected. (3) **Spec ahead of implementation, inherited from v0.275's half of this retirement:** §25.2 says *"There is no exemption for compiler-intrinsic types"*, and `src/sema/TypeResolution_Checks.cpp:2264` still short-circuits the co-declaration check on `t->name == "IntPtr" || t->name == "UIntPtr"` — keyed on the *name*, so any user type so named inherits it — with the retired date-scoped ground restated verbatim in the function comment at `:2247-2248`. This is the completion revision for that retirement, so leaving it undescribed would have left the normative sentence with no delta record at all. **Issues: (1) [#3326](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3326), (2) [#3327](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3327), (3) [#3334](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3334)**, plus [#3333](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3333) for the choice half above. All are reads of the source, not measurements — no build was available in this run.
- **Guides:** untouched; all six keep their pins — no guide teaches this idiom (`grep` for *auto-hashable* over `docs/Bezel_Guide_0*.md`: zero hits). **`Bezel_For_Code_Generation.md`:** edited and re-pinned, per §9's obligation.
- **Conformance corpus:** the stdlib's fenced blocks are extracted, so `IntPtr`/`UIntPtr`/`OwningArray<T>` change; the corpus remains at its v0.247 regeneration with the drift v0.269 measured (#3262).

### v0.277 changelog (v0.276 → v0.277)

**Proposal [0116](proposals/0116-conditional-members.md) graduates, and it graduates having reversed itself.** A **conditionally-admitted member** is a member of a generic type whose *admissibility* — whether it exists on a given receiver at all — is decided per instantiation from the enclosing type's type arguments. The standard library has had them since **v0.186**; the language has never defined them. The rule existed, complete, in exactly one place — §35.2's *"Compiler-provided per-instantiation members (v0.233)"* paragraph, filed in the **Choices** chapter and written entirely about `Result<T, E>` — and the other members defined themselves by pointing at each other. §14.2 now carries the general rule, lifted rather than invented, plus a closed **register**.

**The proposal's first draft would have registered four members as a standing privilege. It was wrong, and the costing that found so is the substance of this revision.** Draft 1 declined the "remove the capability" option after arguing only its weak form — *delete the members*. The strong form is **remove the conditionality**, and on that reading the census of five collapses:

- **`ReadOnlySpan<T>.ToArray()` is deleted.** Not merely ungated — **the member does not exist in the compiler and the call is rejected**: the span family's surface is a closed allow-list ending in a *"no member"* report (`src/sema/ExprTypecheck_Calls.cpp:7903-8188`), and codegen has no arm either. Call sites: zero in `docs/`, zero in `tests/`, zero exercised in the corpus. Draft 1 recorded *"no gate found by reading"*, which reads as *the member works and is ungated*; the opposite was true. **This is the v0.275 defect in mirror image** — that revision restored a member the documents had wrongly denied; this one removes a member the documents wrongly promised.
- **§5's six hashable-element operators are respelled**, not registered: `Contains`, `Distinct`, `Union`, `Intersect`, `Except` and `ToSet` move into a second `extension IEnumerable<T> where T: hashable`. This needs no privilege — `hashable` is an admitted §14.2 constraint, §26.4 defines the block clause, §26.6 merges the blocks, and §5.1 already declares two constrained blocks on this exact type. **It also removes a live self-contradiction**: §1's conventions state that *"absence of a constraint clause means 'any T'"*, so `Distinct()` said *any* `T` while §5's prose said hashable. `GroupBy<TKey>` and both `ToDictionary` overloads gain the ordinary `where TKey: hashable` their siblings already carry.
- **`Result<T, E>`'s combinators are routed, not deleted**, and this is where the first draft's decline actually failed. §26.2's own exclusion sentence names the way out: extensions are closed against the choice kind *because* **no §14.2 constraint names the value-like classification bound** a payload-generic extension surface would need — added at the same v0.233 landing that created the combinators, citing them as its reason. Proposal 0075 §3.3 Option B specified the fix and was declined at v0.233 as *"permanent user-facing constraint vocabulary bought on one program's evidence."* That ground no longer describes the case, which is the new evidence a reopening requires.
- **`Array<T>`/`OwningArray<T>` sorting stays**, and its removal stays declined on v0.275's reasons — which the costing *strengthens*. A rename in either direction does not rescue it: `Array<T>` is a declaration-less builtin (`src/common/BuiltinRegistry.cpp:679`) and the collections are not written in Bezel, so the sort remains a compiler intrinsic under any spelling. Its conditionality is an artifact of the standard library's implementation stage, not a language design commitment.
- **`DangerousPointer()` stays, routed to the subtraction review.** An intermediate draft recommended deleting it outright on the strength of *ninety revisions, zero implementation*. Asked why it was needed in the first place, proposal 0033 answers: it is the fix for the **BLAS double-copy exemplar** found by the 2026-07-07 owner-commissioned FFI review — *"the double-copy exemplar dissolved by `DangerousPointer`"* — and for `execve`/`posix_spawn` argv marshalling. **Both motivating cases are runtime-sized**, which is precisely the residual with no alternative spelling: §32.5's `[N]IntPtr` at a by-address `extern` parameter covers the static case and neither of these. *"Ships nothing"* is evidence about implementation priority, not design merit.

**So the register lands with three rows, and no row is a standing grant.** Each carries its exit: the sorting row an **expiry** (re-examined when the collections are self-hosted), `DangerousPointer()` a **route** (the subtraction review, with its unimplemented status on the row's face), the combinators a **route** (their own ruling). The register is written to empty rather than to grow. That, and not the row count, is what distinguishes it from the standing four-row privilege the first draft proposed — which would have written two fictions into a normative table and given them a growth discipline.

**Also landed: the rejection of a member-level `where` naming an enclosing type parameter** (§14.2 rule 1, Appendix C.1). The form is grammatical — A.4's `MethodDecl` carries `GenericConstraints*` unconditionally — and means nothing. A clause naming the *member's own* parameter is unaffected, including where its bound names an enclosing parameter; that distinction is what lets the `Result` route work without this form.

**⚠ The keystone this revision depends on is not landed, and is not this revision's to land.** [#3336](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3336): §26.4 states that a block `where` clause *"constrains which instantiations of the extended type the extension applies to"*, and the compiler does not implement it — `ExprTC::lookupExtensionMember` (`src/sema/ExprTypecheck.cpp:6937-7218`) reads `genericConstraints` only to collect free variables and to spell an ambiguity diagnostic; **no candidate is ever discarded for failing its clause**, and no test asserts one is. The proof is in the standard library: §5.1's shipped `extension IEnumerable<T> where T: IComparable<T>` needs a hand-written gate to enforce its own clause. So this revision's respell is **correct and inert**: the six operators say what they require, and nothing yet checks it. The alternative — registering them as a privilege because the implementation is behind — would have written an implementation gap into the language.

**Gate round (adversarial composition gate, same revision).** One pass; verdict **BLOCK** — seven blocking findings and nine non-blocking, all applied. `check_docs.sh` saw none of them. Five of the seven were the failure this project keeps naming: *fixed the instance it was shown and did not ask where else the claim was stated.*

- **A shipped API was silently deleted.** `OwningArray<T>.Sort(comparer:)` vanished and a comment line was duplicated in its place — collateral from an edit that was only supposed to re-word the comment on the line below. Four surviving prose claims and this register's own *remedy* column ("the comparer-taking overload") pointed at a member that no longer existed. **This is the exact defect class v0.275 was written to correct, reappearing in the revision that registers the practice** — and it reappeared through a mechanism worth naming: the edit was applied after a uniqueness check, which proves an edit *applies* and never that it is *right*. It was flagged "optional, outside the specified tasks", which is precisely when scrutiny should have risen rather than fallen. *(The same hazard recurred while applying this gate's findings: a reordering script deleted five `DECLINED.md` rows and re-inserted two, losing three. It was caught before the file was written, by a check that counted the rows it expected to find — which is the guard the earlier edit lacked. Recorded because two instances in one revision is a pattern, not an accident: a scripted edit needs a post-condition, not just a pre-condition.)*
- **The closed register was under-inclusive against its own definition.** §14.2's definition captures every member of a **two-presentation** declaration — `Span<T>.Fill()` at value `T`, `Clear()` at class `T`, which the compiler implements — while rule 1 admits a conditional member *only* where a register row names it. On the spec text alone the standard library violated the new rule in about a dozen places. The exclusion existed only in the non-normative proposal; it is now the register's second stated exclusion, which is what makes the closure checkable.
- **Appendix C.1's new row over-rejected**, dropping §14.2 rule 1's carve-out and so forbidding `method M<U>() where U: T`, which §14.2's *Type-parameter bounds* declares grammatical and meaningful. The row contradicted its own first half, and the Migration bullet repeated the over-broad form.
- **An absence was asserted without the grep the process requires** — see the Migration note. The rule this revision adds is exactly the one a live test's program spells.
- **The deletion sweep missed a second `DECLINED.md` row**, whose authoritative record this revision renamed and whose verbatim quotation it deleted. The *sibling* row was amended; this one was not.
- **A new `DECLINED.md` row's cited record said, in terms, that the decline it records is not a decline** — 0116's §9 note still asserted a position §5.3.1 had already reversed.
- **The changelog shipped an unfilled `GATE_ROUND_PLACEHOLDER`** — this paragraph.

Non-blocking, all applied: four stale *"retire four, register one"* assertions inside 0116, one of them a table header contradicting the cells beneath it; a §26.2 misquote that dropped the word *bound*, reproduced in this entry; rule 2's citation of §3.6 rule 2 being broader than that rule's own scope, when two of three register rows carry conditions that are not derived type properties at all; the new `DECLINED.md` rows breaking that file's alphabetical-within-group rule; a misattributed quotation in the amended v0.272 row; one body-locality classification given for two rules of different class; and a citation pointing at §14.2's opening for a clause the opening does not contain.

**One further correction, from the owner rather than the gate, and it is the most substantive.** An earlier draft of this register grounded the sorting row partly on *the standard library's collections not being written in Bezel*, and called that the operative reason. That is not a reason a specification may give: how a member is lowered is invisible to the language, and `Sort(comparer)` is a compiler intrinsic that nobody calls a privilege. The question a specification can answer is whether the **declaration form** is one the language admits — and under a rename it is. The row's stated reason is now §26.5 rule 1 alone, with both ways out named as open questions. What survives is a narrower, genuinely language-level cost: `Array<T>` is an always-available name (§2.3) whose home module is not auto-imported, so an extension over it would need an `import` that naming the type does not. **That asymmetry between §2.3's list and §26.5's resolution is a larger defect than the sorting question that exposed it**, and it is recorded rather than fixed here.

**Migration.**

- **Newly rejected: two shapes.** (i) A member-level `where` clause naming an enclosing type parameter — grammatical before, a compile error now; the affected population is zero in `docs/` and in the conformance corpus, and **one** in `tests/` — `tests/codegen/builtin_closed_ctor_surface_2994_test.cpp:315-329` spells `class Box<Guid> … public static method Make(): int where Guid: new()`, which this rule rejects. That test asserts only the absence of §17.7's no-constructor diagnostic, so it will not fail; re-spelling it (give `Make` its own type parameter) rides [#3330](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3330), which also carries whether the compiler accepts the form at all. **The first draft of this bullet asserted the absence without running §5 item 3b's grep** — in the revision whose own register discipline is that an unimplemented row must say so on its face. (ii) `ReadOnlySpan<T>.ToArray()` at the document level — which the compiler already rejected, so the set of newly non-compiling programs is empty and the documents stop promising a call that never worked.
- **Newly accepted: nothing.** The respell moves six declarations between extension blocks that §26.6 merges; no call site changes and no member changes module. `GroupBy`/`ToDictionary` gain a clause the prose already asserted.
- **Newly defined:** §14.2's *Conditionally-admitted members* and its register; §3.6's pointer sentence (the behavior-dispatch reservation is **not** widened — admissibility is a different mechanism, and the parenthetical *"(not merely admissibility)"* now points somewhere).
- **Unchanged:** every ownership rule and every kernel rule; the axiom register stands at eleven axioms and four tombstones. **Kernel classification: no contact.** **Body-locality classification: two rules, two classes.** §14.2 rules 2–4 are a **carve-out** — a generic-instantiation rule, admissibility decided after substitution at a use site, which proposal 0105 §1 confines to exactly that class; it consumes no per-body fact and reads nothing from any body but the one containing the call. §14.2 rule 1's rejection of a member-level `where` is **local**: it is decided at the declaration from the declaration alone, with no cross-body information. An earlier draft gave one classification for both — conservative rather than unsound, but the checklist asks each added rule to state its own.
- **Deltas filed, not asserted.** [#3336](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3336) (the block `where` clause, the keystone); [#3330](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3330) (is the rejected member-level form currently inert?); [#3331](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3331) (the unenforced conditions, now two rows rather than three); [#3329](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3329) (the `Array<T>.Sort()` diagnostic, against §14.2 rule 3's four-part contract); [#3325](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/3325) (`OwningArray<T>.Sort()`'s missing gate). **No build was available in this run**, so every compiler claim above is a read of the source and is marked as such.
- **Guides:** untouched; all six keep their pins — no guide teaches an admissibility rule this revision moves. Guide 02 *teaches* the `Result` combinators but states no rule and cites no section that moved (verified). **`Bezel_For_Code_Generation.md`:** edited and re-pinned — the `ReadOnlySpan<T>` deletion, the LINQ digest's constrained block, and the `where TKey: hashable` clauses.
- **Conformance corpus:** **zero manifest rows deleted, zero reclassified.** Two case bodies drift (`stdlib_0072`, `stdlib_0073`, both `skip:signature-listing`) and re-extract from the edited blocks; one fence is added by the new extension block. The corpus remains at its v0.247 regeneration with the drift v0.269 measured (#3262).
