### v0.309 changelog (v0.308 → v0.309)

**The ruling train from the 2026-09-29 spec-defect/spec-question docket.** Sixteen items decide cases the documents answered both ways or not at all; every one passed an adversarial critique (six blocking and thirty-six non-blocking findings, all resolved) and the composition gate over the union. Where a ruling reverses a direction the coordinator proposed, the bullet says so and the reason is recorded in `DECLINED.md`: the §25.2 carve-out for constraint-witness operators, and the §28.3 row-4 carve-out for `Array<T>`, were both withdrawn on the text.

- **§7.4 / §6.6 — a declaration's initializer establishes narrowing (ruling; [#4718](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/4718)).** §7.4's assignment bullet now names the declaration form: `var x: T? := expr;` and `const x: T? := expr;` with a non-nullable or narrowed `expr` narrow `x` from the declaration on, the initializer being the declaration's assignment and its narrowing invalidated by exactly the forms §7.4 lists. This is the reading v0.288's #3686 ruling shipped (`n += 1` on a narrowed local); §6.6's worked example, unchanged since v0.267, still called `var m: int? := 0; m += 1;` a compile error. It now shows the admitted `m += 1`, the reassignment from `null` that ends the narrowing, and then the rejection. **Declined:** reading the example as normative, which would reverse a shipped ruling with no ramp and make the one store that proves non-nullness at a declaration invisible to §7.4. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local. **Compiler:** the narrowing fact is recorded at both declaration forms, and the arithmetic, relational and compound gates consume it; the boolean-operator gates (`and`/`or`/`not`) and the `bool?` condition gate (`if`/`while`) read the declared type instead. That is a pre-existing v0.288 delta, which §7.11 already stated (an operand §7.4 has narrowed is non-nullable at every operator); it is now tracked. Corpus: the cases that stated the old reading are re-authored to present a genuinely nullable operand (`int.ParseOrNull(…)` or a nullable-returning helper) — `s7_11_0001`, `s7_11_0003`, `s7_11_0005`, `s7_11_0007`, `s6_6_0013` and `s6_6_0014` (whose `rule:` headers now say the static type is read after §7.4's narrowing), `s7_1_0002`, `s16_6_0005` — and the four §19.3 nullable-scrutinee cases `s16_6_0003`, `s19_3_0003`, `s19_3_0004` and `s7_11_0009` are re-authored the same way, so they hold whichever way §19.3's "nullable scrutinee" is read against a narrowed operand. That reading is filed as its own question, since §16.6's pattern-versus-`in` agreement depends on it. The doc-example case `spec_0012` is hand-edited to the new example (#1380). The code-generation reference's §7.8 narrowing line says a non-null initializer narrows too.
- **§5.2 — no `float`/`double`/`decimal` → `char` conversion (ruling; [#4829](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/4829)).** §5.2 gave a `char` target one numeric source, the integer, and said nothing of a binary-float or `decimal` one; the reference compiler admitted `char(65.5)` as `'A'` by truncating and then applying the code-point check. §25's opening says the explicit-cast expression and the implicit-conversion rules "apply only to the built-in conversions enumerated in §5", and §5.2 enumerates none from a floating source to `char`. §5.2 composes no conversion either; the one composed conversion in §5 (§5.4's `I(e)`) is written out as such. The conversion is now a compile error on the ground §5.2 already gives for `bool`: `char` is a code point, not a number — nor an arithmetic operand (§3.5, #5067 below), which the new sentence says in the same breath so the two rulings read as one fact. `char(int(x))` writes the truncation and the code-point check as the two conversions they are. §5.3's general rule carries the rejection to `char?(x)`, and §6.6's `char` write-back was already integer-only. **Declined:** truncate-then-check (the compiler's reading); `decimal`-only admission; admitting an integral-valued constant. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local. Corpus: no case changes; the coverage gap (a non-constant `char(d)` reject) is recorded. The code-generation reference's §7.1 reject block gains the line.
- **§14.2 clause 2 — the synthesized `Equals(T)` witnesses an `IEquatable<Self>` reached through an extending interface (ruling; [#5104](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5104)).** Clause 2 already admitted a record that "lists I (or any interface extending I)" and counted auto-generated members. The compiler's #5095 narrowing accepted the synthesized witness only for a *direct* `IEquatable<Self>` entry (a disclosed conservative choice), and it vetoes the witness whenever the builtin is reached through another interface at all, even beside a direct listing. The clause now says the witness serves either path, and satisfies no `IEquatable<U>` at a `U` other than the record type itself at its own type parameters, so `record Pair<T>(A: T): IEquatable<Pair<int>>` still needs a written `Equals`. It also says "never inherited" means from a base type, which is the ground sealing gives it. `interface IMy: IEquatable<Point> end IMy; record Point(X: int, Y: int): IMy;` therefore conforms with no written `Equals`, whether or not `Point` also lists `IEquatable<Point>` directly. #5095's rejections all stand on signature matching: a closed non-Self instantiation, a second `IEquatable<U>` entry, a user interface shadowing the name, and `IId: IEquatable<IId>`. **Declined:** the direct-only reading; extending the witness to a non-Self obligation. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local. Sema and codegen widen together, since codegen's predicate trusts sema for Self-ness; #4866's static generic answer below uses the same widened conformance.
- **§2.3 — an imported module's same-named public makes an always-available bare name ambiguous, in every shadowable row (ruling; [#5004](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5004)).** Only the `System.Collections.Generic` row said what happens when a user module exports an always-available name; the other rows said only "shadowable by local declarations", and the reference compiler let an imported `Lib.Task` win over the always-available `Task`. Every shadowable always-available name now stands where an imported bare name does (§2.7 rule 1): a local declaration shadows it, and an imported same-named public makes the bare name ambiguous under §2.2's collision rule. Ground: §2.2 names a current-module declaration as the only thing that shadows an auto-imported name; §2.7 promises that an added import never silently changes a name that already resolved, and "the import wins" does exactly that; and the compiler already treats these names as imported for §2.2's alias-collision rule. The remedy is stated per side: the imported name by qualification (its module name or an alias), the always-available one by its module's qualified name where it has one (`System.Threading.Task` under `import System.Threading;`, §2.7 rule 2). The rule is new for the core-type, disposal, `Task`-family, event/cancellation and standard-exception rows; for the auto-imported-module rows (`System`, `System.Text`, `System.Collections.Linq`) §2.2's collision between imported modules already applied literally, and the `System.Collections.Generic` row already stated it. **Stated cost:** in such a file the bare `Task` is unusable, `async` return types included. `Object` and the §31.4 built-in exception types have no stated module, so a file importing a module that exports one of those names cannot name the built-in at all. Their module homes are a filed follow-up, not decided here. **Declined:** the import wins; the always-available name wins; a per-row split. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local. **Open, filed:** whether §2.2's collision is keyed on generic arity. The text as it stands keys on the name; the ten committed rows that import a non-generic user `Counter` beside the always-available `Counter<K>` are held pending that question, and they falsify rationale §2's "absorbs every in-tree user type" remark. The code-generation reference's bare-name warning now covers every always-available name.
- **Stdlib §2.19 / §25.2 — an `INumber<T>`/`ISteppable<T>` conformer declares the complete comparison group (clarification; [#4754](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/4754)).** #4754 read §2.19's "user types conform by declaring and supplying the statics" against §25.2's complete-group rule as a contradiction, on the strength of rule case `l2_19_0001`, a `Money` conformer declaring only `<`. There is none. §25.2's *Type-parameter operands* paragraph derives the constrained generic body's entitlement to `>`, `<=`, `>=` from exactly that rule binding every conformer, and the v0.181 entry recorded it ("a constraint declaring `<` alone exposes all four comparisons, since every conforming type is forced to declare the full group"). §2.19 now says so beside its conformance sentence. **The coordinator's proposed direction was withdrawn:** a carve-out exempting a constraint-witness `<` from the group rule contradicts §25.2's *Type-parameter operands* paragraph and the v0.181 decision (which makes it a design change, not a ruling); its premise that a witness is reached only through the constraint is false; and a lone-`<` conformer would leave `a > b` in a constrained body with nothing to bind, the #1498 crash `static_interface_dispatch_807.max_via_group_gt_user_type_1498` pins. The withdrawal and its reason are recorded in `DECLINED.md` for the owner queue. **Declined:** that carve-out; widening both interfaces to the full group, which restates §25.2's obligation as members and saves no conformer a line. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: unchanged (the group check stays local). No compiler change. Corpus: `l2_19_0001` re-authored to declare the full group, its `rule:` and `cites:` (`2.19, 25.2`) rewritten and its manifest row rebuilt; it now states the spec's verdict. Coverage gap recorded (a lone-`<` conformer reject; an entitlement run).
- **§17.8 / §17.4 / §28.3 *Producers* — `x!` over an owned binding at an owned sink (ruling; [#4993](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/4993)).** §17.8's owned arm is normative: `x!` over a named owned binding is the read of `x`, classified by position. At a marker-free position of the consume table — for example a K3.1 store into an `owned` field, owning slot or `set(owned)` accessor, a K3.2 return, a K3.5 Pattern B `await`, a K3.7 owning `yield return`, a K3.8 `throw`, a K3.9 discard — `sink._f := x!;` consumes `x`. At a marked position (K3.3 `owned` argument, K3.4 binding or assignment) the transfer is `move x!`, since A.7 already makes `!` transparent to the marker, and an unmarked `x!` reads as an unmarked `x` does (a move for a move-only `x`, K3.12). `move x!` at a marker-free position is §28.3's redundant-marker error. §17.4's borrowed result is `as`-specific: its ground is the nullable result, and `x!` is never `null`; §17.4 says so in one sentence, and §28.3 *Producers* gains an `x!` row. Kernel: derivation — K1.5 with K3.1, K3.2, K3.5–K3.9 and K3.13 for the marker-free rows, K3.3/K3.4 for the marked rows, K3.12 for a move-only operand; the freeze is read off the existing table. No axiom. Body-locality: local. **Declined:** reading `x!` as a borrow at owned sinks with `move x!` as the only spelling — it contradicts one-spelling-per-site, splits `!` from `return x!;` and `x!.Dispose()`, and needs an axiom the kernel does not have; admitting both spellings at K3.1 only. Corpus: no case stated the borrow reading; the owned-arm gap is recorded (suggested `s17_8_0004`/`0005`). The code-generation reference's `move` paragraph says a trailing `!` never changes the spelling.
- **§28.3 *Borrow lifetime rules* (and §22.4) — a borrow stored through a `ref` or `out` location (ruling; [#4819](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/4819)).** A `ref` or plain `out` argument location whose type, after substitution, can carry a borrow — a class or interface type, a function type, or a borrow-bearing record, choice or inline array (§3.6; so an inline array of class elements) — is caller storage the callee may fill. The callee may store into it a borrow sourced at its receiver, a plain parameter or static storage, and a borrow of its own scope-bound locals, temporaries or `owned` parameters is rejected there as at a field. That callee-side sentence is stated here for the first time, derived from K2.3, and the compiler already enforces it. At the call, every borrow the call carries must be admissible into each such location exactly as the direct assignment would be, and a violation is rejected at the call. The pool is the receiver, every plain (non-`owned`, non-`scoped`) argument, a function-typed argument's capture set, and the current value of every such `ref` argument. Admissibility is the local scope comparison at a local or parameter, the field rule at a field, and the setter call at an accessor. After the call the location carries the union. An `out _` discard takes no part. `out var x`'s borrow now has a stated source. The critique widened the drafted scope, which covered class- and interface-typed locations only: a borrow-bearing record (`Put(ref keep, new Holder(t))`) and a function-typed `out` filled with a receiver-capturing closure leave the same hole. Kernel: derivation — K2.3 + K2.4, with K2.2's post-call union and K2.1; after the call the location is a live local borrow of every pooled source, so K5's freeze sees it. No new axiom and no new K4.3 clause: at a field location the admission is the existing field clause. Body-locality: local (the callee's signature and the caller's own body facts). **Declined:** residual trust for a `ref` slot, because K2.3 rejects wherever scopes compare, and a caller local's does. Also declined: rejecting the callee-side store of a parameter-sourced borrow, which would make every borrow-returning `out`/`ref` helper over a parameter unwritable (`Swap<T>` at class `T` included), and pooling only the plain arguments, which is unsound through the receiver and through `Swap`. **Deferred:** a callee-carried storage fact, the recorded simplification's lift (cf. proposal 0132). Corpus: no case changes; the gap is recorded. The code-generation reference's §4.4 gains the bullet.
- **§12.7 / §8.6 — value-typed operands of `is`, `is not` and `as` against a reference target (ruling; [#4866](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/4866)).** For a concrete operand whose static type is a value type or its nullable form, a test against a class, an interface (including one the type implements), `string` or `Object` is a compile error, as the #1984 type pattern is (§19.3). The remedy is the explicit box, `(var o: Object := p; o is IShape)`. For a carrier *type*-narrowed by §12.7 the declared type counts, so a narrowed `Object` or interface carrier stays a boxed reference operand. §7.4's nullability narrowing changes no operand's value or reference kind, so the clause does not touch §7.11's after-narrowing reading. A type-parameter carrier is decided per instantiation (§3.6 rule 2):
  - at a reference substitution, the runtime test;
  - at a value substitution, `is` and `is not` take, statically and with no allocation, the answer the boxed value would give: non-null, and `R` is `Object` or an interface to which the boxed value converts (§14.2 conformance, with §12.9 variance, so it includes #5104's widened witness);
  - at a value substitution, `as` against a reference target is rejected at the instantiation site.

  §8.6 states that a type-test operand and a pattern scrutinee are not boxing positions. The paragraph sits after §12.7's *Narrowing at an `Object` or interface location* paragraphs, on which it depends. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local for the concrete rule; carve-out (generic instantiation, within proposal 0105 §1's two confinements) for the generic arm, whose `as` rejection has the shape of §17.4's inline-array and unit `as` rejection. **Declined:**
  - statically true with an implicit box (#1984's hidden allocation, with `is` disagreeing with `case`);
  - statically false (contradicts §8.1 and the explicit box's answer);
  - rejecting generic tests at the declaration;
  - rejecting generic `is` at value substitutions.

  Value-vs-value tests keep #3120's static decision and are out of scope; that seam against §19.3 is filed. Corpus: no case changes; the gap is recorded. Row 13 of the code-generation reference's trap table carries the rule.
- **§4.4 / §6.4 — decimal results: the value set, and rounding for `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` (ruling; [#4872](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/4872)).** §4.4 states the value set: exactly ±m·10^−s with 0 ≤ m ≤ 2^96 − 1 and 0 ≤ s ≤ 28, which `MaxValue` and `Round`'s 0..28 already implied, with neither the scale nor the sign of a zero part of the value. §6.4 states one result rule for all four operators, since none had a stated rounding and a `/`-only rule would leave `*` rounding half-up beside a half-even `/`. An exact representable result is exact. Otherwise the result is rounded at the largest scale ≤ 28 whose rounded mantissa fits, to nearest with ties to even, the rounding `Decimal.Round` and the format specifiers already use. Overflow is a result that does not fit at scale 0, and a nonzero result that rounds to zero is zero (`-1e-28m / 3m` is `0`). `1m / 1.0000000000000000000000000001m` is now `0.9999999999999999999999999999` (was `0`), `decimal.MaxValue / 10m` is `7922816251426433759354395033.5`, and `10m / 3m` has 28 threes. `mod` is exact and needs no statement. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: no compile-time rule is added or altered (constant folding follows the runtime). **Declined:**
  - the operand-derived-scale truncation;
  - maximal-scale truncation (biased; disagrees with `Round` at a midpoint);
  - whole-value-set nearest, which differs only just above a (2^96 − 1)/10^(s+1) boundary, departs from the .NET rule the representation mirrors, and buys nothing a program can rely on;
  - ties away from zero.

  **Seam, filed:** decimal literals, `decimal.Parse` and `decimal(x)` round to the nearest value over the whole set (§4.3, §5.2) and #4876 reads the literal midpoint half-up. They therefore differ from §6.4 just above such a boundary and at an even midpoint. They are not restated here. Corpus: no case changes; the gap is recorded.
- **§9.8 step 2 — a record's auto-generated primary is the fallback `Deserialize` candidate (ruling; [#4775](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/4775) Q2).** Under v0.308's clash reading of §9.3, a combined-form record whose storage is all positional could declare no explicit constructor binding exactly its components, so serialization and any convenience constructor were mutually exclusive. The synthesized `Deserialize` now calls the unique matching explicit constructor, or, when no explicit constructor matches, the auto-generated primary of a record declaring positional fields. The step's compile error applies when none matches and the primary does not match either, or when more than one explicit constructor matches. The primary is a **fallback**, not a peer. A heterogeneous positional record may declare a validating body constructor binding the same components in another type order (`constructor(y: string, x: int)` beside `record P(X: int, Y: string)`), which §9.8's contract-clause paragraph is written for, and a peer primary would have turned that accepted conformance into "more than one matches". **Declined:** the primary as a peer candidate. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local (the record's own constructor set and component names). Corpus: no case changes; the gap is recorded.
- **§3.5 / §6.6 / §17.6 — `char` is not an arithmetic operand (ruling, owner-ruled 2026-09-29; [#5067](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5067)).** §3.5's operator lists name operand types **as written, before §5.1 conversion**, so §5.1's `char` → `int` widening does not make `c + 1`, `c * 2` or a `char` shift count well-typed; the arithmetic is `int(c) + 1`. `c < 'z'` and `c < 122` are unaffected, because ordering lists `char`. §6.6's write-back, whose example `c := char(c + 1)` presupposed the rejected expression, now takes R from `int(x) op e`: `c += 1` is `c := char(int(c) + 1)`, and `c++` is the same through §17.6. **The compound-form sub-decision is the coordinator's:** a `char` target admits only `+=` and `-=`, the code-point advance §17.6's `c++`/`c--` desugar to. `c *= 2`, `c /= 2` and `c mod= n` are rejected on the owner's ground that `char` is not an arithmetic type (a code point is advanced, never scaled). The drafted text had kept all five arithmetic forms; the critique found that decline "weak against that stated principle". The right operand is typed as in `int op e`: `sbyte` through `int`, or `long`, or an integer constant. A `char` right operand (`c -= d`) is not arithmetic either, and a non-constant `uint`/`ulong` operand has no §6.2 promotion with `int`. Bitwise and shift forms on a `char` target stay errors, now stated in terms because the `int(x)` form would otherwise type them. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local (operand and target static types). **Declined:** the §5.1-widening reading (the issue's reading 1); keeping the scaling compound forms. Corpus: `s17_6_0012`'s `rule:` header re-quoted (verdict unchanged); `spec_0012` carries §6.6's new example comment. The code-generation reference's §7.1 reject block gains the `ch - '0'` / `char(ch + 1)` / `ch *= 2` line, merged with #4829's.
- **§12.8 / Appendix C.5 — a `this(...)` chain must end (ruling; [#5036](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5036)).** Following each constructor's `this(...)` to the constructor it resolves to (§22.6) must reach a constructor that does not chain with `this(...)`. The resolution happens at the declaration, not per instantiation, so a generic type has one chain graph. A constructor that reaches itself is rejected at its declaration, reported naming the participating constructors, as §12.10 does for an inheritance cycle. The rule reaches records through §9.3's "governed by §12.8 unchanged". **Ground:** §12.8 already says "another" constructor, and §22.8 runs field initializers in "the constructor at the end of any `this(...)` chain". §22.7 also enters a chaining constructor's body with the chained-to constructor's §7.9 obligation discharged. A cycle has no end, so its initializers never run and that credit is circular: §7.9 is discharged by nothing. Kernel: not applicable. Body-locality: local; the chain position is outside the body and resolves against the type's own signatures. **Declined:** admitting a cycle as a runtime non-termination (unsound under §7.9); detecting only syntactic self-chains (the issue's defaulted-sibling case is a self-edge only after resolution). Appendix C.5 gains the row. Corpus: none affected; three cases recorded as a gap. The code-generation reference's constructor row says so.
- **§35.5 — an owning match's non-destructuring binding receives the value it consumes (ruling; [#4821](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/4821)).** In an owning match (either trigger), a whole-value arm binding (`var y => …`) names the consumed value, which the construct holds until it completes. The boundary is K8.3's; K8.3's borrow reading of pattern bindings holds during trial, as §35.5's *Guards: borrow during trial, transfer on selection* already says, and K8.5 gives the named-temporary shape. A consume of the binding in the arm body receives the value (K3.12), after which the completion pass has nothing to dispose. On a path that leaves the arm without consuming it, the value is disposed at construct completion as before, with no must-use warning; form 1's parenthetical is restated per path, since a conditional consume joins per path (K7.4). The borrowing match is unchanged: its whole-value binding is a borrow, and consuming it stays rejected (#4803). **Declined:** rejecting the consume (option (a)), which would make the one binding of a consuming construct unable to consume, for no soundness gain. Kernel: derivation (K8.3 + K8.5 + K3.12 + K3.14 + K3.15, with K7.4). Body-locality: local. The compiler accepts both forms already; the unconsumed path's disposal is a filed probe. Corpus: none affected; two cases recorded as a gap. The code-generation reference's owning-match sentence says so.
- **§28.3 — announcement-table row 4 names trivial-dispose classes (clarification; [#5123](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5123)).** A static method whose declared return is a plain trivial-dispose class, `Array<T>` among them, is row 4's rejection at the declaration, like any concrete class. §3.1 names `Array<T>`/`OwningArray<T>` "class types", which answers the question directly. K1.6 gives a trivial-dispose instance the classification and the free obligation, and stdlib §4.4 frees an `Array<T>` "at the array's owner's release point", so a sourceless static return names no responsible party. `Array<T>` is not runtime-managed: §28.9's tier is exhaustive, and the runtime reclaim for trivial-dispose instances is retired (rationale §5.28; `DECLINED.md`). Spell `owned Array<T>`, or re-expose static storage through a static property. **The coordinator's proposed direction was withdrawn:** a row-4 carve-out for trivial-dispose or builtin collection types would reinstate the retired reclaim with no responsible party for a fresh array, which makes it a design change; the reason is recorded in `DECLINED.md`. Kernel: derivation (K1.6 + K2.4 + K6.2). Body-locality: unchanged (local). **Compiler (tracked, #5123 retitled):** admits the shape today; the catch-up lands with its own fixture sweep. Corpus: none affected; one reject case recorded as a gap.
- **§22.12 — a base class's static member named through a derived type is the declaring type's cell (ruling; [#4974](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/4974), reading 2).** A static member declared on a base class is a member of every class derived from it: §2.7's enclosing-type rule counts inherited statics, and §12.2's inherited members are visible at the derived declaration site. It may therefore be named through a derived type. Where `class D<T>: B<T>` declares no `_c` of its own, `D<string>._c` names the declaring type's cell at the substitution the base clause supplies, `B<string>._c`, and the two spellings are one cell: one cell per declaring instantiation, whatever type name reaches it. **Declined:** reading 1, rejecting a static member named through a derived type, which would contradict §2.7 and §12.2's membership. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local (the declaring type and the base clause's substitution). Corpus: no case states either reading; the gap is recorded.
- **§29.11 — the consumption diagnostic names the remedy for the source's provenance (clarification; [#5133](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5133)).** v0.308 scoped the mandated `.ToArray()` remedy as the re-enumeration remedy over a live backing. Over a *minting* source at a class or interface element type, that remedy itself yields dead borrows, because the materialized slots are borrows of elements the enumerator disposes on the next advance. The mandate now conditions the named remedy on provenance, in the remedies paragraph's own terms. Over a collection-backed or owning source it is the `.ToArray()` re-enumeration remedy. Over a minting source at a class or interface element type it is consumption inside the borrowing loop body or owning iteration, and never materialization. No verdict moves; what the diagnostic says at a minting source is newly stated. This closes the question v0.308 filed at landing. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: unchanged (the diagnostic's content, not its trigger).

Where the name is `Object` or a §31.4 exception type, no qualified spelling of the built-in exists yet (filed).

The owner reads v0.307's §3.5 as already rejecting the binary forms, which the compiler admitted until the #5054 series; the scaling compound forms are rejected from this revision on, with no warning ramp (a verdict ruling, not a ratchet).

This is observable in programs that compile today: inexact quotients gain digits and round instead of truncating, and sums and products round half-even instead of half-up at an even-mantissa midpoint. Also newly defined: consuming an owning match's whole-value arm binding (#4821; the compiler already accepts it); a base class's static named through a derived type as the declaring type's cell (#4974; the compiler today mints a second cell); and the remedy §29.11's consumption diagnostic names over a minting source (#5133).

### v0.310 changelog (v0.309 → v0.310)

**The follow-up train to v0.309.** Six spec questions the v0.309 rulings filed, and one editorial line. Every item decides a case the documents answered both ways or not at all; every one passed an adversarial critique (seven blocking and twenty-three non-blocking findings, all resolved) and the composition gate over the union. Where a ruling departs from the direction the coordinator proposed, the bullet says so and the reason is recorded in `DECLINED.md`: #5141's consequence (three of the ten held `Counter` rows import a generic `Counter<T>` and still collide), #5142's `Object` half (answered only for the import collision; no module is stated for `Object`), #5148's wording and scope (§6.4's largest-fitting-scale rule stated by reference, not "the nearest representable value", which v0.309 declined; the literal and `Parse` sites only, with `decimal(x)` filed), and #5156's binding patterns (rejected at a value instantiation, as `as` is, not given the static answer).

- **§2.2 — a bare name is compared together with its generic arity (ruling; [#5141](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5141)).** §2.2's collision rule and its current-module shadowing rule spoke of "the same public name" without saying whether arity is part of a name. It is. §2.8.3 rule 3 already makes arity part of a type's identity, and §14.1 *Instantiation and its site* with Appendix C.1 makes every reference supply exactly the declared number of type arguments, so no use can reach both of two names that differ only in arity. The standard library already declares `TaskCompletionSource` beside `TaskCompletionSource<T>` in `System.Threading`. A non-generic `Counter` therefore neither collides with nor shadows the always-available `Counter<K>`, and a file importing a library's `Counter` uses both `Counter.Bump()` and `Counter<string>`; an imported `Counter<T>` still collides with `Counter<K>`. §2.2 also states how arity selects at a use: among the types §2.7 rule 1 finds for an identifier, a reference resolves to the first, in that rule's order, whose arity its type-argument list fixes, and where none has that arity it resolves to the first of them and is C.1's arity error — never an alias, a member or a module prefix. So §2.7's precedence is unchanged, the §22.12 "requires type arguments" diagnostic on a bare generic head stands, and §2.2's alias-collision ground ("a same-named alias would be unreachable in every chain-head position") stays true, since a generic-only name still takes an arity-0 head. **Correction to the issue's premise:** three of the ten committed rows #5140 holds import a generic `Counter<T>`, `Counter<K>`'s arity, and collide under #5004; the #5140 catch-up renames the library type in each. **v0.309's recorded cost for #5004 narrows:** in a file importing a module that exports a non-generic `Task`, only the arity-0 `Task` is ambiguous (`async` return types written `Task` included); `Task<int>` stays usable. Rationale §2's "absorbs every in-tree user type" parenthetical, false on the generic rows, now states the rule. **Declined:** the identifier-only key, which contradicts §2.8.3's identity and makes the library's own `TaskCompletionSource` pair a self-collision; arity for the collision but the identifier for shadowing, which would make a current-module `Counter` hide `Counter<K>` while an imported one does not; arity for the always-available rows only (the per-row split #5004 declined); an arity-keyed lookup that lets a generic-only head fall through to an alias, a member or a module prefix, which §14.1's arity error forbids. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local (the reference's own tokens and the file's import set). The code-generation reference's bare-name warning says "of the same arity" and shows `System.Threading.Task` with its `import System.Threading;`.
- **§2.3 / stdlib §2.17 — the §31.4 built-in exception hierarchy's module is `System`; no import collides with `Object` (ruling; [#5142](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5142)).** v0.309's #5004 ruling left two names with no qualified spelling for the built-in. The exception hierarchy now has one. Stdlib §2.17 states, for the first time in words, that `Exception` and the types available without `import` have the module `System`, and §2.3's row reads "the §31.4 built-in hierarchy (`Exception` and the types in its tree), whose module is `System`", so the domain-specific exceptions §31.4 declares elsewhere (`KeyNotFoundException` in `System.Collections.Generic`) keep their homes. This is the one module the documents associate with the hierarchy: stdlib §2.17 sits in stdlib §2, which §2.3 calls `System`'s full catalog; §31.4 already declares the built-in-derived `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` in `System`; and §8.5 and §31.4's `ToString()` already required a module-qualified name. The compiler's `System.<Name>` rendering of the hierarchy agrees. So `System.Exception` reaches the built-in under an import that exports `Exception`, and §2.3's remedy sentence drops "where it has one": `System.Exception`, and `System.Threading.Task` under `import System.Threading;`. **`Object`, narrowed to the question asked:** §2.3's core-type cell now says an import never collides with `Object`, because no module exports a type `Object` (§8.1). No module is stated for `Object`, and whether a type parameter, nested type, local type or generic `Object<T>` named `Object` may shadow it is filed rather than decided in a table cell. **Declined:** exempting the rows with no stated module from the collision (option (b)), the per-row split #5004 declined; a new module home for the exceptions, which no document names. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local (name resolution).
- **§19.3 — an ordering pattern reads the scrutinee after §7.4 narrowing (ruling; [#5143](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5143)).** §19.3 rejects a relational or range pattern over a "nullable scrutinee" and says "pattern position performs no narrowing". It did not say whether a scrutinee §7.4 has already narrowed counts as nullable. It does not. The rejection now reads nullability from the scrutinee's static type after narrowing, as §7.11 reads an operand, which is the rule §7.11 says "pattern position takes"; a relational or range pattern over a narrowed scrutinee is admitted, as `v in r` over it is (§17.5). This is the only reading under which §16.6's pattern-versus-`in` agreement holds. "Pattern position performs no narrowing of its own" keeps its meaning: the pattern establishes no fact of its own, so an earlier `null` arm narrows nothing for a later arm. The new sentence is scoped to this rejection. Since v0.309's declaration clause, `var n: int? := 80; case n of > 70 => …` is the common shape. **Declined:** the declared-type reading, which one committed test pinned as a deliberate disagreement the spec never stated; a §16.6 carve restricting the agreement to un-narrowed operands. **Not decided:** the same question for §19.3's type-pattern sentence and §19.6's nullable-scrutinee coverage bullet, both conservative as written, and through §19.6 the §21.7 totality verdict (filed). Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local (the body's own §7.4 facts at the `case`). **Compiler (tracked):** the ordering-pattern gate reads the declared type; the catch-up gates on the narrowing fact for every nullable kind and unwraps the scrutinee before lowering. Corpus: the four v0.309 cases keep their genuinely nullable scrutinees and still test the rejection; `s19_3_0003` and `s7_11_0009` have their `rule:` headers re-quoted to "no narrowing of its own" (verdicts unchanged); the accept gap is recorded.
- **§4.4 / §4.3, stdlib §9.3 — a `decimal` literal and `decimal.Parse` round by §6.4's rule (ruling; [#5148](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5148)).** v0.309 gave `+`, `-`, `*` and `/` one result rule (§6.4: largest fitting scale, ties to even). A `decimal` literal still read §4.3's "nearest representable value", with no tie rule, the stdlib said nothing of over-precision `Parse` input, and the compiler rounds both half-up (#4876). At an even-mantissa midpoint that makes `39614081257132168796771975166.5m` differ from `39614081257132168796771975166m + 0.5m`, the disagreement #4876 was fixed to close. §4.4 now states, beside the value set, that a literal or parsed string whose magnitude does not exceed `decimal.MaxValue` but whose value the set cannot hold denotes that value rounded as §6.4 rounds an inexact result: the rule is stated once, by reference, so the two cannot drift. §4.3 and the stdlib `Parse` entry point at it (`"0.12345678901234567890123456785"` parses to `0.1234567890123456789012345678`). The coordinator's drafted wording ("the nearest representable value, ties to even") was not used: whole-set nearest is the rule v0.309 declined for §6.4, and it differs from §6.4 just above each (2^96 − 1)/10^(s+1) boundary. **Scope:** the literal and `Parse` halves only. `decimal(x)` (§5.2) is held and filed: rounding once from `x`'s exact binary value would flip `decimal(0.1)` from the `0.1` the compiler's 15-significant-digit conversion (the .NET conversion) gives, so the input value and its tie rule are one question. **Declined:** half-up for literals and `Parse` "as written"; whole-set nearest (v0.309's row, amended to say the literal and `Parse` sites now take §6.4's rule). **Not decided:** the range edge between `MaxValue` and `MaxValue + ½`, where §4.3 and stdlib §9.3 read magnitude and §6.4 reads fit at scale 0 (filed); `decimal(x)` (filed). Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: no compile-time rule is added or altered (constant folding follows the runtime). Corpus: no case changes; the even-midpoint gap is recorded.
- **§19.3 — a type-parameter scrutinee against a reference-type pattern is decided per instantiation (ruling; [#5156](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5156)).** v0.309 decided `is` and `as` over a generic carrier `v: T` per instantiation (§12.7) and left the `case` form silent. Against a reference type `R` (a class, an interface, `string` or `Object`) it now mirrors them. At a reference substitution the pattern is the runtime test. At a value substitution a type pattern without binding, and a named destructuring's class head, takes the answer `v is R` takes, with no allocation; an arm that can never match there is admitted and never selected, since §19.6 makes no dead arm an error. The destructuring's slot bindings are member reads and are not rejected, and at a value substitution its head never matches. A type pattern with binding is rejected at the instantiation site whatever the static answer, as `as` is (§12.7): where the answer is true the binding would be the implicit box §19.3 forbids, and §12.7 does not split `as` by answer. **The coordinator's uniform static-answer wording was narrowed:** it gave the binding form the answer too, and so the box. A per-instantiation answer neither supplies nor removes a §19.6 static proof, which is a verdict about the generic body (§19.6 already counts a generic choice with no per-instantiation analysis). **Declined:** rejecting the pattern at the declaration, or at every value substitution (reading (b), the generic-test rejection v0.309 declined for §12.7); the static answer for binding patterns. **Not decided:** a type-parameter scrutinee against a value-type pattern (filed with #5157's generic question). Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: carve-out (generic instantiation), within proposal 0105 §1's confinements, as §12.7's generic arm. Corpus: none affected; three cases recorded as a gap.
- **§12.7 — a value operand tested against a different value type is a compile error (ruling; [#5157](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5157)).** v0.309 aligned §12.7's value-operand/reference-target case with §19.3's type pattern and left value-versus-other-value on #3120's implementation, which answers `i is long` over an `int` statically `false` while §19.3 rejects the pattern `long` over an `int` scrutinee. The two now agree. A concrete value-typed operand under `is`, `is not` or `as` against a value type other than its own or its own nullable form, not a type parameter, is a compile error: a value's runtime type is its static type (§8.2), so the test could never succeed. It is not a range check either: `is` tests the type, never whether the value would convert (§5.2). A test naming the operand's own type is admitted: statically true (for `as`, the value wrapped as `T?`), or, over the nullable form, the null test. The sentence closes §12.7's value-operand paragraph, after the type-parameter carrier sentence, so that sentence keeps its reference-target scope; a type-parameter operand or target keeps its per-instantiation answer, not restated here. No recorded use of a statically false `is` exists; #3120 itself left the diagnostic question open. #5157's reading (b) rested on a §19.6 dead-arm error the text does not contain. **Declined:** the static `false`; a warning. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local (the operand's declared type and the target). Appendix C.1's type-test line gains the clause, and the code-generation reference's row 13 says it.
- **Appendix C.1 — the value-operand/reference-target type-test rejection is listed (editorial).** §12.7's v0.309 rule (#4866) and §19.3's type-pattern rule (v0.221, #1984) were enforced invariants absent from Appendix C. C.1 gains one line after the box-write line, naming §19.3's scrutinee kinds (a primitive, record, enum or inline array) as §19.3 states them, and #5157's value-versus-other-value clause (above) extends it. No rule changes.

- **Migration.** *Newly rejected:*

Test the value instead (`long(i) = …`, a range check), or box explicitly. The compiler answered these statically `false` or `null` with no diagnostic. This is a verdict ruling, not a ratchet.
  - A type pattern **with binding** against a class, interface, `string` or `Object` over a type-parameter scrutinee, at a value instantiation, rejected at the instantiation site whatever the static answer (#5156; box explicitly, or constrain `where T: class`).

  - A name used beside a same-identifier name of a different generic arity, imported, current-module or always-available: a library's `Counter` with `Counter<int>`, a current-module non-generic `Counter` with `Counter<int>` reaching the always-available `Counter<K>`, and `Task<int>` in a file importing a module that exports a non-generic `Task` (#5141).

This is observable in programs that compile today: an even-mantissa midpoint rounds to the even neighbour where the compiler rounds half-up, and a value with more than one dropped digit is rounded once (#5148).

### v0.311 changelog (v0.310 → v0.311)

**The follow-up train to v0.310.** The eight spec questions v0.310 filed, decided, and one editorial line. Seven are rulings or clarifications on the text; one, the value of `decimal(x)` (#5169), is an owner decision, with its survey recorded in rationale §14.8. Every item passed an adversarial critique (four blocking and twenty-six non-blocking findings, all resolved as proposed) and the composition gate over the union. #5164 answers **no**, as the owner ruled on the drafted comparison: the text, v0.303's recorded decline and v0.310's arity keying reject the bare self-name, and the precedent the question cited is C++'s injected-class-name, not C#. #5166 corrects the proposed direction on one form: §21.10 already rejects a method-local type named `Object`.

- **§14.1 / §22.12 — a bare generic type name is not the current instantiation inside its own declaration (clarification; [#5164](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5164)).** v0.310 filed whether `Counter.n` inside `class Counter<T>` means `Counter<T>.n`, as the compiler admits. It does not. §14.1's "`Box` bare … compile errors at a `class Box<T>`" and Appendix C.1 carry no body exception, and v0.303 recorded the decline of the bare form. v0.310's arity keying rests on every reference fixing its arity by its type-argument list; a self-name meaning `Counter<T>` would be a reference whose tokens do not fix it, outranking a same-identifier arity-0 type. The current instantiation is spelled `Counter<T>.n`, or the member is reached by its bare name `n` through §2.7's enclosing-type lookup. §14.1 now says the rule holds inside a generic type's own declaration (member bodies, field initializers and member signatures), and §22.12 says the same of static-member access. With a non-generic `Tag` in scope, `Tag.disposed` inside `Tag<T>` names that type's member, as C# resolves it (C# reports CS0305 where no arity-0 type exists); the "current instantiation" reading is C++'s injected-class-name. The change class is clarification: no document verdict moves. **Declined:** the self-name as a §2.7 rule-1 entry ahead of the current module's declarations, which would hide a non-generic companion such as `TaskCompletionSource` inside its generic twin's body and contradict v0.303's recorded decline; the self-name as a fall-through, which would let an added import silently change what a resolved chain means (§2.7). v0.303's raw-reference row in `DECLINED.md` now states its scope over a generic type's own declaration and keeps its note that the compiler tolerates bare type-position references (#4181). Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local. The code-generation reference's §7.1 gains the reflex line (`Registry.n` inside `class Registry<T>`).
- **§8.1 / §2.3 / §3.4 / §8.5, stdlib §2.13 — `Object`'s module is `System` (ruling; [#5165](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5165)).** v0.310 filed the question: §8.5's class default and stdlib §2.13's `FullName` rule (1) need a module path for every named non-keyword type, and none was stated for `Object`. It is `System`, as `Type`'s already is (§2.3's `System` row). §2.8.3 rule 3 identifies every type by its declaring module, and §3.4 says `Object` is a class with no keyword alias, so rule (2)'s keyword exemption does not reach it. The root's family is already in `System`: the keyword types' library names (§3.4) and `Type`, the token `GetType()` returns. `System.Object` is therefore the root's qualified name, reached by §2.7 rule 2. `typeof(Object).FullName` and the default `ToString` of `new Object()` render `"System.Object"`, and `Object` as a type argument renders `"System.Object"` under `FullName` and `"Object"` under `Name`. §8.1 states the module, §2.3's core-type row names it, §8.5 gains the example, stdlib §2.13 rule (1) renders both `Object` and `Type`, and §3.4's "referenced as `Object` unconditionally" becomes "named `Object` or, qualified, `System.Object`", since the qualified spelling now exists and a shadowing declaration (#5166) can hide the bare one. **Declined:** a keyword-style unqualified rendering, and a module-less root, both contrary to §2.8.3 rule 3. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local. The code-generation reference's `Type` line gives the root's `FullName`.
- **§8.1 / §2.3 — "cannot redeclare or replace `Object`" bans a user module-level non-generic declaration (ruling; [#5166](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5166)).** §8.1 named no scope, while §2.3 marks `Object` shadowable. The ban covers a user module-level class, record, enum, interface, choice or type alias named `Object` with no type parameters, in any user module and at any visibility: the declaration that would stand in for the root, `System.Object` (#5165), across a module, or collide with it in importers. A generic `Object<T>` is a different name under §2.2's arity keying. A nested type or type parameter named `Object` shadows the root as any declaration shadows an always-available name, and `System.Object` still reaches it. §3.4's wider reserved-name ban rests on the keyword/PascalCase dual form, which `Object` lacks. **Correction to the proposed direction:** a method-local type named `Object` is not ordinary shadowing but §21.10's error, since a local type may not shadow any visible type name. §8.1 also says the specification's own uses of `Object` mean the root. §2.3's core-type cell now reads "no module other than `System`, the root's own, declares a non-generic type `Object`", since #5165 gives the root a module in the same revision; `DECLINED.md`'s #5142 option-(b) row says the same. **Declined:** barring every declaration of the name, which would falsify §2.3's "Yes"; barring `Object<T>`. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local. **Compiler (tracked):** it accepts a module-level `public class Object` (`s8_1_0001`, banked divergence, unchanged), and resolves every bare `Object` in type position to the root before scope lookup.
- **§19.3 / Appendix C.1 — choice and unit scrutinees take the value-scrutinee type-pattern rejection (ruling; [#5171](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5171)).** §12.7 (v0.309, #4866) makes a value operand against a reference target a compile error "as the §19.3 type pattern is" over six kinds, and §19.3 listed four. v0.310 restated §19.3's four in C.1 as written and filed the question. The lists now agree: a primitive, record, enum, choice, inline-array or unit scrutinee (or its nullable form) against a class, interface, `string` or `Object` type pattern, with or without binding, is a compile error. A choice is a value type (§3.1), a scrutinee is not a boxing position (§8.6), and an owning choice cannot be boxed at all (§35.8). Otherwise `c is IShape` and `case c of IShape => …` would disagree on one question, which is the disagreement #4866 removed. A choice's case patterns, a case name or a case destructuring (`Some(var x)`, a payload-free `None`), are not type patterns (§35.5), and §19.3 now says so in place. §19.3's box-explicitly remedy now notes that a move-only value (an owning choice or owning inline array) cannot be boxed and its conformance is static. C.1's other-value-type clause (v0.310) reads the aligned list. **Declined:** narrowing §12.7's list instead, which would need the implicit box #4866 rejected; a runtime test through an implicit box. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local. The code-generation reference's row 13 lists the six kinds. **Compiler (tracked):** sema's pattern predicate covers a non-nullable primitive, record or enum scrutinee in the binding form only.
- **§19.1 / §19.3 / §19.6 / Appendix C.7 — a scrutinee narrowed non-null at the `case` is non-nullable for every pattern rule and every exhaustiveness proof (ruling; [#5167](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5167)).** v0.310 (#5143) read the relational/range rejection after §7.4 narrowing and filed the same question for §19.3's type-pattern clause and §19.6's bullets. The answer is the same rule, stated once in §19.1: wherever §19 reads a scrutinee's nullability, it reads the static type after §7.4 narrowing, and only the null fact counts (a §12.7 type narrowing leaves the declared type in place). So over a narrowed `T?` the `T` pattern always matches, and `var r: R? := new R(1); case r of R(var x, var y) => return x + y; end;` is statically exhaustive with no `null` arm and, by §19.6's registry, total under §21.7. Reading §19.3 one way for ordering patterns and the other way for type patterns would give one scrutinee two nullabilities in one `case`, and it would demand the provably dead arm v0.307 declined for the record bullet. The verdict changes are accept-only. A defensive `null` arm over a scrutinee that cannot hold `null` (non-nullable by its declared type, a type parameter only under a constraint implying non-null (§14.2), or narrowed non-null) stays admitted and is never selected: §19 has no dead-arm error, and the §19.6 bullet now says so. An unconstrained type parameter is not such a scrutinee: at `T = string?` a `null` arm is selected. **Declined:** the declared-type reading for the type-pattern clause and §19.6; rejecting a `null` arm over a scrutinee that cannot hold `null`. Kernel: no contact (the ownership arm-join only loses an input edge, which can only drop a rejection). Body-locality: local (the body's own §7.4 facts at the `case`). The code-generation reference's nullable-operator paragraph says a narrowed scrutinee is not nullable. **Compiler (tracked):** the exhaustiveness walk and the totality gate read the declared type.
- **§21.7 — the qualifying-bullet list names §19.6's record bullet (editorial).** §21.7's statement-`case` totality grant lists the §19.6 bullets it keys on and omitted the record bullet v0.307 (#4372) added, though §19.6 calls its list the registry §21.7 is keyed to and rule case `s21_7_0005` already states record totality. No verdict changes.
- **§4.4 / §4.3, stdlib §9.3 — a `decimal` literal or parse is out of range exactly when its rounding does not fit at scale 0 (ruling; [#5168](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5168)).** v0.310 gave literals and `Parse` §6.4's rounding and left the range read by magnitude, so `79228162514264337593543950335.4m` was out of range while `MaxValue + 0.4m` is `MaxValue` (§6.4 overflows only when the result "does not fit at scale 0"). The range now takes §6.4's definition. §4.4 states once, for the literal, `Parse` and the form `decimal(x)` reads (#5169), that such a value is out of range exactly when its rounding does not fit at scale 0; §4.3 says a `decimal` literal out of that range is likewise a compile error and points at §4.4, and the stdlib `Parse` entry points at it too. `MaxValue` ends in an odd digit, so `…335.4m` is `MaxValue` and the tie `…335.5m` rounds to the even 2^96 and is out of range: the admitted interval is open at `±(MaxValue + ½)`. By source read the compiler already draws the boundary there (the literal check and `Parse` share one parser, which stores `MaxValue` for `.4` and raises for `.5`). **Declined:** the magnitude reading, which gives one value two verdicts by spelling and would reject what the compiler admits. **Not decided:** the same edge for binary-float literals between the largest finite value and half an ulp above it (§4.3's float clause reads magnitude; the compiler rounds; filed). Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local (the literal's own text).
- **§5.2 / §4.4, stdlib §2.18, rationale §14.8 — `decimal(x)` reads `x`'s shortest round-trip form (ruling, owner decision; [#5169](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5169)).** §5.2's "the nearest representable `decimal` value" read literally as the double's exact binary expansion (`decimal(0.1)` = `0.1000000000000000055511151231`), while the compiler converted through 15 significant digits and a committed row expects `0.1`. `decimal(x)` now yields the value of `x`'s shortest round-trip form: the digits `x`'s no-format `ToString()` prints (stdlib §2.18), the shortest decimal string that parses back to `x` in `x`'s own type and, of several such, the one nearest `x`. §4.4's rounding applies where that value is not in the set, which for a `double` happens only below 10^−12 in magnitude, and the rounding reads the shortest form, not the binary expansion. So `decimal(0.1)` is `0.1`, `decimal(0.1 + 0.2)` is `0.30000000000000004`, `decimal(0.1f)` is `0.1`, `decimal(2.5e-28)` is a tie that goes to the even `0.0000000000000000000000000002`, and distinct doubles of magnitude at least 10^−12 give distinct decimals. `decimal(x)` is the value of the `decimal` literal written with `x.ToString()`'s digits; the identity with `decimal.Parse(x.ToString())` holds for values only, since `Parse` admits no exponent. Stdlib §2.18's round-trip sentence gains "of several such, the one nearest it": several strings of the minimal length can parse back to one double (`0.30000000000000003`, `…04` and `…05` for `0.1 + 0.2`), so "the shortest" alone did not determine the digits `ToString()` prints or the value `decimal(x)` takes. **Refinement of the owner's wording, acknowledged by the owner:** a `float` operand reads `float`'s own shortest form, so `decimal(x)` equals the value of `x.ToString()` for every binary float; `decimal(0.1f)` and `decimal(double(0.1f))` therefore differ. Rationale §14.8 records the three candidate values and the survey, labelled as the owner's (Java `BigDecimal.valueOf`, Kotlin `toBigDecimal` and Go shopspring `NewFromFloat` convert through the shortest form; Python `Decimal(float)` and Java `new BigDecimal(double)` take the exact expansion; .NET rounds to 15 digits). **Declined:** the exact expansion (28 digits of binary noise; breaks `decimal(0.1)` → `0.1`); a fixed significant-digit rounding (a second precision constant; not injective). Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: no compile-time rule is added (the constant-operand check calls the runtime conversion). **Compiler (tracked).** `DECLINED.md`'s #4872 whole-set row now records that `decimal(x)` rounds by the same rule.
- **§19.3 / §12.7 / Appendix C.1 — a type parameter against a value type is decided per instantiation, in every position (ruling; [#5170](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5170)).** v0.310 made a concrete value operand against a different value type a compile error and left type parameters out, and §19.3's "all type-pattern rules then apply to the substituted type" read literally as that rejection re-applied at each instantiation. Where a type parameter stands on either side of a type test (operand `v is long`, scrutinee `case v of int`, pattern `case p of T`, target `p is T`) and both sides are value types at an instantiation, the test is now answered per instantiation with no allocation: `true` (the pattern matches) when the substituted types are identical, a nullable substitution of the target or pattern parameter counting as its underlying type, and `false` otherwise, a never-matching arm being admitted and never selected. The binding form is included. An instantiation-site rejection tracks the box, not the answer: #5156 rejects a reference binding at a value substitution because a true answer would need the implicit box; between two value types no box is ever formed, so the test is answered. §19.3's sentence says so as its one exception ("save one"), so the null rule, §17.4's per-instantiation inline-array/unit `as` rejection and #5156's reference-pattern rule stay in force; §19.3's #5156 sentence points at it, and §12.7's carrier gloss ("the answer the boxed value would give") is scoped to a reference target. §3.6 rule 2's instantiation-site rejection is for property-dependent requirements, not for a test's answer. Every committed row that exercises the shape already pins this answer. **Declined:** re-applying the other-value-type rejection per instantiation; rejecting the value binding form; rejecting at the declaration. **Not decided:** a reference type arriving by substitution against a value, as a pattern or target over a concrete value (`case p of T`, `p is T` over `p: int` at `T = Object`) or as a type-parameter pattern over a type-parameter scrutinee (`v: T`, pattern `U`, at `T = int`, `U = IShape`), where the text, the compiler and a #5156 mirror give different answers (filed). Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: carve-out (generic instantiation), within proposal 0105 §1's confinements, as §12.7's generic arm and #5156. **v0.310 correction:** three committed rows (`case_generic_value_scrutinee_ref_pattern_1936.*_no_match`) exercise #5156's binding shape, which v0.310's absence check and Migration said no row did; they flip under v0.310's text, and the #5156 tracker now names them.

- **Migration.** *Newly rejected:*
  - A type pattern naming a class, interface, `string` or `Object`, with or without binding, or naming a different value type, over a concrete choice or unit scrutinee or its nullable form (#5171; the documents gave no verdict before). Box explicitly first, except an owning choice, which cannot be boxed. By source read the compiler admits these today, and no committed row uses them.
  - A bare generic type name used as its own current instantiation inside its declaration (`Counter.n` inside `class Counter<T>` with no arity-0 `Counter` in scope) (#5164). The documents' verdict is unchanged (it was already C.1's arity error); it is listed here because the compiler admits it: two committed rows pin the admission and flip, and five use it incidentally and are respelled (Spec-ahead-of-impl below).

  *Newly accepted:*

  - A `decimal` literal or `Parse`/`TryParse`/`ParseOrNull`/`Convert.ToDecimal` input in (`MaxValue`, `MaxValue + ½`), which is `MaxValue` (symmetrically `MinValue`); `MaxValue + ½` and above stay out of range (#5168). The compiler already accepts it.

The compiler already answers statically.

  *Newly defined:*
  - `System.Object` as the root's qualified name; `typeof(Object).FullName` and `new Object()`'s default `ToString` are `"System.Object"`, and `Object` as a type argument renders `"System.Object"` under `FullName` (#5165). A concrete `Object` argument in an extension head is now spellable, `extension IEnumerable<System.Object>` (`<Object>` binds a type parameter, §26).
  - A generic `Object<T>`, a nested type named `Object`, and a type parameter named `Object`: admitted, shadowing as ordinary declarations, with `System.Object` reaching the root (#5166).
  - The value of `decimal(x)` for a binary float, observable in programs that compile today: a `double` whose shortest form has 16 or 17 significant digits (`decimal(0.1 + 0.2)` is `0.30000000000000004`, not `0.3`), a non-dyadic `float` (`decimal(0.1f)` is `0.1`, not `0.100000001490116`), a tiny magnitude at a scale-28 tie (`decimal(2.5e-28)` rounds to even), and a runtime `double` equal to 2^96, which now raises `OverflowException` (a constant one is a compile error) (#5169).

  *Clarified, verdict unchanged:*
  - §8.1's ban is on a user module-level non-generic declaration named `Object`, any user module and visibility; a method-local `Object` is §21.10's error (#5166).
  - A `null` arm over a scrutinee that cannot hold `null` is admitted and never selected (#5167).

### v0.312 changelog (v0.311 → v0.312)

**The two questions v0.311 filed, decided.** Both follow a principle v0.311 stated for a neighbouring case. The binary-float literal edge takes the rounding reading #5168 gave `decimal`. A reference type arriving by substitution against a value takes the per-instantiation answer #5156 gives a type-parameter scrutinee, under #5170's "an instantiation-site rejection tracks the box, not the answer". Both items passed an adversarial critique (one blocking and fifteen non-blocking findings, all resolved as proposed) and the composition gate over the union.

- **§4.3 / §5.2 — a `double` or `float` literal is out of range exactly when its IEEE rounding is not finite, and `float(d)` overflows at the same threshold (ruling; [#5181](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5181)).** v0.311 (#5168) bounded `decimal` literals by their rounding and left §4.3's binary-float clause on magnitude. So `1.7976931348623158e308`, whose nearest `double` is `double.MaxValue`, was a compile error by the text, while `double.MaxValue + 9e291` is `double.MaxValue` by §6.3's IEEE arithmetic. A literal now denotes its value rounded to nearest with ties to even, and it is out of range exactly when that rounding is not finite. That happens at or above the largest finite value plus half an ulp; the tie itself rounds up, because that value's significand is odd. This is IEEE 754's overflow boundary, and it is where `strtod` and `strtof` put it. So `1.7976931348623158e308` is `double.MaxValue`, `1.7976931348623159e308` is out of range, and `3.4028235e38f` (the digits `float.MaxValue.ToString()` prints) is `float.MaxValue` rather than a compile error. §4.3's sentence is split in two, and its "never rounds to `±Infinity`" now reads "a literal never denotes `±Infinity`", which the rejection guarantees. §5.2's `float(d)` narrowing said "a magnitude beyond `float`'s finite range yields `±Infinity`", which carries the same ambiguity, so it is decided with the literal: `float(d)` rounds `d`'s value to the nearest `float` with ties to even and yields `±Infinity` exactly when that rounding is not finite, so `float(3.4028235e38)` is `float.MaxValue`. The threshold is the same at the edge; in general `float(<double literal>)` rounds twice, the literal first to `double`, so `float(1.0000001788139343)` and `1.0000001788139343f` differ. **Declined:** the magnitude reading, which gives one value two verdicts by spelling, rejects the literal spelled with `float.MaxValue`'s own printed digits, and reads §4.3's float half against the decimal half v0.311 decided. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: local (the literal's own text). **Compiler (tracked):** it agrees for `double`, and its `float(d)` (`fptrunc`) already agrees. For `float` literals, all six sites (the range check, the constant folder, three codegen sites and an imported `float` constant's folding) materialise `(float)strtod`, which rounds twice. That rejects a sliver just below the tie, which the ruling admits, and it misrounds some in-range literals against §4.3's unchanged nearest-value rule (`1.0000001788139343f`, `7.038531e-26f`). Binary-float `Parse`/`TryParse` and a JSON `float` field share the cause, so `float.Parse(x.ToString()) = x` fails today for the one `float` magnitude whose shortest form is `7.038531e-26`, against stdlib §2.18's unchanged round trip.
- **§19.3 / §12.7 / Appendix C.1 — a reference type arriving by substitution against a value takes the per-instantiation answer, and `as` and binding are rejected at the instantiation site (ruling; [#5182](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5182)).** v0.311 (#5170) answered type-parameter tests between two value types. It filed the value/reference case in which the reference type arrives by substitution: `case p of T`, `var x: T`, `p is T` and `p as T` over `p: int` at `T = Object` or `IShape`, and `case v of U` over `v: T` at `T = int`, `U = IShape`. Read literally, "all type-pattern rules then apply to the substituted type" re-applied §19.3's concrete reference-pattern rejection there, while #5156 answers the same pair when the reference type is written. The ruling mirrors #5156 on both sides. A bare test takes, allocating nothing, the answer the boxed value would give: `true` exactly when the value is non-null and `R` is `Object` or an interface the boxed value converts to (for a move-only value, which is never boxed, the answer its type's conformance gives). A never-matching arm is admitted. `as` and a type pattern with binding are rejected at the instantiation site whatever the answer, since a true answer would be the implicit box. An instantiation-site rejection tracks the box, not the answer, so no concrete rejection is re-applied through a substitution, whether the result is a value type or a reference type; only the forms that would form the box are rejected. So `case p of T` over `p: int` matches at `T = Object`, never matches at `T = string`, and `var x: T` is rejected at both. §19.3's "save one" now names both rejections of a pattern over a value scrutinee and routes the value/reference case to #5156's answer. #5156's sentence reaches a substituted `R` and a concrete value scrutinee, and its answer clause names §12.7's `is R` test. §12.7's carrier sentence covers a type-parameter target as well as a carrier, and its value/value sentence refers back to that head rather than restating it. C.1 says the same. **Declined:** the concrete rejection re-applied per instantiation, which rejects a bare test that forms no box and gives one instantiated pair two verdicts by which side is generic; the compiler's static `false`, which answers a different question than #5156 answers for the same pair and admits the forms whose true answer is the implicit box. Kernel: no contact. Body-locality: carve-out (generic instantiation), within proposal 0105 §1's confinements, as §12.7's generic arm, #5156 and #5170 are. **Compiler (tracked), by source read:** it answers `false` at a class or non-implemented interface target, which agrees, and for every pattern form, which does not at `Object` or an implemented interface; it drops `p is T` silently at `T = Object` or `string`; it answers the null test for a nullable operand whatever the target; and it admits the `as` and binding forms.

- **Migration.** *Newly rejected:*
  - `p as T` and a type pattern with binding (`var x: T`, `var x: U`) where, at an instantiation, a value (a concrete operand or scrutinee, or a type parameter's value substitution) meets a type parameter's reference substitution (#5182). The documents gave no stated verdict for the target side, and the literal reading of §19.3 already rejected the pattern side. The compiler admits both today, and no committed row uses them.

  *Newly accepted:*
  - A `double` literal of magnitude in (`double.MaxValue`, `double.MaxValue` + ½ ulp) is `±double.MaxValue`, and a `float` literal of magnitude in (`float.MaxValue`, `float.MaxValue` + ½ ulp) is `±float.MaxValue`, for example `3.4028235e38f`, the digits `float.MaxValue.ToString()` prints (#5181). `MaxValue` + ½ ulp and above stay out of range. The compiler already accepts the `double` interval, and the `float` interval except its top 2^−29 part next to the tie (tracked).
  - `float(d)` for a `double` `d` of magnitude in (`float.MaxValue`, `float.MaxValue` + ½ ulp) is `±float.MaxValue`, where §5.2's magnitude words read `±Infinity` (#5181). The compiler's `fptrunc` already gives `float.MaxValue`.
  - A bare `is`/`is not`/type pattern between a value and a type parameter's reference substitution, which the literal reading of §19.3 rejected at the instantiation site (#5182).

  *Newly defined:*
  - That bare test's answer: `true` exactly when the value is non-null and `R` is `Object` or an interface the boxed value converts to, `false` otherwise, with no allocation (#5182). The compiler answers `false` or drops the test today (tracked).

  *Clarified, verdict unchanged:*
  - §4.3 states that a binary-float literal's tie rounds to the even significand, IEEE 754's default, which §6.3 already adopts; a literal's value away from the edge is unchanged (#5181).

  *Doc-only:* none beyond the above.

  *Spec-ahead-of-impl (tracking issues filed at landing):*
  - single rounding of `float` literals at the six `(float)strtod` sites, which also fixes the misrounding of some in-range literals against §4.3's unchanged nearest-value rule; binary-float `Parse`/`TryParse` and JSON `float` deserialisation share the cause (#5181; no row flips; new failing rows listed in the tracker);
  - the value/reference-substitution answer and the instantiation-site rejection of `as` and binding, landing with #5176's #5156 catch-up (#5182; no row flips; new failing rows listed in the tracker).
  - **Correction to v0.311 (#5170):** its Migration (*Newly accepted* and *Spec-ahead-of-impl*) says the compiler already answers value/value tests statically. By source read, a nullable concrete operand (`p: int?`, `p is T` at `T = long`) takes a `hasValue` branch that ignores the target (`LlvmBackend_Layout.cpp:3637-3642`); the `v: T?` carrier probably does too (a tracker probe). No committed row exercises either; #5170's tracker ([#5191](https://github.com/s8lap/bezel-lang/issues/5191)) takes the correction, and #5182's tracker names the shared branch.

  *Filed as questions:*
  - stdlib §9.2 / §2.3: the range contract of `double.Parse`/`float.Parse` (with `TryParse` and `ParseOrNull`) and `Convert.ToDouble`. §9.2 states none, while §2.3 says `Convert.To*` raise `OverflowException` "when the value does not fit — the same contract as the §9 per-type `Parse` family"; the runtime returns `±Infinity` for both. Raise, or yield `±Infinity`? Either way, the boundary is v0.312's §4.3 rounding criterion (#5181).

  *Guides:* no idiom a guide teaches changed; their re-validation pins stay. The code-generation reference is unchanged in substance (it states no rule either item changes); its three pins move to v0.312.

  *Corpus:* the rule corpus stays at 2,185 cases, none added or deleted and no verdict flipped. `s4_3_0003`, `s4_3_0004` and `s5_2_0005` have their `rule:` headers re-quoted for §4.3's and §5.2's rounding sentences, and `s4_3_0003` is retitled ("a floating-point literal whose IEEE rounding is not finite is a compile error"); verdicts and `s4_3_0003`'s `diagnostic: magnitude` needle unchanged (#5181). No case exercises #5182's shapes, and none quotes a sentence it changes. Gaps are recorded per item. The manifest is rebuilt from the case headers.
